import numpy as np, pandas as pd, re
from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "cabin":  ["B5", "C23", "D41", "C85", None, "E12", "B20"],   # CASE 1
    "ticket": ["A/5 21171", "PC 17599", "3101282", "113803",     # CASE 1, messy
               "STON/O2. 3101282", "17463", "349909"],
    "col":    [7, 3, 1, "AB", 4, "XY", 9],                        # CASE 2
})

# =====================================================================
# 0. DIAGNOSIS -- pandas gives no warning; both look like `object`
# =====================================================================
def diagnose(s: pd.Series) -> str:
    s = s.dropna().astype(str)
    numeric_frac = pd.to_numeric(s, errors="coerce").notna().mean()
    has_digit    = s.str.contains(r"\d").mean()
    has_alpha    = s.str.contains(r"[A-Za-z]").mean()
    if numeric_frac > .99:                    return "purely numeric"
    if numeric_frac < .01 and has_digit < .1: return "purely categorical"
    if has_digit > .8 and has_alpha > .8:     return "MIXED - case 1 (both in every cell)"
    return f"MIXED - case 2 ({numeric_frac:.0%} of rows parse as numbers)"

for c in df.columns:
    print(f"{c:8s} dtype={str(df[c].dtype):8s} -> {diagnose(df[c])}")
# cabin  object -> MIXED - case 1
# ticket object -> MIXED - case 2 (43% parse)   <- messier than it looks
# col    object -> MIXED - case 2 (71% parse)

# =====================================================================
# 1. CASE 1 -- SPLIT each cell into its letter and number parts
# =====================================================================
df["cabin_letter"] = df.cabin.str.extract(r"^([A-Za-z]+)")          # 'C'
df["cabin_number"] = pd.to_numeric(df.cabin.str.extract(r"(\d+)")[0])  # 23
print(df[["cabin", "cabin_letter", "cabin_number"]])

# A registration plate has FOUR parts, not two:
plates = pd.Series(["MH12AB1234", "DL8CAF5678", "KA05MN9012"])
parts = plates.str.extract(r"^([A-Z]{2})(\d{1,2})([A-Z]{1,3})(\d{4})$")
parts.columns = ["state", "rto", "series", "number"]
print(parts)
# Each part is a genuinely different signal. Glued together they are 3 useless
# high-cardinality categories.

# The messy real case: Titanic tickets have an OPTIONAL prefix
tk = df.ticket.str.extract(r"^(?:(?P<prefix>[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9/. ]*?)\s+)?(?P<num>\d+)$")
tk["prefix"] = tk.prefix.fillna("NONE").str.replace(r"[./]", "", regex=True).str.upper()
tk["num"] = pd.to_numeric(tk.num)
print(tk)
# 'NONE' is itself informative -- it means a plain numeric ticket.

# =====================================================================
# 2. CASE 2 -- SEPARATE the rows into two columns
# =====================================================================
s = df["col"]
df["col_numeric"]     = pd.to_numeric(s, errors="coerce")   # non-numbers -> NaN
df["col_categorical"] = s.where(df.col_numeric.isna())      # numbers    -> NaN
df["col_was_coded"]   = df.col_numeric.isna().astype(int)   # THE INDICATOR
print(df[["col", "col_numeric", "col_categorical", "col_was_coded"]])
#   col  col_numeric col_categorical  col_was_coded
#     7          7.0            NaN               0
#    AB          NaN             AB               1     <- often the real signal

# The two NaN patterns are complementary by construction:
assert (df.col_numeric.isna() ^ df.col_categorical.isna()).all()

# =====================================================================
# 3. WHY THE NAIVE FIXES ARE WRONG -- measured
# =====================================================================
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 3000
deck  = rng.choice(list("ABCDEFG"), n, p=[.05,.10,.20,.25,.20,.15,.05])
room  = rng.integers(1, 120, n)
cabin = pd.Series([f"{d}{r}" for d, r in zip(deck, room)])
# survival depends on the DECK LETTER only
y = (rng.random(n) < np.array([.75,.70,.60,.45,.35,.30,.25])[
        [ord(d) - 65 for d in deck]]).astype(int)

X_whole = pd.get_dummies(cabin)                       # one-hot the WHOLE string
X_split = pd.concat([pd.get_dummies(cabin.str[0]),
                     pd.to_numeric(cabin.str.extract(r"(\d+)")[0])], axis=1)

print("columns  whole-string:", X_whole.shape[1], " split:", X_split.shape[1])
print("auc whole-string:", cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000),
        X_whole, y, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc").mean().round(3))
print("auc after split :", cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000),
        X_split, y, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc").mean().round(3))
# ~700 sparse columns and a mediocre score, vs 8 columns and a good one.

# And the truly destructive option:
print("coerced to numeric -> all NaN:",
      pd.to_numeric(cabin, errors="coerce").isna().mean())      # 1.0

# =====================================================================
# 4. AS A REUSABLE TRANSFORMER, so it lives inside a Pipeline
# =====================================================================
class SplitMixed(BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin):
    """Case 1: split 'C23' into ('C', 23). Case 2: split rows by type."""

    def __init__(self, mode="case1", pattern=r"^([A-Za-z]+)(\d+)$"):
        self.mode, self.pattern = mode, pattern

    def fit(self, X, y=None):
        self.col_ = X.columns[0] if hasattr(X, "columns") else 0
        return self

    def transform(self, X):
        s = (X[self.col_] if hasattr(X, "columns") else pd.Series(np.ravel(X))
             ).astype("string")
        if self.mode == "case1":
            ext = s.str.extract(self.pattern)
            return pd.DataFrame({
                "cat": ext[0].fillna("UNKNOWN"),
                "num": pd.to_numeric(ext[1], errors="coerce"),
            })
        num = pd.to_numeric(s, errors="coerce")
        return pd.DataFrame({
            "num":        num,
            "cat":        s.where(num.isna()).fillna("NUMERIC"),
            "was_coded":  num.isna().astype(int),
        })

    def get_feature_names_out(self, input_features=None):
        return (np.array(["cat", "num"]) if self.mode == "case1"
                else np.array(["num", "cat", "was_coded"]))

out = SplitMixed(mode="case1").fit_transform(df[["cabin"]])
print(out)

# =====================================================================
# 5. THE FULL PIPELINE -- split, then treat each part correctly
# =====================================================================
data = pd.DataFrame({"cabin": cabin})
data["cabin_letter"] = cabin.str[0]
data["cabin_number"] = pd.to_numeric(cabin.str.extract(r"(\d+)")[0])
data["cabin_missing"] = data.cabin_letter.isna().astype(int)

pre = ColumnTransformer([
    ("letter", Pipeline([("imp", SimpleImputer(strategy="constant",
                                               fill_value="UNKNOWN")),
                         ("ohe", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"))]),
               ["cabin_letter"]),
    ("number", Pipeline([("imp", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
                         ("sc",  StandardScaler())]), ["cabin_number"]),
    ("flag",   "passthrough", ["cabin_missing"]),
], remainder="drop")

pipe = Pipeline([("pre", pre), ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))])
print("pipeline auc:", cross_val_score(pipe, data, y, cv=5,
                                       scoring="roc_auc").mean().round(3))
print("features:", pipe.fit(data, y).named_steps["pre"].get_feature_names_out())

q.q:
The Titanic Cabin column looks like C85, B20, E46. How do you
handle it?
q.a:
Split it: the leading letter is the deck (a strong survival signal, because deck
position determined distance to the lifeboats) and the digits are the room number
(weak, but it encodes position along the ship). One-hot the letter, scale the
number, and add a missingness indicator — most cabins are missing, and that
absence correlates with passenger class.

q.q: A column contains 7, 3, 1, "AB", 4. What do you do?
q.a:
Separate it into a numeric column and a categorical column, with NaN where
each does not apply, and add a binary flag marking which rows were coded. Then
ask the data owner what "AB" means — it is a business rule, and it usually
matters more than the numbers do.

q.q: Why not just one-hot encode the whole mixed column?
q.a:
Because it destroys the shared structure. C23 and C24 become
unrelated categories despite both being on deck C, cardinality explodes to
hundreds of nearly-singleton columns, and unseen values at prediction time have
no encoding at all.

q.q: How do you detect a mixed column programmatically?
q.a:
Apply pd.to_numeric(s, errors="coerce") and measure the fraction that
parses. Zero or one means the column is homogeneous; anything strictly in between
is Case 2. For Case 1, check whether almost every value contains both a digit and
a letter.

q.q: After splitting you have many NaNs. Is that a problem?
q.a:
Not in itself — it is expected, and the pattern is informative. Add an indicator
column recording which type each row was, then impute (Topics 23–27). Imputing
without the indicator throws away exactly the signal the split revealed.

22.idea: Dates encode seasonality, cycles and trends. Parse to datetime, extract parts (year, month, weekday, day of year, weekend flag), and encode periodic parts cyclically.
22.intuition: A month number treats December and January as 11 apart, but they are one month apart. Cyclic encoding puts them on a circle.
22.formula: sin(2π m/12), cos(2π m/12) for month m. For weekday use period 7.
steps: Convert with pd.to_datetime.
Extract year, month, day, weekday, is_weekend, day of year.
Encode periodic features with sin and cos.
Create elapsed time features (days since an event) if relevant.
22.example: 2026-08-30 is a Sunday, day of year 242. Month 8 encodes as sin = −0.866, cos = −0.5.
pitfalls: Using the raw string or integer timestamp without parsing.
Random train/test splits on time series leak the future: split by time.
22.tip: Cyclic encoding for periodic features; time-based splits for temporal data.
22.hook: sin(2π m/12), cos(2π m/12) put December next to January.
22.pit: Using month as a plain integer: December and January look far apart.
22.code:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.preprocessing import FunctionTransformer, StandardScaler
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit, cross_val_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
idx = pd.date_range("2024-01-01", "2026-03-01", freq="h")
df = pd.DataFrame({"ts": idx})

# a realistic signal: weekly + daily seasonality + trend + noise
t = np.arange(len(idx))
df["demand"] = (100
    + 30 * np.sin(2*np.pi*df.ts.dt.hour/24)          # daily cycle
    + 20 * (df.ts.dt.dayofweek >= 5)                 # weekend effect
    + 15 * np.sin(2*np.pi*df.ts.dt.dayofyear/365.25) # annual cycle
    + 0.002 * t                                      # trend
    + rng.normal(0, 6, len(idx)))

# =====================================================================
# 1. STEP ZERO -- convert to datetime. Nothing works before this.
# =====================================================================
df["ts"] = pd.to_datetime(df["ts"])
print(df.ts.dtype)                       # datetime64[ns]
# From a messy source you often need:
#   pd.to_datetime(s, format="%d/%m/%Y", errors="coerce", utc=True)
# `errors="coerce"` turns unparseable strings into NaT rather than crashing.

# =====================================================================
# 2. EXTRACT THE PARTS
# =====================================================================
d = df.ts.dt
feat = pd.DataFrame({
    # --- date parts ---
    "year":        d.year,
    "month":       d.month,
    "day":         d.day,
    "dayofweek":   d.dayofweek,          # Monday = 0
    "dayofyear":   d.dayofyear,
    "quarter":     d.quarter,
    "weekofyear":  d.isocalendar().week.astype(int),
    # --- time parts ---
    "hour":        d.hour,
    "minute":      d.minute,
    # --- derived flags ---
    "is_weekend":     (d.dayofweek >= 5).astype(int),
    "is_month_start": d.is_month_start.astype(int),
    "is_month_end":   d.is_month_end.astype(int),
    "is_business_hr": ((d.hour >= 9) & (d.hour < 18) & (d.dayofweek < 5)).astype(int),
})
print(feat.head(3).T)

# =====================================================================
# 3. CYCLICAL ENCODING -- both components, always
# =====================================================================
def cyclic(values, period):
    ang = 2 * np.pi * np.asarray(values) / period
    return np.sin(ang), np.cos(ang)

for name, col, period in [("hour", d.hour, 24),
                          ("dow",  d.dayofweek, 7),
                          ("month", d.month, 12),
                          ("doy",  d.dayofyear, 365.25)]:
    feat[f"{name}_sin"], feat[f"{name}_cos"] = cyclic(col, period)

# PROOF that the wrap-around is fixed:
def dist(h1, h2, period=24):
    s1, c1 = cyclic(h1, period); s2, c2 = cyclic(h2, period)
    return float(np.hypot(s1 - s2, c1 - c2))

print(f"raw integer distance 23 vs 0 : {abs(23 - 0)}")     # 23  -- WRONG
print(f"cyclic distance      23 vs 0 : {dist(23, 0):.3f}") # 0.26 -- adjacent
print(f"cyclic distance      12 vs 0 : {dist(12, 0):.3f}") # 2.00 -- maximal

# WHY BOTH COMPONENTS: sin alone is not injective
print("sin(3h) == sin(9h):", np.isclose(cyclic(3, 24)[0], cyclic(9, 24)[0]))   # True
print("(sin,cos) differ  :", not np.allclose(cyclic(3, 24), cyclic(9, 24)))    # True

# =====================================================================
# 4. ELAPSED TIME -- generalises where absolute dates do not
# =====================================================================
signup = pd.to_datetime(rng.choice(pd.date_range("2020-01-01", "2025-12-31"), 5))
now = pd.Timestamp("2026-03-01")
users = pd.DataFrame({"signup": signup})
users["days_since_signup"]  = (now - users.signup).dt.days
users["months_since_signup"] = users.days_since_signup / 30.44
users["tenure_years"]        = users.days_since_signup / 365.25
print(users)
# `days_since_signup` means the same thing in 2026 and 2030.
# `signup.year` does not -- the model has never seen 2030.

# =====================================================================
# 5. LAG AND ROLLING FEATURES -- and the shift that prevents leakage
# =====================================================================
daily = df.set_index("ts").demand.resample("D").mean().to_frame()

daily["lag_1"] = daily.demand.shift(1)          # yesterday
daily["lag_7"] = daily.demand.shift(7)          # same weekday last week

# WRONG -- the window at row t INCLUDES row t, i.e. the target itself
daily["roll7_leaky"] = daily.demand.rolling(7).mean()

# RIGHT -- shift first, so the window ends at t-1
daily["roll7"]     = daily.demand.shift(1).rolling(7).mean()
daily["roll7_std"] = daily.demand.shift(1).rolling(7).std()
daily["diff_1"]    = daily.demand.diff(1)

print(daily[["demand", "roll7_leaky", "roll7"]].head(10).round(2))
print("leaky rolling correlates with the target:",
      daily[["demand", "roll7_leaky"]].corr().iloc[0, 1].round(3))   # inflated
print("correct rolling                        :",
      daily[["demand", "roll7"]].corr().iloc[0, 1].round(3))

# =====================================================================
# 6. DOES CYCLICAL ENCODING ACTUALLY HELP? -- model-dependent
# =====================================================================
y = df.demand.values
raw_cols    = ["hour", "dayofweek", "month"]
cyclic_cols = ["hour_sin","hour_cos","dow_sin","dow_cos","month_sin","month_cos"]

tscv = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5)      # NEVER a shuffled split on time data
for model_name, model in [("Ridge (linear)", Ridge()),
                          ("RandomForest", RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=60,
                                                                 random_state=0))]:
    r = cross_val_score(model, feat[raw_cols],    y, cv=tscv, scoring="r2").mean()
    c = cross_val_score(model, feat[cyclic_cols], y, cv=tscv, scoring="r2").mean()
    print(f"{model_name:16s} raw {r:6.3f}   cyclic {c:6.3f}")
# Ridge: large gain -- it cannot represent a cycle from an integer.
# Forest: little difference -- it can isolate hour 23 with two splits.

# =====================================================================
# 7. TEMPORAL SPLIT -- train on the past, validate on the future
# =====================================================================
cut = "2025-10-01"
train = df[df.ts <  cut]
test  = df[df.ts >= cut]
print(f"train {train.ts.min().date()} -> {train.ts.max().date()}  ({len(train)})")
print(f"test  {test.ts.min().date()} -> {test.ts.max().date()}  ({len(test)})")

# And what a RANDOM split would wrongly allow:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
a, b = train_test_split(df, test_size=.25, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
print("random split test range:", b.ts.min().date(), "->", b.ts.max().date())
# The "test" set spans the whole history -- the model trains on the future.

# =====================================================================
# 8. AS A PIPELINE-SAFE TRANSFORMER
# =====================================================================
def datetime_features(X):
    s = pd.to_datetime(pd.Series(np.ravel(X)))
    d = s.dt
    out = pd.DataFrame(index=s.index)
    for name, col, period in [("hour", d.hour, 24), ("dow", d.dayofweek, 7),
                              ("month", d.month, 12)]:
        ang = 2 * np.pi * col / period
        out[f"{name}_sin"], out[f"{name}_cos"] = np.sin(ang), np.cos(ang)
    out["is_weekend"] = (d.dayofweek >= 5).astype(int)
    out["hour"] = d.hour
    return out.values

dt_tf = FunctionTransformer(datetime_features,
                            feature_names_out=lambda s, n: np.array(
                                ["hour_sin","hour_cos","dow_sin","dow_cos",
                                 "month_sin","month_cos","is_weekend","hour"]))

pipe = Pipeline([
    ("dt",    ColumnTransformer([("time", dt_tf, "ts")], remainder="drop")),
    ("scale", StandardScaler()),
    ("model", Ridge()),
])
print("pipeline r2:", cross_val_score(pipe, df[["ts"]], y, cv=tscv,
                                      scoring="r2").mean().round(3))
# Raw timestamps in, predictions out -- the extraction is part of the model.

q.q: Why encode the hour as sin and cos rather than as an integer?
q.a:
Because the hour is cyclical. As an integer, 23 and 0 are 23 apart — the maximum
possible distance — when they are actually adjacent. Mapping onto the unit
circle makes the distance correct.

q.q: Why do you need both sin and cos?
q.a:
$\sin$ alone is not injective over a full cycle: 3 a.m. and 9 a.m. give the same
sine. The pair identifies a unique point on the circle.

q.q: Should you use cyclical encoding for XGBoost?
q.a:
Rarely worth it. A tree isolates hour 23 with a couple of splits, so the
wrap-around costs it little. Cyclical encoding is for models that treat the
feature as a position on a line — linear models, KNN, SVM, neural networks.

q.q:
Your demand forecast has $R^2 = 0.99$ in backtest and fails live.
Most likely cause?
q.a:
A rolling or aggregate feature that includes the current row — rolling(7)
without a .shift(1). The feature contains the target. Check every
window-based feature's alignment.

q.q: How do you split time-series data for validation?
q.a:
Chronologically: train on the past, validate on the future, mirroring production.
Use TimeSeriesSplit for cross-validation. A shuffled split lets the model
learn from the future and inflates every metric.

q.q: Should you include year as a feature?
q.a:
Only with care. It captures a genuine trend but cannot extrapolate — every
future year is outside the training range, and a tree will simply clamp to the
last year it saw. Prefer an explicit trend term, a time index, or elapsed-time
features.

23.t: Missing Data I: Complete Case Analysis
23.idea: Complete case analysis (listwise deletion) drops every row that has any missing value. It is simple and unbiased only when data is missing completely at random and few rows are lost.
23.intuition: Throwing away incomplete forms is fine if very few forms are incomplete. It becomes harmful when many columns each have a little missing data.
23.formula: Rows kept ≈ (1 − missing rate)^(number of independent columns). 5% per column over 30 columns keeps about 21%.
steps: Count missing values per column and per row.
Estimate the share of rows that survive.
Only delete if the loss is small (under about 5%) and missingness looks random.
Otherwise impute.
23.example: 10 rows, 2 incomplete: keep 8 (80%). With 30 columns each missing 5%, only about 21% of rows are complete.
pitfalls: Deleting rows can bias the data if missingness depends on the value (MNAR).
Losing many rows silently shrinks the training set.
23.tip: Always report how many rows were lost, not just that you dropped them.
23.pit: Dropping 5% per column across 30 columns keeps only about 21% of rows.
23.code:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from scipy import stats
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 5000
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "age":     rng.uniform(20, 70, n),
    "tenure":  rng.integers(1, 120, n).astype(float),
    "n_calls": rng.poisson(2, n).astype(float),
})
df["income"] = 2000 * df.age + rng.normal(0, 12_000, n)
y = (0.00002 * df.income + 0.01 * df.n_calls + rng.normal(0, .5, n) > 1.2).astype(int)

# =====================================================================
# 1. THE THREE MECHANISMS, SIMULATED
# =====================================================================
full = df.copy()

mcar = full.copy()
mcar.loc[rng.random(n) < .30, "income"] = np.nan          # independent of all

mar = full.copy()
mar.loc[rng.random(n) < (full.age - 20) / 60, "income"] = np.nan   # depends on AGE

mnar = full.copy()
mnar.loc[full.income > full.income.quantile(.70), "income"] = np.nan  # depends on ITSELF

for name, d in [("MCAR", mcar), ("MAR", mar), ("MNAR", mnar)]:
    obs = d.income.dropna()
    print(f"{name:5s} missing {d.income.isna().mean():.0%}  "
          f"true mean {full.income.mean():9.0f}  "
          f"observed mean {obs.mean():9.0f}  "
          f"bias {obs.mean() - full.income.mean():+9.0f}")
# MCAR bias ~ 0        -> deletion is safe
# MAR  bias large      -> deletion is biased, imputation can help
# MNAR bias enormous   -> the top 30% is simply GONE; nothing recovers it

# =====================================================================
# 2. COMPLETE CASE ANALYSIS -- the one-liner, and what it costs
# =====================================================================
work = mar.copy()
work["y"] = y

before = len(work)
cca = work.dropna()                       # list-wise deletion
print(f"rows: {before} -> {len(cca)}  ({1 - len(cca)/before:.1%} lost)")

# THE 5% RULE, checked properly -- on ROWS lost, not per-column rate
loss = 1 - len(cca) / before
print("CCA acceptable?" , "YES" if loss < .05 else f"NO -- {loss:.1%} of rows lost")

# =====================================================================
# 3. HOW FAST IT COMPOUNDS ACROSS COLUMNS
# =====================================================================
wide = pd.DataFrame(rng.normal(0, 1, (5000, 20)))
for p in [.01, .05, .10]:

          f"{w.dropna().shape[0]/5000:.1%} of rows survive  "
          f"(theory {(1-p)**20:.1%})")

# =====================================================================
work["income_missing"] = work.income.isna()

q.q: When is it acceptable to just drop rows with missing values?
q.a:
When the data is MCAR and the row loss is small — the usual guidance is under
5%. Verify MCAR by checking that the other columns and the target base rate do
not differ between complete and incomplete rows.

q.q: Explain MCAR, MAR and MNAR with an example each.
q.a:
MCAR: a sensor drops readings at random intervals. MAR: younger respondents skip
the income question — missingness depends on age, which you observe. MNAR: high
earners skip the income question — missingness depends on income itself, which
you do not observe. Only the third is unfixable from the data alone.

q.q:
Each of your 20 columns is 5% missing. What fraction of rows survives
CCA?
q.a:
Roughly $(0.95)^{20}\approx36%$ if missingness is independent — so you would
discard nearly two-thirds of the data. In practice missingness often clusters in
the same rows, so measure the real number rather than computing it.

q.q: How can you tell whether data is MNAR?
q.a:
You cannot, from the data — by definition the evidence is missing. You diagnose
it from domain knowledge about the collection process. Mitigate by adding a
missingness indicator, modelling the missingness explicitly, or collecting a
small validated sample of the missing cases.

q.q: What is wrong with dropping rows at training time?
q.a:
Beyond bias and lost power: production will still send requests with missing
fields, and you cannot drop a customer. You end up with a separate imputation
rule at serving time — two different treatments of missingness, and a direct
source of training/serving skew.

q.q: A column is 80% missing. Drop it?
q.a:
Probably drop the column, but first create a was_missing indicator. The
fact of recording is often predictive — Titanic Cabin is 77% missing,
and having a recorded cabin correlates strongly with first class and survival.

24.idea: Numerical imputation replaces missing numbers with a statistic: the mean for symmetric data, the median for skewed data. Random-sample and end-of-distribution imputation are alternatives.
24.intuition: Fill the gap with the most typical value. The mean is the centre of mass; the median is the middle person, which resists outliers.

Fit the statistic on training data only.
Optionally add a missing-indicator column so the model knows the value was filled.

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer, MissingIndicator
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline, FeatureUnion
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, GridSearchCV, train_test_split
from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 6000
income = rng.lognormal(3.4, .65, n)                 # right-skewed
score  = 0.8 * np.log(income) + rng.normal(0, .35, n)
y = (0.9 * np.log(income) + 0.5 * score + rng.normal(0, 1, n) > 4.4).astype(int)

# MNAR: the highest earners decline to answer
missing = income > np.percentile(income, 68)
obs = income.copy(); obs[missing] = np.nan
df = pd.DataFrame({"income": obs, "score": score})
print(f"missing {np.isnan(obs).mean():.0%}")

# =====================================================================
# 1. MEAN / MEDIAN -- and the variance shrinkage, verified
# =====================================================================
mean_imp   = SimpleImputer(strategy="mean").fit_transform(df[["income"]]).ravel()
median_imp = SimpleImputer(strategy="median").fit_transform(df[["income"]]).ravel()

f = np.isnan(obs).mean()
print(f"true std      {income.std():.2f}")
print(f"mean-imputed  {mean_imp.std():.2f}   theory sigma*sqrt(1-f) = "
      f"{np.nanstd(obs) * np.sqrt(1 - f):.2f}")
print(f"shrinkage factor observed {mean_imp.std()/income.std():.3f}  "
      f"predicted {np.sqrt(1-f):.3f}")

# The "creates outliers" problem is about the JOINT distribution:
r_true = np.corrcoef(np.log(income), score)[0, 1]
r_mean = np.corrcoef(np.log(mean_imp), score)[0, 1]
print(f"correlation with score:  true {r_true:.3f}   after mean imputation {r_mean:.3f}")
# Attenuated -- a real signal made to look weaker than it is.

# =====================================================================
# 2. ARBITRARY VALUE
# =====================================================================
arb = SimpleImputer(strategy="constant", fill_value=-999).fit_transform(df[["income"]]).ravel()
print("sentinel rows:", (arb == -999).sum())

# WHY NOT ZERO: it collides with a legitimate value
counts = np.where(rng.random(n) < .2, 0, rng.poisson(3, n)).astype(float)
counts[rng.random(n) < .1] = np.nan
zero_imp = SimpleImputer(strategy="constant", fill_value=0).fit_transform(
    counts.reshape(-1, 1)).ravel()
print("rows that are now 0:", (zero_imp == 0).sum(),
      "-- genuinely zero AND missing, indistinguishable")

# =====================================================================
# 3. END OF DISTRIBUTION -- both formulas from the notes
# =====================================================================
class EndOfDistributionImputer(BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin):
    """mu + 3*sigma for normal data;  Q3 + 1.5*IQR for skewed data."""
    def __init__(self, method="iqr", tail="right"):
        self.method, self.tail = method, tail
    def fit(self, X, y=None):
        X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
        v = X[~np.isnan(X)]
        if self.method == "gaussian":
            m, s = v.mean(), v.std()
            self.value_ = m + 3*s if self.tail == "right" else m - 3*s
        else:
            q1, q3 = np.nanpercentile(v, [25, 75]); iqr = q3 - q1
            self.value_ = q3 + 1.5*iqr if self.tail == "right" else q1 - 1.5*iqr
        return self
    def transform(self, X):
        X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float).copy()
        X[np.isnan(X)] = self.value_
        return X

eod = EndOfDistributionImputer(method="iqr").fit(df[["income"]])
print(f"IQR fence      Q3+1.5IQR = {eod.value_:.2f}")
print(f"gaussian fence mu+3sigma = "
      f"{EndOfDistributionImputer(method='gaussian').fit(df[['income']]).value_:.2f}")

# =====================================================================
# 4. RANDOM SAMPLE -- the only method that preserves the shape
# =====================================================================
class RandomSampleImputer(BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin):
    """Draw from the observed TRAINING values. Seeded per row for determinism."""
    def __init__(self, random_state=0):
        self.random_state = random_state
    def fit(self, X, y=None):
        X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
        self.pool_ = X[~np.isnan(X)]          # stored for use at SERVING time
        return self
    def transform(self, X):
        X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float).copy()
        idx = np.isnan(X)
        if idx.any():
            r = np.random.default_rng(self.random_state)
            X[idx] = r.choice(self.pool_, idx.sum())
        return X

rs = RandomSampleImputer().fit_transform(df[["income"]]).ravel()
print(f"\nstd:      true {income.std():.2f}  mean-imp {mean_imp.std():.2f}  "
      f"random-sample {rs.std():.2f}")
print(f"skew:     true {pd.Series(income).skew():.2f}  "
      f"mean-imp {pd.Series(mean_imp).skew():.2f}  "
      f"random-sample {pd.Series(rs).skew():.2f}")
# Random sampling matches the original on BOTH moments. Nothing else does.

# =====================================================================
# 5. THE MISSING INDICATOR -- usually worth more than the imputed value
# =====================================================================

out = imp.fit_transform(df[["income"]])
print("columns out:", out.shape[1], "(value + indicator)")

# =====================================================================
# 6. COMPARE THEM ALL, PROPERLY -- inside cross-validation
# =====================================================================

setups = {
    "mean":            SimpleImputer(strategy="mean"),
    "median":          SimpleImputer(strategy="median"),
    "median + flag":   SimpleImputer(strategy="median", add_indicator=True),
    "arbitrary -999":  SimpleImputer(strategy="constant", fill_value=-999),
    "end of dist":     Pipeline([("e", EndOfDistributionImputer()),
                                 ("nothing", "passthrough")]),
    "random sample":   RandomSampleImputer(),
}
print(f"\n{'imputer':18s} {'LogReg':>9s} {'Forest':>9s}")
for name, tf in setups.items():
    lr = Pipeline([("imp", tf), ("sc", StandardScaler()),
                   ("m", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))])
    rf = Pipeline([("imp", tf),
                   ("m", RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=150, random_state=0))])
    a = cross_val_score(lr, X, y, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc").mean()
    b = cross_val_score(rf, X, y, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc").mean()
    print(f"{name:18s} {a:9.4f} {b:9.4f}")
# Note the pattern: "arbitrary -999" and "end of dist" are competitive for the
# FOREST and terrible for LOGISTIC REGRESSION -- exactly as the theory predicts.

# =====================================================================
# 7. LET GRIDSEARCH CHOOSE -- the notes' own advice
# =====================================================================
pipe = Pipeline([("imp", SimpleImputer()),
                 ("sc",  StandardScaler()),
                 ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))])
gs = GridSearchCV(pipe, {
    "imp__strategy":      ["mean", "median", "most_frequent", "constant"],
    "imp__fill_value":    [0, -1, -999],
    "imp__add_indicator": [False, True],
    "clf__C":             [0.1, 1.0, 10.0],
}, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc", n_jobs=-1, error_score="raise").fit(X, y)
print("\nbest imputation:", {k: v for k, v in gs.best_params_.items() if "imp" in k})
print("best cv auc:", round(gs.best_score_, 4))

# =====================================================================
# 8. FIT ON TRAIN ONLY -- the median is a learned parameter
# =====================================================================
X_tr, X_te = train_test_split(X, test_size=.25, random_state=0)
imp = SimpleImputer(strategy="median").fit(X_tr)
print("\nmedian learned from TRAIN:", imp.statistics_.round(2))

q.q: What is wrong with mean imputation?
q.a:
It shrinks the variance by $\sqrt{1-f}$, plants an artificial spike at a single
value, attenuates correlations with other columns, and understates uncertainty in
any downstream inference. It is acceptable only when very little is missing.

q.q: Mean or median?
q.a:
Median by default — robust to skew and outliers, and it always lands on a
plausible value. Use the mean only after checking that the column is close to
symmetric.

q.q: When would you deliberately impute with an extreme value?
q.a:
When the data is MNAR and you are using a tree-based model. Pushing the imputed
rows to the tail lets the tree isolate them with a single split, so it can learn a
separate rule for "this was missing". Never do it for a linear or
distance-based model — it becomes a dominating outlier.

q.q: Which imputation method preserves the distribution?
q.a:
Random sample imputation — drawing from the observed values of the same column.
It preserves the shape, the variance and the quantiles. Its drawback is
non-determinism, which you fix by seeding from a stable row key.

q.q: Why add a missing indicator?
q.a:
Because imputation destroys the information that the value was absent, and that
absence is frequently predictive — under MNAR it can be the strongest signal in
the column. It costs one binary feature and lets the model learn a separate
effect for imputed rows.

q.q: Why is imputing a numeric column with 0 dangerous?
q.a:
Zero is usually a legitimate value. After imputation you cannot distinguish
"no purchases" from "we do not know", and the model learns a blended,
incorrect effect for both.

from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, GridSearchCV

n = 4000
cities = ["Mumbai", "Delhi", "Pune", "Kochi", "Jaipur"]
p = [.42, .24, .16, .11, .07]

    "city":      rng.choice(cities, n, p=p),

# =====================================================================

print("target rate | city missing:", y[miss].mean().round(3))

# =====================================================================
# 5. ORDINAL COLUMNS -- the median category DOES exist

edu = df.education.copy()

q.q: How do you impute a categorical column?
q.a:
With the mode if very little is missing — under roughly 10%. Above that,
create an explicit "Missing" category. Mean and median do not exist for
nominal data.

q.q: Why does mode imputation get worse as the missing rate rises?
q.a:
Because every imputed row is assigned to the same category. The mode's share
grows by roughly $f(1-p_m)$ while every other category shrinks by a factor
$(1-f)$. At 45% missing you have rewritten the distribution rather than repaired
it.

q.q: Why is a "Missing" category often better than the mode?
q.a:
Because it is honest. Mode imputation asserts a fact you do not have; the
"Missing" category asserts only that the value was absent. It preserves
the observed categories' proportions and lets the model learn a separate effect
for absence — which under MAR or MNAR is frequently the strongest signal
available.

q.q: How do you decide between them for a given column?
q.a:
Two checks. First the missing rate against the 10% threshold. Second, and more
important: compare the target rate between rows where the value is present and
rows where it is missing. If they differ significantly, the absence is
informative and you should keep it as a category regardless of the rate.

q.q:
Your model crashes in production on city="Chennai". Why, and
what do you do?
q.a:
The one-hot encoder has no column for an unseen category. Set
handle_unknown="ignore" so it encodes as all zeros, or — better — map
any unrecognised category into the same "Missing" bucket, so unseen and
absent values share a learned effect rather than one of them having no
representation.

q.q: Does imputing a categorical column change the number of features?
q.a:
Mode imputation does not. The "Missing" category adds exactly one column
after one-hot encoding — which is the price of retaining the information, and a
cheap one.

26.idea: The KNN imputer fills a missing value using the average of the k nearest rows, measuring distance on the features that are present.
26.intuition: Similar rows probably have similar values. Ask the most similar neighbours what their value was.
26.formula: Filled value = average of the k nearest neighbours' values for that feature.
steps: Scale the features first, so distance is fair.
For a row with a gap, find the k nearest complete-enough rows.
Average their values for the missing feature.
Impute train and test with the train neighbours.
26.example: Query (3, ?) with complete rows (1, 2), (2, 3), (10, 11) and k = 2: neighbours by feature A are (2,3) at distance 1 and (1,2) at distance 2. Fill = (3 + 2) / 2 = 2.5.
pitfalls: Unscaled features make the large-range feature dominate distance.
Slow on large datasets, since each query scans neighbours.
26.tip: KNN imputation is more accurate than mean but needs scaling and costs more time.
26.hook: Fill = average of the k nearest neighbours' values.

steps: Distance on the observed feature A only: |3-1| = 2, |3-2| = 1, |3-10| = 7.
k = 2 nearest rows: row 2 (distance 1) and row 1 (distance 2).
Fill B = (3 + 2) / 2 = 2.5. Row 3 is ignored because it is far away.

# =====================================================================
# 2. THE nan_euclidean DISTANCE, FROM SCRATCH
# =====================================================================
def nan_euclidean(x, y):
    """Distance over shared columns, rescaled to the full dimension."""
    present = ~np.isnan(x) & ~np.isnan(y)
    if present.sum() == 0:
        return np.nan
    p, k = len(x), present.sum()
    return np.sqrt(p / k * ((x[present] - y[present]) ** 2).sum())

a = np.array([3.0, np.nan, 7.0, 2.0])

        nearest = donors[good][np.argsort(d[good])[:k]]
        X[i, col] = X[nearest, col].mean()
    return X

q.q: How does the KNN Imputer differ from median imputation?
q.a:
Median imputation is univariate — it uses only the column being filled, so
every missing value gets the same number. KNN imputation is multivariate: it
finds the $k$ most similar rows using the other columns and averages their
values, so the imputed value is conditioned on the rest of the row. It preserves
correlations that median imputation destroys.

q.q:
How do you compute the distance when the neighbour rows also have
missing values?
q.a:
With nan_euclidean: sum the squared differences over the columns present
in both rows, then multiply by $p/|P|$ to rescale as if all columns had been
present. Without that rescaling, rows sharing fewer columns would appear closer.

q.q: Why must you scale before KNN imputation?
q.a:
Because it is distance-based. An unscaled salary column with variance $10^8$
dominates an age column with variance $10^2$, so the "nearest" rows are chosen
almost entirely on salary, and every other column contributes nothing.

q.q: What happens as $k$ grows?
q.a:
The imputed value converges to the column mean — averaging over more and more
neighbours washes out the local information. You have paid $O(n^2p)$ for mean
imputation. Tune $k$ by cross-validation.

q.q: When would you not use it?
q.a:
On large datasets (past roughly $10^5$ rows the quadratic cost is prohibitive),
in high dimensions (distances become uninformative — Topic 32), when the
columns are close to independent (no benefit over the median), and when you
cannot afford to ship the training matrix as part of the model artefact.

q.q: Does the KNN Imputer leak?
q.a:
Not if it is inside a pipeline. It is a fitted transformer: it learns the
training matrix in fit and uses only that matrix to find donors in
transform. Fitting it on the combined train and test data would leak, as
with any transformer.

27.idea: MICE fills each column with missing values by regressing it on the other columns, cycling through columns until the imputed values stop changing. It is multivariate imputation by chained equations.
27.intuition: Each gap is predicted from everything else, then the other gaps are refined using that improved picture, repeated until stable.
27.formula: Start: mean fill. Repeat: for each column j with gaps, fit model on observed rows and predict missing rows of j; stop when changes are near 0.
steps: Fill all gaps with the mean or median.
Pick one column at a time and treat it as the target.
Train a model on the other columns, using rows where the target is observed.
Replace that column's gaps with predictions.
Repeat over all columns until the change between cycles is tiny.
27.example: Age and income both have gaps. Fill both with the mean, regress age on income to refine age's gaps, then regress income on age, and repeat.
pitfalls: Assumes data is missing at random (MAR); MNAR breaks it.
Can be slow and overfit if the regression models are too complex.
27.tip: MICE uses the other features, which is why it beats single mean fills; say it works best under MAR.
27.hook: Start with mean fill, then regress each column on the rest, repeat.
27.pit: Works best when data is missing at random (MAR).

steps: Start: fill B's gap with its mean of observed values, (2+3+6)/3 = 3.67.
Iteration 1: regress B on A using the observed rows 1, 2, 4. Fit: slope 1.357, intercept 0.5.
Predict B at A = 3: 1.357 x 3 + 0.5 = 4.57. Replace the gap with 4.57.
Only one column has a gap here, so the next iteration gives the same value: converged.

      f"{(M.any(axis=1)).mean():.0%} of rows affected")

# =====================================================================
# 1. THE ALGORITHM, IMPLEMENTED FROM THE NOTES' SEVEN STEPS
# =====================================================================
def mice_scratch(X, max_iter=10, tol=1e-3, verbose=True):
    X = X.copy()
    missing = np.isnan(X)

    # STEP 1: fill all NaN with the column mean
    col_mean = np.nanmean(X, axis=0)
    for j in range(X.shape[1]):
        X[missing[:, j], j] = col_mean[j]

    for it in range(max_iter):
        prev = X[missing].copy()

        # STEP 6: do this for ALL columns
        for j in range(X.shape[1]):
            if not missing[:, j].any():
                continue
            # STEP 2: treat column j as the target
            # STEP 3: the OTHER columns are the input
            others = [c for c in range(X.shape[1]) if c != j]
            obs = ~missing[:, j]

            # STEP 4: train a model on the rows where j IS observed
            model = BayesianRidge().fit(X[obs][:, others], X[obs, j])

            # STEP 5: replace the missing values with the predictions
            X[missing[:, j], j] = model.predict(X[missing[:, j]][:, others])

        # STEP 7: stop when the change is near zero
        delta = np.abs(X[missing] - prev).mean()
        if verbose:
            print(f"  iter {it+1:2d}  mean change {delta:.6f}")
        if delta < tol:
            break
    return X

q.q: Explain MICE in one paragraph.
q.a:
Fill every gap with the column mean as a starting point. Then take one column at
a time, blank out its originally-missing cells, fit a model predicting that
column from all the others on the rows where it is observed, and write the
predictions back. Do this for every column, then repeat the whole cycle until the
imputed values stop changing. It replaces a single unconditional average with a
set of conditional models that inform each other.

q.q: Why does it need to iterate?
q.a:
Because when you impute column 1 you use columns 2 and 3, which are themselves
still filled with crude means. Once columns 2 and 3 improve, column 1's model has
better inputs and can be improved in turn. The cycle propagates information until
it stabilises.

q.q: Which missingness mechanism does MICE assume?
q.a:
MAR — missingness depends on the observed data. That is exactly what
conditioning on the other columns can capture. It is unbiased under MCAR too
(and merely more efficient), and it reduces but does not eliminate bias under
MNAR.

q.q:
What is the difference between IterativeImputer and true
MICE?
q.a:
IterativeImputer produces one completed dataset — single imputation.
True MICE produces $m$ datasets from $m$ runs with different random draws, fits
the model $m$ times, and pools the results with Rubin's rules so that the
uncertainty about the missing values propagates into the standard errors.

q.q: When would you use median imputation instead?
q.a:
When under about 5% is missing, when the columns are nearly independent, when
the dataset is large enough that the extra fits are prohibitive, or when the
model is a gradient-boosted tree that handles missingness natively. Always verify
the choice by cross-validation rather than assuming the sophisticated method
wins.

q.q: How do you know MICE has converged?
q.a:
Track a summary of the imputed values — their mean or standard deviation —
across iterations and check that it has plateaued. n_iter_ tells you
whether it stopped on the tolerance or simply hit max_iter; the latter
means it had not converged.

28.t: Outliers I: Detection and the Z-Score Method
28.idea: The z-score measures how many standard deviations a point sits from the mean. Points beyond plus or minus 3 are flagged as outliers under a roughly normal assumption.
28.intuition: If the data is bell-shaped, almost everything lies within 3 standard deviations. Anything further is unusual.
steps: Compute μ and σ on the column.
Compute z for each value.
Flag |z| > 3 (or another threshold you justify).
Decide: cap, remove, or keep and flag.
28.example: [10,11,12,11,10,12,11,10,40]: mean 14.1, std 9.2. The value 40 has z = 2.82, so it is NOT flagged, because the outlier inflated the std itself.
pitfalls: Masking: a big outlier inflates σ and hides itself, especially with small n.
Assumes normality; skewed columns get false flags.
28.tip: Mention masking: it is the reason to prefer IQR on small or skewed data.
28.pit: Outliers inflate μ and σ, hiding themselves (masking).

y_out = np.r_[y, [60.0, 65.0, 58.0]]

clean = LinearRegression().fit(x.reshape(-1,1), y)
dirty = LinearRegression().fit(x_out.reshape(-1,1), y_out)
print(f"clean fit: slope {clean.coef_[0]:.3f}  intercept {clean.intercept_:.3f}")
print(f"3 outliers: slope {dirty.coef_[0]:.3f}  intercept {dirty.intercept_:.3f}")
# 3 points out of 203 (1.5%) move the slope by ~40%.

# A TREE barely notices -- it splits on rank order
t1 = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=3, random_state=0).fit(x.reshape(-1,1), y)
t2 = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=3, random_state=0).fit(x_out.reshape(-1,1), y_out)
grid = np.linspace(0, 10, 50).reshape(-1, 1)
print("tree prediction change:", np.abs(t1.predict(grid) - t2.predict(grid)).mean().round(3))
print("linear prediction change:", np.abs(clean.predict(grid) - dirty.predict(grid)).mean().round(3))

# A ROBUST loss also resists them:
hub = HuberRegressor(epsilon=1.35).fit(x_out.reshape(-1,1), y_out)
print(f"Huber slope on dirty data: {hub.coef_[0]:.3f}  (true = 2.5)")

# =====================================================================
# 2. THE EMPIRICAL RULE, VERIFIED
# =====================================================================
d = rng.normal(50, 10, 200_000)
for k in [1, 2, 3]:
    inside = np.mean(np.abs(d - d.mean()) <= k * d.std())
    print(f"within {k} sigma: {inside:.4%}   (theory "
          f"{stats.norm.cdf(k)-stats.norm.cdf(-k):.4%})")

# =====================================================================
# 3. Z-SCORE TREATMENT -- detection, trimming, capping
# =====================================================================
income = rng.normal(60_000, 15_000, 5000)
income[rng.choice(5000, 12, replace=False)] = rng.uniform(300_000, 500_000, 12)

mu, sigma = income.mean(), income.std()
lower, upper = mu - 3*sigma, mu + 3*sigma
z = (income - mu) / sigma
outlier = np.abs(z) > 3

print(f"\nmu {mu:,.0f}   sigma {sigma:,.0f}")
print(f"limits: [{lower:,.0f}, {upper:,.0f}]")
print(f"flagged: {outlier.sum()} rows ({outlier.mean():.2%})")

trimmed = income[~outlier]                            # TRIMMING: fast, loses rows
capped  = np.clip(income, lower, upper)               # CAPPING: keeps every row

print(f"trimming: {len(income)} -> {len(trimmed)} rows")
print(f"capping : {len(capped)} rows, {np.sum(capped != income)} values changed")
print(f"std  original {income.std():,.0f}  trimmed {trimmed.std():,.0f}  "
      f"capped {capped.std():,.0f}")

# =====================================================================
# 4. FAILURE 1 -- THE NORMALITY ASSUMPTION
# =====================================================================
skewed = rng.lognormal(3, 0.9, 5000)
m, s = skewed.mean(), skewed.std()
print(f"\nSKEWED column, skew = {stats.skew(skewed):.2f}")
print(f"  mu-3sigma = {m-3*s:8.1f}   but the minimum is {skewed.min():.1f} "
      f"-> flags NOTHING on the left")
print(f"  mu+3sigma = {m+3*s:8.1f}   flags {np.mean(skewed > m+3*s):.2%} "
      f"-- ALL on one side")
_, p = stats.normaltest(skewed)
print(f"  normality test p = {p:.2e} -> the assumption is violated; use IQR (Topic 29)")

# The correct move: transform FIRST, then apply the rule
logged = np.log(skewed)
zl = (logged - logged.mean()) / logged.std()
print(f"  after log transform: skew {stats.skew(logged):+.2f}, "
      f"flagged {np.mean(np.abs(zl) > 3):.2%} -- now symmetric")

# =====================================================================
# 5. FAILURE 2 -- MASKING
# =====================================================================
base = rng.normal(50, 5, 300)
print(f"\n{'planted':>8s} {'sigma':>8s} {'flagged':>8s}")
for k in [0, 1, 3, 10, 30]:
    dd = np.r_[base, [400.0]*k] if k else base
    zz = (dd - dd.mean()) / dd.std()
    print(f"{k:8d} {dd.std():8.1f} {np.sum(np.abs(zz)>3):8d}")
# 1 planted outlier is caught. 30 planted outliers inflate sigma so much
# that NONE of them is caught. They mask each other.

# =====================================================================
# 6. THE ROBUST Z-SCORE -- immune to masking
# =====================================================================
def robust_z(a):
    med = np.median(a)
    mad = np.median(np.abs(a - med))
    return 0.6745 * (a - med) / (mad + 1e-12)   # 0.6745 = Phi^-1(0.75)

for k in [0, 1, 3, 10, 30]:
    dd = np.r_[base, [400.0]*k] if k else base
    print(f"planted {k:3d}: classic z flags {np.sum(np.abs((dd-dd.mean())/dd.std())>3):3d}, "
          f"robust z flags {np.sum(np.abs(robust_z(dd))>3):3d}")
# The robust version catches all of them, every time.

# =====================================================================
# 7. AS A PIPELINE TRANSFORMER, FITTED ON TRAIN ONLY
# =====================================================================
class ZScoreCapper(BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin):
    """Cap at mu +/- k*sigma. Boundaries are LEARNED from training data."""
    def __init__(self, k=3.0, robust=False):
        self.k, self.robust = k, robust

    def fit(self, X, y=None):
        X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
        if self.robust:
            centre = np.nanmedian(X, axis=0)
            spread = np.nanmedian(np.abs(X - centre), axis=0) / 0.6745
        else:
            centre = np.nanmean(X, axis=0)
            spread = np.nanstd(X, axis=0)
        self.lower_ = centre - self.k * spread
        self.upper_ = centre + self.k * spread
        return self

    def transform(self, X):
        return np.clip(np.asarray(X, dtype=float), self.lower_, self.upper_)

    def get_feature_names_out(self, input_features=None):
        return np.asarray(input_features, dtype=object)

X = np.c_[income, rng.normal(35, 8, 5000)]
y = (0.00003 * income + rng.normal(0, 1, 5000) > 2).astype(int)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.25, random_state=0)

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
for name, steps in [
    ("no capping", [("sc", StandardScaler())]),
    ("z-score cap", [("cap", ZScoreCapper(3.0)), ("sc", StandardScaler())]),
    ("robust cap",  [("cap", ZScoreCapper(3.0, robust=True)), ("sc", StandardScaler())]),
]:
    pipe = Pipeline(steps + [("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))])
    print(f"{name:12s} cv auc "
          f"{cross_val_score(pipe, X_tr, y_tr, cv=5, scoring='roc_auc').mean():.4f}")

capper = ZScoreCapper(3.0).fit(X_tr)
print("\nboundaries learned from TRAIN:", capper.upper_.round(0))
# These SAME numbers are applied to test and to production. Recomputing them
# on test would give the two sets different definitions of "outlier".

# =====================================================================
# 8. CHECK BEFORE YOU DELETE: are the outliers the TARGET?
# =====================================================================
print("\ntarget rate | normal rows :", y[~outlier].mean().round(3))
print("target rate | outlier rows:", y[outlier].mean().round(3))
# If the second number is much higher, you are looking at an anomaly-detection
# problem and removing the outliers deletes every positive case.

q.q: Should you always remove outliers?
q.a:
No. First decide whether the point is a data error, a genuine rare event, or a
different population. Errors get fixed or removed; genuine rare events are often
the signal — in fraud or defect detection they are the entire target; different
populations should be segmented, not deleted.

q.q: Why are linear models so much more sensitive than trees?
q.a:
Squared loss weights a point by its residual, so influence grows without bound
and least squares has a breakdown point of zero. A tree only asks whether a value
falls above or below a threshold, so an extreme value is simply "large".

q.q: Trimming or capping?
q.a:
Capping is usually better: it keeps the row, and therefore all the other
columns' good values, while bounding the influence. Trimming is faster but
reduces the data size, and on a wide dataset the row loss compounds. Trim when
the value is genuinely an error.

q.q: What is masking?
q.a:
Outliers hiding each other. $\mu$ and $\sigma$ are computed from data that
includes them, so a cluster of extreme points inflates $\sigma$, widening the
$3\sigma$ boundary until those same points fall inside it. Use the robust
Z-score — median and MAD — which cannot be moved by up to half the data.

q.q: Your income column is right-skewed. Can you use the Z-score rule?
q.a:
Not directly. The rule assumes normality; on skewed data $\mu-3\sigma$ can fall
below the minimum while $\mu+3\sigma$ flags ordinary high earners. Either
log-transform the column first and then apply the rule, or use the IQR method,
which makes no distributional assumption.

q.q: Why 3 sigma rather than 2?
q.a:
Because $|z|>2$ flags 4.6% of genuinely normal data — one row in 22, which is
an unacceptable false-positive rate for a routine cleaning step. $|z|>3$ flags
0.27%.

29.idea: The IQR method uses quartiles, which outliers cannot pull. Values beyond Q1 minus 1.5 IQR or Q3 plus 1.5 IQR are flagged. Robust for skewed data.
29.intuition: The middle half of the data defines the normal range. Points far outside that box are outliers, whatever the tails do.
29.formula: IQR = Q3 − Q1; lower fence = Q1 − 1.5 IQR; upper fence = Q3 + 1.5 IQR.
steps: Compute Q1 and Q3 (linear interpolation).
IQR = Q3 − Q1.
Lower = Q1 − 1.5 IQR; upper = Q3 + 1.5 IQR.
Flag points outside [lower, upper].
29.example: [12,13,14,15,16,17,18,95]: Q1 = 13.75, Q3 = 17.25, IQR = 3.5. Fences [8.5, 22.5]. Only 95 is flagged. The z-score (2.64) misses the same point.
pitfalls: Removing outliers may remove real rare events, like fraud.
Standard fences assume a moderately skewed distribution.
29.tip: IQR is the default choice for skewed or small data because quartiles resist outliers.
29.pit: Deleting outliers can remove real rare events (e.g. fraud).

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from scipy import stats
from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, train_test_split, GridSearchCV

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
income = np.r_[rng.lognormal(3.2, .55, 3000), [180., 205., 230., 12., 9.]]

# =====================================================================
# 1. THE RULE
# =====================================================================
q1, q3 = np.percentile(income, [25, 75])
iqr = q3 - q1
lower, upper = q1 - 1.5*iqr, q3 + 1.5*iqr

print(f"Q1 (25th pct) {q1:7.2f}")
print(f"Q3 (75th pct) {q3:7.2f}")
print(f"IQR           {iqr:7.2f}")
print(f'"minimum" Q1-1.5*IQR = {lower:7.2f}')
print(f'"maximum" Q3+1.5*IQR = {upper:7.2f}')

outlier = (income < lower) | (income > upper)
print(f"flagged: {outlier.sum()} rows ({outlier.mean():.2%})")
print(f"actual min {income.min():.2f}, max {income.max():.2f} "
      f"-- note these are NOT the fences")

# pandas, in three lines:
s = pd.Series(income)
Q1, Q3 = s.quantile([.25, .75])
mask = ~s.between(Q1 - 1.5*(Q3-Q1), Q3 + 1.5*(Q3-Q1))
print("pandas agrees:", bool((mask.values == outlier).all()))

# =====================================================================
# 2. WHERE 1.5 COMES FROM -- verified on normal data
# =====================================================================
z = rng.normal(0, 1, 500_000)
a, b = np.percentile(z, [25, 75])
print(f"\nQ1 {a:+.4f}  (theory {stats.norm.ppf(.25):+.4f})")
print(f"Q3 {b:+.4f}  (theory {stats.norm.ppf(.75):+.4f})")
print(f"IQR {b-a:.4f}  (theory 1.3490)")
print(f"upper fence {b+1.5*(b-a):.4f} sigma  (theory 2.698)")
print(f"flagged {np.mean((z<a-1.5*(b-a))|(z>b+1.5*(b-a))):.4%}  (theory 0.6977%)")

for k in [1.5, 3.0]:
    fence = 0.6745 + k*1.349
    print(f"k={k}: equivalent to {fence:.2f} sigma, "
          f"flags {2*(1-stats.norm.cdf(fence)):.6%} of normal data")

# =====================================================================
# 3. IQR vs Z-SCORE ACROSS DISTRIBUTIONS
# =====================================================================
def flags(v):
    m, sd = v.mean(), v.std()
    a, b = np.percentile(v, [25, 75]); r = b - a
    return (np.mean((v < m-3*sd) | (v > m+3*sd)),
            np.mean((v < a-1.5*r) | (v > b+1.5*r)))

print(f"\n{'distribution':22s} {'z-score':>9s} {'IQR':>9s}")
for name, v in [("normal",          rng.normal(50, 10, 20_000)),
                ("right-skewed",    rng.lognormal(3.2, .7, 20_000)),
                ("heavy-tailed t3", rng.standard_t(3, 20_000)),
                ("uniform",         rng.uniform(0, 100, 20_000)),
                ("bimodal",         np.r_[rng.normal(20,4,10_000),
                                          rng.normal(70,4,10_000)])]:
    zf, qf = flags(v)
    print(f"{name:22s} {zf:9.2%} {qf:9.2%}")
# uniform: BOTH flag 0% -- there is no tail, so neither rule fires.
# bimodal: both flag ~0% -- the rules cannot see that there are TWO populations.

# =====================================================================
# 4. MASKING -- the IQR method is immune
# =====================================================================
base = rng.normal(50, 5, 300)
print(f"\n{'planted':>8s} {'z detects':>10s} {'IQR detects':>12s}")
for k in [0, 1, 3, 10, 30, 60, 120]:
    d = np.r_[base, [400.]*k] if k else base
    m, sd = d.mean(), d.std()
    a, b = np.percentile(d, [25, 75]); r = b - a
    zc = int(np.sum(np.abs(d-m) > 3*sd))
    qc = int(np.sum((d < a-1.5*r) | (d > b+1.5*r)))
    print(f"{k:8d} {zc:10d} {qc:12d}")
# The IQR method finds all of them until they reach ~25% of the data --
# its breakdown point. The z-score method collapses almost immediately.

# =====================================================================
# 5. TRIMMING vs CAPPING
# =====================================================================
trimmed = income[~outlier]
capped  = np.clip(income, lower, upper)
print(f"\ntrimming: {len(income)} -> {len(trimmed)} rows")
print(f"capping : {len(capped)} rows, {int((capped != income).sum())} values changed")
print(f"std   original {income.std():.2f}  trimmed {trimmed.std():.2f}  "
      f"capped {capped.std():.2f}")
print(f"skew  original {stats.skew(income):+.2f}  capped {stats.skew(capped):+.2f}")

# =====================================================================
# 6. THE WEAKNESS -- symmetric fences on an asymmetric column
# =====================================================================
skewed = rng.lognormal(3.5, 1.0, 10_000)
a, b = np.percentile(skewed, [25, 75]); r = b - a
lo, hi = a - 1.5*r, b + 1.5*r
print(f"\nstrongly skewed (skew {stats.skew(skewed):.1f}):")
print(f"  lower fence {lo:8.2f}  vs minimum {skewed.min():8.2f} "
      f"-> flags {np.mean(skewed<lo):.2%} on the left")
print(f"  upper fence {hi:8.2f}  vs maximum {skewed.max():8.2f} "
      f"-> flags {np.mean(skewed>hi):.2%} on the right")

# THE FIX: transform first, then apply the rule
lg = np.log(skewed)
a2, b2 = np.percentile(lg, [25, 75]); r2 = b2 - a2
print(f"  after log: skew {stats.skew(lg):+.2f}, "
      f"flags {np.mean((lg<a2-1.5*r2)|(lg>b2+1.5*r2)):.2%} -- balanced")

# =====================================================================
# 7. IT IS UNIVARIATE -- a multivariate outlier slips through
# =====================================================================
h = rng.normal(170, 8, 2000)                  # height cm
w = 0.9*(h-100) + rng.normal(0, 5, 2000)      # weight kg, correlated
h = np.r_[h, [150.]]; w = np.r_[w, [120.]]    # short AND heavy -> impossible pair

for name, v in [("height", h), ("weight", w)]:
    a, b = np.percentile(v, [25, 75]); r = b - a
    flagged = (v[-1] < a-1.5*r) or (v[-1] > b+1.5*r)
    print(f"\n{name}: last point {v[-1]:.0f}, fences "
          f"[{a-1.5*r:.0f}, {b+1.5*r:.0f}] -> flagged: {flagged}")
# Neither column flags it. But jointly it is absurd:
iso = IsolationForest(contamination=0.001, random_state=0).fit(np.c_[h, w])
print("Isolation Forest flags it:", iso.predict([[150., 120.]])[0] == -1)

# =====================================================================
# 8. AS A PIPELINE TRANSFORMER -- fences LEARNED from train
# =====================================================================
class IQRCapper(BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin):
    """Cap at Q1 - k*IQR and Q3 + k*IQR, per column."""
    def __init__(self, k=1.5):
        self.k = k

    def fit(self, X, y=None):
        X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
        q1, q3 = np.nanpercentile(X, [25, 75], axis=0)
        iqr = q3 - q1
        self.lower_, self.upper_ = q1 - self.k*iqr, q3 + self.k*iqr
        return self

    def transform(self, X):
        return np.clip(np.asarray(X, dtype=float), self.lower_, self.upper_)

    def get_feature_names_out(self, input_features=None):
        return np.asarray(input_features, dtype=object)

n = 4000
X = np.c_[np.r_[rng.lognormal(3.2, .6, n-20), rng.uniform(300, 900, 20)],
          rng.normal(35, 8, n)]
y = (0.02*np.clip(X[:, 0], 0, 120) + 0.05*X[:, 1] + rng.normal(0, 1, n) > 3.2).astype(int)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.25, random_state=0)

for name, steps in [
    ("none",       [("sc", StandardScaler())]),
    ("IQR cap 1.5",[("cap", IQRCapper(1.5)), ("sc", StandardScaler())]),
    ("IQR cap 3.0",[("cap", IQRCapper(3.0)), ("sc", StandardScaler())]),
]:
    pipe = Pipeline(steps + [("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))])
    print(f"{name:12s} cv auc "
          f"{cross_val_score(pipe, X_tr, y_tr, cv=5, scoring='roc_auc').mean():.4f}")

# k is a hyperparameter -- tune it rather than assuming 1.5
gs = GridSearchCV(Pipeline([("cap", IQRCapper()), ("sc", StandardScaler()),
                            ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))]),
                  {"cap__k": [1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0, 5.0]},
                  cv=5, scoring="roc_auc", n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print("best k:", gs.best_params_["cap__k"], round(gs.best_score_, 4))

capper = IQRCapper(1.5).fit(X_tr)
print("fences learned from TRAIN:", capper.upper_.round(2))
# Applied UNCHANGED to test and to production.

q.q: IQR or Z-score — when do you use which?
q.a:
Z-score when the column is approximately normal. IQR when it is skewed, heavy
tailed, or you do not want to assume a distribution. IQR is also immune to
masking, so it is the safer default; the Z-score rule is preferable only when
normality genuinely holds.

q.q: Where does the 1.5 come from?
q.a:
Tukey chose it so the fences sit at roughly $\mu\pm2.7\sigma$ on normal data,
flagging about 0.7%. The arithmetic: $Q_3=\mu+0.6745\sigma$ and
$IQR=1.349\sigma$, so $Q_3+1.5 IQR=\mu+2.698\sigma$. The stricter
$k=3$ fence corresponds to $\mu\pm4.7\sigma$.

q.q: Why doesn't the IQR method suffer masking?
q.a:
Because the quartiles are computed from the middle of the distribution and have a
25% breakdown point. Adding extreme values barely moves $Q_1$ and $Q_3$, so the
fences stay put. The mean and standard deviation have a 0% breakdown point, so
outliers widen the very boundary meant to catch them.

q.q:
Your income column flags 8% of rows as outliers. Is something
wrong?
q.a:
Probably not with the data — with the method. Income is strongly right-skewed,
and a symmetric fence flags a lot of genuinely ordinary high earners.
Log-transform first and re-apply, or use an adjusted box plot that scales the
fences by the skewness.

q.q:
A point is within the fences on every column. Can it still be an
outlier?
q.a:
Yes. The rule is univariate. Someone 150 cm tall weighing 120 kg is
unremarkable on each column separately but implausible jointly. Multivariate
detection needs Mahalanobis distance, Isolation Forest or Local Outlier Factor.

q.q: What does the IQR rule flag on uniformly distributed data?
q.a:
Nothing. $Q_1-1.5 IQR$ falls below the minimum and
$Q_3+1.5 IQR$ above the maximum. That is correct behaviour — a uniform
distribution has no tail — and a useful reminder that the method describes
tails, not errors.

30.t: Outliers III: Percentile Method and Winsorisation
30.idea: Percentile capping (winsorisation) replaces values beyond chosen percentiles with the percentile values, instead of deleting rows.
30.intuition: Keep the row but stop one extreme value from dominating. Cap at the 5th and 95th percentiles, for example.
steps: Choose the lower and upper percentiles (for example 5 and 95).
Compute those percentiles on training data.
Clip train and test values to the same bounds.
30.example: [1..9, 100] with P5 = 1.45 and P95 = 59.05: the 100 becomes 59.05, and the mean drops from 14.5 to 10.45.
pitfalls: Capping hides genuinely extreme but valid values.
Choosing percentiles to make a metric look better.
30.tip: Winsorise when you want to keep rows; delete only when outliers are errors.
30.pit: Capping hides genuinely extreme but valid values.

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from scipy import stats
from scipy.stats.mstats import winsorize
from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, GridSearchCV, train_test_split

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
income = np.r_[rng.lognormal(3.3, .6, 3000), rng.uniform(300, 900, 25)]

# =====================================================================
# 1. PERCENTILES -- the definitions from the notes
# =====================================================================
print("50th percentile:", np.percentile(income, 50).round(2))
print("median         :", np.median(income).round(2), " <- the same thing")
print("100th percentile:", np.percentile(income, 100).round(2))
print("maximum         :", income.max().round(2), " <- the same thing")

# "99% means 99% of people are behind me"
v99 = np.percentile(income, 99)
print(f"\n99th percentile = {v99:.2f}")
print(f"fraction of the data at or below it: {np.mean(income <= v99):.2%}")

# =====================================================================
# 2. THE PERCENTILE METHOD -- decide a min and max threshold
# =====================================================================
LOWER_PCT, UPPER_PCT = 1, 99
lo, hi = np.percentile(income, [LOWER_PCT, UPPER_PCT])
outlier = (income < lo) | (income > hi)

print(f"\nthresholds: [{lo:.2f}, {hi:.2f}]")
print(f"flagged: {outlier.sum()} rows ({outlier.mean():.2%})")
# EXACTLY 2% -- because you asked for 1% per tail. The data had no say.

# THE DISTINGUISHING PROPERTY: it flags 2% even on perfectly clean data
clean = rng.normal(50, 10, 5000)
a, b = np.percentile(clean, [1, 99])
print(f"on CLEAN normal data, percentile flags {np.mean((clean<a)|(clean>b)):.2%}")
print(f"                      z-score    flags "
      f"{np.mean(np.abs(clean-clean.mean())>3*clean.std()):.2%}")

# =====================================================================
# 3. TRIMMING vs WINSORIZATION
# =====================================================================
trimmed = income[~outlier]                       # rows DELETED
wins    = np.clip(income, lo, hi)                # rows KEPT, values capped

print(f"\n{'':14s} {'n':>6s} {'mean':>9s} {'std':>9s} {'skew':>7s} {'max':>9s}")
for name, v in [("original", income), ("trimmed", trimmed), ("winsorized", wins)]:
    print(f"{name:14s} {len(v):6d} {v.mean():9.2f} {v.std():9.2f} "
          f"{stats.skew(v):7.2f} {v.max():9.2f}")

print(f"\nvalues changed by winsorizing: {int((wins != income).sum())}")
print(f"rows sitting exactly at the cap: {int((wins == hi).sum())}  <- the spike")

# scipy has it built in (note: limits are FRACTIONS, not percents)
sp = np.asarray(winsorize(income, limits=[0.01, 0.01]))
print("matches scipy:", np.allclose(np.sort(sp), np.sort(wins)))

# pandas one-liner:
s = pd.Series(income)
print("pandas clip:", np.allclose(s.clip(*s.quantile([.01, .99])).values, wins))

# =====================================================================
# 4. THE EFFECT ON THE MEAN -- symmetric vs skewed
# =====================================================================
sym = rng.normal(100, 15, 20_000)
skw = rng.lognormal(3.3, .8, 20_000)
for name, v in [("symmetric", sym), ("skewed", skw)]:
    a, b = np.percentile(v, [1, 99])
    w = np.clip(v, a, b)
    print(f"{name:10s} mean {v.mean():9.2f} -> winsorized {w.mean():9.2f}  "
          f"({(w.mean()-v.mean())/v.mean():+.2%})")
# Symmetric: the two tails cancel, the mean barely moves.
# Skewed:    the mean is pulled DOWN. You have deliberately biased it.

# =====================================================================
# 5. ASYMMETRIC THRESHOLDS -- usually the correct choice
# =====================================================================
# income has a natural floor; there is no meaningful left tail to cap
lo_sym, hi_sym = np.percentile(income, [1, 99])
lo_asym, hi_asym = income.min(), np.percentile(income, 99)
print(f"\nsymmetric 1/99 removes {np.mean(income < lo_sym):.2%} from the left "
      f"-- real low incomes, deleted for no reason")
print(f"asymmetric 0/99 removes 0% from the left, "
      f"{np.mean(income > hi_asym):.2%} from the right")

# =====================================================================
# 6. ALL FOUR TECHNIQUES ON THE SAME COLUMN
# =====================================================================
m, sd = income.mean(), income.std()
q1, q3 = np.percentile(income, [25, 75]); iqr = q3 - q1
techniques = {
    "z-score 3sigma": (m - 3*sd,          m + 3*sd),
    "IQR 1.5":        (q1 - 1.5*iqr,      q3 + 1.5*iqr),
    "percentile 1-99":  tuple(np.percentile(income, [1, 99])),
    "percentile 5-95":  tuple(np.percentile(income, [5, 95])),
}
print(f"\n{'technique':18s} {'lower':>9s} {'upper':>9s} {'flagged':>9s}")
for name, (a, b) in techniques.items():
    print(f"{name:18s} {a:9.2f} {b:9.2f} {np.mean((income<a)|(income>b)):9.2%}")

# =====================================================================
# 7. AS A PIPELINE TRANSFORMER, WITH THE THRESHOLD TUNED
# =====================================================================
class PercentileCapper(BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin):
    """Winsorize at the given percentiles. Thresholds LEARNED from train."""
    def __init__(self, lower=1.0, upper=99.0):
        self.lower, self.upper = lower, upper

    def fit(self, X, y=None):
        X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
        self.lower_ = np.nanpercentile(X, self.lower, axis=0)
        self.upper_ = np.nanpercentile(X, self.upper, axis=0)
        return self

    def transform(self, X):
        return np.clip(np.asarray(X, dtype=float), self.lower_, self.upper_)

    def get_feature_names_out(self, input_features=None):
        return np.asarray(input_features, dtype=object)

n = 4000
X = np.c_[np.r_[rng.lognormal(3.2, .6, n-25), rng.uniform(300, 900, 25)],
          rng.normal(35, 8, n)]
y = (0.03*np.clip(X[:, 0], 0, 90) + 0.05*X[:, 1] + rng.normal(0, 1, n) > 3.4).astype(int)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.25, random_state=0)

for name, steps in [
    ("none",           [("sc", StandardScaler())]),
    ("winsorize 1/99", [("cap", PercentileCapper(1, 99)),  ("sc", StandardScaler())]),
    ("winsorize 5/95", [("cap", PercentileCapper(5, 95)),  ("sc", StandardScaler())]),
    ("right tail only",[("cap", PercentileCapper(0, 99)),  ("sc", StandardScaler())]),
]:
    pipe = Pipeline(steps + [("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))])
    print(f"{name:17s} cv auc "
          f"{cross_val_score(pipe, X_tr, y_tr, cv=5, scoring='roc_auc').mean():.4f}")

# The threshold is a hyperparameter -- let the data choose it
gs = GridSearchCV(
    Pipeline([("cap", PercentileCapper()), ("sc", StandardScaler()),
              ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))]),
    {"cap__lower": [0, 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5], "cap__upper": [95, 97.5, 99, 99.5, 100]},
    cv=5, scoring="roc_auc", n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print("\nbest thresholds:", gs.best_params_, round(gs.best_score_, 4))

capper = PercentileCapper(1, 99).fit(X_tr)
print("thresholds learned from TRAIN:", capper.upper_.round(2))
# Applied UNCHANGED to test and to production. A test value above the
# training 99th percentile is capped to the TRAINING threshold -- correct,
# because that is the boundary the model was fitted under.

q.q: What is winsorization?
q.a:
Capping using percentiles: values below the $p$th percentile are set to the $p$th
percentile and values above the $(100-p)$th are set to that. It keeps every row,
unlike trimming, and bounds the influence of extreme values while preserving the
ordering.

q.q: How does the percentile method differ from the IQR method?
q.a:
The IQR method derives its boundaries from the data's own spread, so the number
of flagged rows depends on the distribution. The percentile method fixes the
flagged fraction in advance — 1% per tail means exactly 1% per tail, always.
That makes it distribution-free but also means it flags rows even when the data
is clean.

q.q: When is winsorization the wrong choice?
q.a:
When the extreme values are the signal — fraud, defects, catastrophic claims —
and when the target's total matters. Capping claim amounts at the 99th percentile
and then forecasting total payouts systematically under-forecasts, because the
tail is where the money is.

q.q: Should you always cap both tails equally?
q.a:
No. For a variable with a natural floor — income, price, duration, counts —
there is no meaningful left tail, and capping at the 1st percentile deletes real
low values for no reason. Use an asymmetric threshold: 0 on the left, 99 on the
right.

q.q: How do you choose the percentile threshold?
q.a:
Treat it as a hyperparameter. Put the capper in a pipeline and grid-search the
thresholds against the downstream metric. Start from 1/99 as a default and let
cross-validation adjust it.

q.q:
Your model sees a production value above the training 99th percentile.
What happens?
q.a:
It is capped to the training threshold, because that is the fitted
parameter. This is correct — the model was estimated under that boundary — but
it means the model cannot distinguish "slightly above the cap" from "far above
the cap". If that distinction matters, keep a was_capped indicator
alongside.

31.idea: Feature construction creates new columns from existing ones using domain knowledge. Feature splitting breaks one column into several, such as a full name into first and last name.
31.intuition: A raw column often hides a useful quantity. Revenue divided by visits is more informative than either alone.
31.formula: New feature = f(existing features), chosen by domain logic.
steps: List the quantities the decision depends on.
Check which combinations of existing columns express them.
Create the feature, then test whether it improves validation score.
Drop the originals if they are now redundant.
31.example: From order_time: hour of day; from price and quantity: unit price; from name: title and surname.
pitfalls: Creating features that use the target (leakage).
Adding many weak features that only add noise.
31.tip: Justify each constructed feature with a domain reason before testing it.
