import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures, StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, train_test_split

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 3000
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "name":     rng.choice(["Mr. Ankit Sharma", "Mrs. Priya Rao",
                            "Miss. Anita Das", "Master. Arjun Rao"], n),
    "sibsp":    rng.integers(0, 5, n),
    "parch":    rng.integers(0, 4, n),
    "fare":     rng.lognormal(3.2, .7, n),
    "weight":   rng.normal(70, 12, n),
    "height_m": rng.normal(1.70, .09, n),
    "user_id":  rng.integers(0, 200, n),
    "amount":   rng.lognormal(3.0, .8, n),
})

# =====================================================================
# 1. RATIO -- a linear model CANNOT construct this for itself
# =====================================================================
df["bmi"] = df.weight / df.height_m ** 2
y_health = (df.bmi > 25).astype(int)          # the truth depends ONLY on the ratio

raw = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000),
                      df[["weight", "height_m"]], y_health, cv=5,
                      scoring="roc_auc").mean()
built = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000),
                        df[["bmi"]], y_health, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc").mean()
print(f"raw weight+height auc {raw:.4f}   constructed BMI auc {built:.4f}")

# Even a random forest struggles, because the boundary is a CURVE:
rf_raw = cross_val_score(RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, random_state=0),
                         df[["weight", "height_m"]], y_health, cv=5,
                         scoring="roc_auc").mean()
print(f"forest on raw columns auc {rf_raw:.4f} -- it approximates with a staircase")

# =====================================================================
# 2. AGGREGATE -- the Titanic family_size example
# =====================================================================
df["family_size"] = df.sibsp + df.parch + 1        # +1 for the passenger
# survival is NON-MONOTONE in family size
p = np.where((df.family_size >= 2) & (df.family_size <= 4), .70, .25)
y_surv = (rng.random(n) < p).astype(int)

print("\nsurvival rate by family size:")
print(df.assign(y=y_surv).groupby("family_size").y.agg(["mean", "size"]).round(3))

for label, cols in [("raw sibsp+parch", ["sibsp", "parch"]),
                    ("+ family_size",   ["sibsp", "parch", "family_size"])]:
    s = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000), df[cols], y_surv,
                        cv=5, scoring="roc_auc").mean()
    print(f"{label:18s} auc {s:.4f}")

# The non-monotone shape needs one more step (feature construction + binning):
df["is_alone"]         = (df.family_size == 1).astype(int)
df["is_small_family"]  = df.family_size.between(2, 4).astype(int)
df["is_large_family"]  = (df.family_size > 4).astype(int)
s = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000),
                    df[["is_alone", "is_small_family", "is_large_family"]],
                    y_surv, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc").mean()
print(f"{'+ shape encoded':18s} auc {s:.4f}")

# =====================================================================
# 3. FEATURE SPLITTING -- "Mr Ankit" into several columns
# =====================================================================
parts = df.name.str.extract(r"^(?P<title>[A-Za-z]+)\.\s+"
                            r"(?P<first>[A-Za-z]+)\s+(?P<last>[A-Za-z]+)$")
df = pd.concat([df, parts], axis=1)
print("\n", df[["name", "title", "first", "last"]].drop_duplicates().to_string(index=False))

# The title encodes SEX, AGE BAND and MARITAL STATUS at once:
title_meaning = {"Mr": "adult male", "Mrs": "married adult female",
                 "Miss": "unmarried female", "Master": "boy under ~13"}
print("\n", title_meaning)
# On the Titanic "Master" is the ONLY column identifying young boys -- and
# age is missing for 20% of passengers, so this recovers it for free.

# Surname enables family grouping -- a genuinely relational feature:
df["surname_group_size"] = df.groupby("last")["last"].transform("size")

# =====================================================================
# 4. GROUP-RELATIVE -- "unusual FOR THIS USER"
# =====================================================================
# WRONG: computed on all the data, including validation rows
df["amount_vs_user_LEAKY"] = df.amount / df.groupby("user_id").amount.transform("mean")

# RIGHT: statistics learned on TRAIN and stored for serving
class GroupRelative(BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin):
    """x / group_mean(x), with the group means LEARNED from training data."""
    def __init__(self, group_col, value_col):
        self.group_col, self.value_col = group_col, value_col

    def fit(self, X, y=None):
        self.means_ = X.groupby(self.group_col)[self.value_col].mean()
        self.global_ = X[self.value_col].mean()      # fallback for unseen groups
        return self

    def transform(self, X):
        g = X[self.group_col].map(self.means_).fillna(self.global_)
        return (X[self.value_col] / g).to_frame("ratio_to_group")

tr, te = train_test_split(df, test_size=.25, random_state=0)
gr = GroupRelative("user_id", "amount").fit(tr)
print("\ntrain ratios:", gr.transform(tr).head(3).values.ravel().round(3))
print("test  ratios:", gr.transform(te).head(3).values.ravel().round(3))
print("unseen user falls back to the global mean:",
      gr.transform(pd.DataFrame([{"user_id": 9999, "amount": 50.0}])).values.round(3))

# =====================================================================
# 5. THE FRAUD EXAMPLE -- physics as a feature
# =====================================================================
txn = pd.DataFrame({
    "user":  [1, 1, 1, 2, 2],
    "ts":    pd.to_datetime(["2026-03-01 10:00", "2026-03-01 10:06",
                             "2026-03-01 14:00", "2026-03-01 09:00",
                             "2026-03-01 11:30"]),
    "lat":   [19.07, 28.61, 19.07, 12.97, 13.08],
    "lon":   [72.87, 77.20, 72.87, 77.59, 80.27],
})
txn = txn.sort_values(["user", "ts"])
txn["dt_hours"] = txn.groupby("user").ts.diff().dt.total_seconds() / 3600
# crude great-circle distance in km
dlat = txn.groupby("user").lat.diff(); dlon = txn.groupby("user").lon.diff()
txn["dist_km"] = np.sqrt((dlat*111)**2 + (dlon*111*np.cos(np.radians(txn.lat)))**2)
txn["implied_kmh"] = txn.dist_km / txn.dt_hours.replace(0, np.nan)
txn["impossible"] = txn.implied_kmh > 900          # faster than a jet
print("\n", txn[["user", "ts", "dist_km", "dt_hours", "implied_kmh", "impossible"]]
        .round(1).to_string(index=False))
# NEITHER raw column says anything. The ratio says "this cannot have happened."

# =====================================================================
# 6. THE AUTOMATED ALTERNATIVE, AND ITS COST
# =====================================================================
base = df[["weight", "height_m", "fare", "sibsp", "parch"]]
poly = PolynomialFeatures(degree=2, include_bias=False).fit(base)
print(f"\nPolynomialFeatures: {base.shape[1]} columns -> "
      f"{len(poly.get_feature_names_out())} columns")
print("but it generates PRODUCTS, never RATIOS:",
      [c for c in poly.get_feature_names_out() if "/" in c] or "none")
# BMI = weight / height^2 is simply not in the space it searches.

# =====================================================================
# 7. THE WHOLE THING AS A PIPELINE-SAFE TRANSFORMER
# =====================================================================
class FeatureConstructor(BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin):
    """Domain features. Stateless here, so fit() has nothing to learn."""
    def fit(self, X, y=None):
        return self

    def transform(self, X):
        X = X.copy()
        X["bmi"]             = X.weight / X.height_m ** 2
        X["family_size"]     = X.sibsp + X.parch + 1
        X["is_alone"]        = (X.family_size == 1).astype(int)
        X["is_small_family"] = X.family_size.between(2, 4).astype(int)
        X["fare_per_person"] = X.fare / X.family_size
        X["title"]           = X.name.str.extract(r"^([A-Za-z]+)\.")[0]
        return X.drop(columns=["name"])

    def get_feature_names_out(self, input_features=None):
        return np.array(["sibsp", "parch", "fare", "weight", "height_m",
                         "user_id", "amount", "bmi", "family_size", "is_alone",
                         "is_small_family", "fare_per_person", "title"])

cols = ["name", "sibsp", "parch", "fare", "weight", "height_m", "user_id", "amount"]
pipe = Pipeline([
    ("construct", FeatureConstructor()),
    ("prep", ColumnTransformer([
        ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), ["title"]),
        ("num", StandardScaler(), ["bmi", "family_size", "fare_per_person",
                                   "is_alone", "is_small_family", "fare"]),
    ], remainder="drop")),
    ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)),
])
print("\nfull pipeline auc:",
      cross_val_score(pipe, df[cols], y_surv, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc").mean().round(4))
# Construction lives INSIDE the pipeline, so production applies the identical
# derivations -- no chance of computing family_size differently at serve time.

q.q: Give an example of a constructed feature that beat the raw columns.
q.a:
BMI. Neither weight nor height predicts obesity well on its own — a heavy person
may simply be tall. The ratio $weight/height^2$ is what medicine
actually uses, and a linear model cannot form it because a ratio is not in its
hypothesis space.

q.q: Can't a gradient-boosted tree just learn the interaction itself?
q.a:
Only approximately, and expensively. A ratio boundary $x_1/x_2 = c$ is a diagonal
line, which axis-aligned splits approximate as a staircase — many splits, and
many data points to justify each one. Handing the model the ratio directly costs
one column.

q.q:
Why is family_size better than sibsp and parch
separately?
q.a:
Because survival depends on the total, and the dependence is non-monotone: solo
travellers and large families both fared badly, small families well. Neither raw
column shows that. Adding a binary is_small_family on top encodes the
shape a linear model otherwise cannot express.

q.q: What does splitting a passenger name give you?
q.a:
The title — Mr, Mrs, Miss, Master — which encodes sex, marital status and age
band at once. On the Titanic, "Master" identifies boys under about thirteen,
which is genuinely useful when age is missing for a fifth of the passengers.
The surname additionally enables family grouping.

q.q: How do group-relative features leak, and how do you prevent it?
q.a:
The group mean is computed from data that includes the row being encoded, and, if
computed on the full dataset, indirectly from validation rows. Compute group
statistics on the training set only, store them for serving with a global-mean
fallback for unseen groups, and for temporal problems use a window that ends
strictly before the prediction timestamp.

q.q: Why not just use PolynomialFeatures and let the model choose?
q.a:
It generates products and powers, never ratios, so it misses the most productive
pattern. It also produces $O(p^2)$ columns, most of them meaningless, which costs
compute and invites overfitting through multiple testing. Domain knowledge
produces the right candidate without searching thousands of wrong ones.

32.t: Curse of Dimensionality and Feature Extraction
32.idea: As the number of features grows, data becomes sparse and distances lose meaning. More dimensions need exponentially more data. The remedy is dimensionality reduction: selection (keep some features) or extraction (build new ones).
32.intuition: A line of 100 points is dense; a square needs 100 points per side; a 100-D cube is almost empty. The space grows faster than the data.
32.formula: Fraction of a unit cube inside the central region [0.1, 0.9]^d = 0.8^d: 0.64 at d = 2, 0.107 at d = 10, 2×10⁻¹⁰ at d = 100.
steps: Notice poor performance as features grow.
Try feature selection first (domain knowledge, univariate tests, model importance).
If that does not help, use extraction (PCA, LDA, t-SNE for visualisation).
Compare validation scores before and after.
32.example: In 100 dimensions 99.999...% of uniform random points lie in the outer shell, so nearest neighbours are almost as far as any other point.
pitfalls: Adding features without adding data makes models worse.
Distance-based methods (KNN, K-means) suffer most.
32.tip: Give the 0.8^d example; it makes the curse concrete.
32.pit: Adding features without adding data makes models worse.

import numpy as np, time
from scipy.special import gammaln
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression, LassoCV
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.discriminant_analysis import LinearDiscriminantAnalysis
from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest, mutual_info_classif
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# =====================================================================
# 1. SPARSITY -- the sample size needed grows EXPONENTIALLY
# =====================================================================
print(f"{'d':>4s} {'cells (10 bins)':>18s} {'points/cell, n=1e6':>20s}")
for d in [1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20]:
    cells = 10.0 ** d
    print(f"{d:4d} {cells:18.2e} {1e6/cells:20.2e}")

# To keep 10 points per cell you would need n = 10 * 10^d rows:
for d in [5, 10, 20]:
    print(f"d={d:2d} needs n = {10 * 10.0**d:.1e} rows for 10 points per cell")

# =====================================================================
# 2. THE HYPERCUBE IS ALMOST ALL CORNER
# =====================================================================
def ball_fraction(d):
    """Volume of the inscribed unit ball / volume of the unit cube."""
    return np.exp(d/2*np.log(np.pi) - gammaln(d/2 + 1) - d*np.log(2))

print(f"\n{'d':>4s} {'ball / cube':>14s} {'in the corners':>16s}")
for d in [2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 50]:
    f = ball_fraction(d)
    print(f"{d:4d} {f:14.6f} {1-f:15.4%}")
# At d=10, 99.75% of the volume is in the corners. There is no "middle".

# =====================================================================
# 3. DISTANCE CONCENTRATION -- nearest stops meaning near
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'d':>5s} {'d_min':>8s} {'d_max':>8s} {'min/max':>9s} {'sd/mean':>9s}")
for d in [1, 2, 5, 10, 50, 100, 500, 1000]:
    X = rng.uniform(0, 1, (1000, d))
    q = rng.uniform(0, 1, (1, d))
    dist = np.sqrt(((X - q) ** 2).sum(axis=1))
    print(f"{d:5d} {dist.min():8.3f} {dist.max():8.3f} "
          f"{dist.min()/dist.max():9.3f} {dist.std()/dist.mean():9.4f}")
# min/max -> 1.0 and sd/mean -> 0: every point is the same distance away.

# =====================================================================
# 4. IT IS THE IRRELEVANT DIMENSIONS THAT DO THE DAMAGE
# =====================================================================
n = 500
signal = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, 3))
y = (signal[:, 0] + .7*signal[:, 1] - .5*signal[:, 2] + rng.normal(0, .4, n) > 0).astype(int)

print(f"\n{'total features':>15s} {'KNN':>8s} {'LogReg':>8s} {'Forest':>8s}")
for d in [3, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 300, 800]:
    X = np.c_[signal, rng.normal(0, 1, (n, max(d-3, 0)))]      # noise columns
    k = cross_val_score(KNeighborsClassifier(5), X, y, cv=5).mean()
    l = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=800), X, y, cv=5).mean()
    f = cross_val_score(RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100,
                                               random_state=0), X, y, cv=5).mean()
    print(f"{d:15d} {k:8.3f} {l:8.3f} {f:8.3f}")
# The SIGNAL is unchanged throughout -- only noise columns were added.
# KNN collapses fastest (distance-based). Forests resist best (they select).

# =====================================================================
# 5. n < d -- the design matrix becomes singular
# =====================================================================
for n_, d_ in [(200, 50), (200, 200), (200, 500)]:
    X = rng.normal(0, 1, (n_, d_))
    print(f"n={n_:4d} d={d_:4d}  rank {np.linalg.matrix_rank(X):4d}  "
          f"cond(X'X) {np.linalg.cond(X.T @ X):.2e}")
# Once d >= n the matrix is rank-deficient: infinitely many perfect fits,
# none of which generalise. Regularisation (Topics 41-43) is mandatory.

# =====================================================================
# 6. THE SOLUTION -- selection vs extraction, measured
# =====================================================================
X = np.c_[signal, rng.normal(0, 1, (n, 297))]        # 300 features, 3 real
base = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=800))
print(f"\nall 300 features         : "
      f"{cross_val_score(base, X, y, cv=5).mean():.3f}")

sel = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                    SelectKBest(mutual_info_classif, k=5),
                    LogisticRegression(max_iter=800))
print(f"selection, k=5           : {cross_val_score(sel, X, y, cv=5).mean():.3f}")

chosen = SelectKBest(mutual_info_classif, k=5).fit(X, y).get_support(indices=True)
print(f"  columns kept: {chosen}  (the true signal is 0,1,2)")

# FEATURE EXTRACTION -- builds NEW columns
ext = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), PCA(n_components=5),
                    LogisticRegression(max_iter=800))
print(f"PCA, 5 components        : {cross_val_score(ext, X, y, cv=5).mean():.3f}")

# LDA is SUPERVISED, and capped at C-1 components
lda = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LinearDiscriminantAnalysis(n_components=1),
                    LogisticRegression(max_iter=800))
print(f"LDA, 1 component (C-1=1) : {cross_val_score(lda, X, y, cv=5).mean():.3f}")

# EMBEDDED selection -- Lasso drives irrelevant coefficients to exactly zero
las = LassoCV(cv=5, random_state=0).fit(StandardScaler().fit_transform(X), y)
print(f"Lasso kept {np.sum(las.coef_ != 0)} of {X.shape[1]} features; "
      f"the true 3 are among them: {set(range(3)) <= set(np.flatnonzero(las.coef_))}")

# NOTE: unsupervised PCA can discard the signal, because maximum variance
# is not the same as maximum relevance. That is exactly what LDA fixes.

# =====================================================================
# 7. COMPUTATION INCREASES -- the notes' other claim
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'d':>6s} {'KNN fit+predict':>18s} {'LogReg fit':>13s}")
for d in [10, 100, 1000, 3000]:
    X_ = rng.normal(0, 1, (3000, d)); y_ = rng.integers(0, 2, 3000)
    t = time.perf_counter()
    KNeighborsClassifier(5).fit(X_[:2000], y_[:2000]).predict(X_[2000:])
    tk = time.perf_counter() - t
    t = time.perf_counter()
    LogisticRegression(max_iter=200).fit(X_, y_)
    tl = time.perf_counter() - t
    print(f"{d:6d} {tk:17.3f}s {tl:12.3f}s")

# =====================================================================
# 8. THE MANIFOLD HYPOTHESIS -- why reduction works in practice
# =====================================================================
t = rng.uniform(0, 2*np.pi, 2000)                     # ONE intrinsic dimension
X_manifold = np.c_[np.cos(t), np.sin(t), 0.5*np.cos(2*t)]

X_manifold += rng.normal(0, .01, X_manifold.shape)

cum = np.cumsum(p.explained_variance_ratio_)
print(f"\nnominal dimensions: {X_manifold.shape[1]}")
print(f"components for 95% variance: {np.searchsorted(cum, .95) + 1}")
print(f"components for 99% variance: {np.searchsorted(cum, .99) + 1}")

q.q: What is the curse of dimensionality?
q.a:
As the number of features grows, the volume of the space grows exponentially, so
a fixed sample becomes exponentially sparse. Distances concentrate — every point
becomes roughly equidistant from every other — and the number of parameters to
estimate grows while the evidence per parameter shrinks. Past an optimum, adding
features makes the model worse.

q.q: Why does it hurt KNN more than a random forest?
q.a:
KNN's entire mechanism is distance, and distance concentration destroys it
directly: with 300 features of which three matter, the 297 irrelevant ones drown
the signal in every distance computation. A forest evaluates one feature at a
time and effectively performs selection, so irrelevant columns are largely
ignored.

q.q: If more information is better, how can adding a feature hurt?
q.a:
Because the model estimates from a finite sample. An extra dimension spreads the
same rows over an exponentially larger space, so the evidence supporting any
estimate collapses. The information exists; the sample is too small to exploit
it, and the extra parameter adds variance.

q.q: Feature selection or feature extraction?
q.a:
Selection when you must explain the model — the surviving columns are still
"age" and "income". Extraction when you want maximum compression and can
tolerate synthetic components. Selection discards whatever information the
dropped columns held; extraction combines information from all of them.

q.q: Why might PCA hurt a supervised model?
q.a:
Because PCA is unsupervised: it maximises variance, and the direction of greatest
variance need not be the direction that separates the classes. A low-variance
component can carry all the signal and be discarded. LDA fixes this by maximising
class separation instead — but is limited to $C-1$ components.

q.q: MNIST images have 784 pixels. Is that 784 real dimensions?
q.a:
No. Digits lie on a low-dimensional manifold inside pixel space — adjacent
pixels are highly correlated and almost every point in the space is noise rather
than a digit. PCA retains 95% of the variance in roughly 150 components. This
manifold structure is why dimensionality reduction works in practice despite the
worst-case theory.

33.intuition: A photographer shooting a 3D stadium chooses the angle that shows the most spread. PCA chooses the angle where the data spreads out most.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA, KernelPCA
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.discriminant_analysis import LinearDiscriminantAnalysis
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, GridSearchCV, train_test_split

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# =====================================================================
# 1. PCA FROM SCRATCH -- the four steps of the derivation
# =====================================================================
n, p = 500, 4
latent = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, 2))
X = latent @ rng.normal(0, 1, (2, p)) + rng.normal(0, .35, (n, p))

# STEP 1: centre
mean = X.mean(axis=0)
Xc = X - mean

# STEP 2: covariance matrix  Sigma = (1/n) Xc' Xc
Sigma = (Xc.T @ Xc) / n
print("covariance is symmetric:", np.allclose(Sigma, Sigma.T))
print("matches numpy:", np.allclose(Sigma, np.cov(Xc, rowvar=False, bias=True)))

# STEP 3: eigendecomposition  Sigma u = lambda u
eigvals, eigvecs = np.linalg.eigh(Sigma)          # eigh: symmetric matrices
order = np.argsort(eigvals)[::-1]                 # descending
eigvals, eigvecs = eigvals[order], eigvecs[:, order]

print("\neigenvalues:", eigvals.round(4))
print("explained variance ratio:", (eigvals / eigvals.sum()).round(4))
print("sum of eigenvalues:", eigvals.sum().round(4),
      " == trace(Sigma):", np.trace(Sigma).round(4))   # variance is PRESERVED

# The variance along an eigenvector IS its eigenvalue -- verify it:
for k in range(2):
    u = eigvecs[:, k]
    print(f"  PC{k+1}: var(Xc @ u) = {np.var(Xc @ u):.6f}   lambda = {eigvals[k]:.6f}")

# Orthogonality comes FREE from the spectral theorem:
print("\nPCs are orthogonal:", np.allclose(eigvecs.T @ eigvecs, np.eye(p)))
print("PC1 . PC2 =", float(eigvecs[:, 0] @ eigvecs[:, 1]).__round__(12))

# STEP 4: project
k = 2
W = eigvecs[:, :k]
Z = Xc @ W
print("\nreduced shape:", Z.shape)

# =====================================================================
# 2. MATCHES SKLEARN
# =====================================================================
sk = PCA(n_components=k).fit(X)
print("\nsklearn explained variance ratio:", sk.explained_variance_ratio_.round(4))
print("scratch                          :", (eigvals[:k]/eigvals.sum()).round(4))
# components may differ by an overall SIGN -- that is not an error, an
# eigenvector is only defined up to sign.
for j in range(k):
    same = (np.allclose(sk.components_[j],  W[:, j], atol=1e-6) or
            np.allclose(sk.components_[j], -W[:, j], atol=1e-6))
    print(f"  component {j+1} matches (up to sign): {same}")

# =====================================================================
# 3. THE SVD ROUTE -- what libraries actually compute
# =====================================================================
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(Xc, full_matrices=False)
print("\nlambda from SVD:", (S**2 / n)[:k].round(6))
print("lambda from eig:", eigvals[:k].round(6))
print("V matches eigenvectors (up to sign):",
      all(np.allclose(np.abs(Vt[j]), np.abs(eigvecs[:, j]), atol=1e-6)
          for j in range(k)))
# SVD avoids forming Xc'Xc, which would SQUARE the condition number.
print(f"cond(Xc) = {np.linalg.cond(Xc):.2e},  "
      f"cond(Xc'Xc) = {np.linalg.cond(Xc.T @ Xc):.2e}")

# =====================================================================
# 4. RECONSTRUCTION -- max variance == min squared error
# =====================================================================
X_hat = Z @ W.T + mean
err = ((X - X_hat) ** 2).sum()
print(f"\nreconstruction error {err:.4f}")
print(f"n * sum of DISCARDED eigenvalues {n * eigvals[k:].sum():.4f}")   # identical

for kk in range(1, p + 1):
    Wk = eigvecs[:, :kk]
    e = (((Xc - Xc @ Wk @ Wk.T) ** 2).sum())
    print(f"  k={kk}: retained {eigvals[:kk].sum()/eigvals.sum():6.2%}, error {e:9.4f}")

# =====================================================================
# 5. SCALING IS MANDATORY
# =====================================================================
age    = rng.normal(40, 10, 500)
salary = rng.normal(60_000, 15_000, 500) + (age - 40) * 900
raw = np.c_[age, salary]

pu = PCA().fit(raw)
ps = PCA().fit(StandardScaler().fit_transform(raw))
print(f"\nunscaled PC1 explains {pu.explained_variance_ratio_[0]:.4%}, "
      f"loadings {np.abs(pu.components_[0]).round(4)}")
print(f"scaled   PC1 explains {ps.explained_variance_ratio_[0]:.4%}, "
      f"loadings {np.abs(ps.components_[0]).round(4)}")
# Unscaled, PC1 IS the salary axis -- age's loading is ~0.0000.
print("column variances:", raw.var(axis=0).round(1))   # 1e2 vs 1e8

# =====================================================================
# 6. CHOOSING k
# =====================================================================
Xh = rng.normal(0, 1, (600, 5)) @ rng.normal(0, 1, (5, 40)) + rng.normal(0, .45, (600, 40))
Xh = StandardScaler().fit_transform(Xh)
full = PCA().fit(Xh)
cum = np.cumsum(full.explained_variance_ratio_)
for lvl in [.90, .95, .99]:
    print(f"{lvl:.0%} of variance needs {np.searchsorted(cum, lvl)+1} of 40 components")

# Kaiser criterion on standardised data: keep lambda > 1
print("Kaiser (lambda > 1):", int((full.explained_variance_ > 1).sum()), "components")

# Or let sklearn hit a variance target directly:
print("PCA(n_components=0.95) picks:",
      PCA(n_components=0.95).fit(Xh).n_components_)

# =====================================================================
# 7. IT IS UNSUPERVISED -- variance is NOT relevance
# =====================================================================
n2 = 800
signal = rng.normal(0, 1, n2)                    # LOW variance, ALL the signal
noise  = rng.normal(0, 12, (n2, 9))              # HIGH variance, no signal
X2 = np.c_[signal, noise]
y2 = (signal > 0).astype(int)

base = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=800), X2, y2, cv=5).mean()
pca1 = cross_val_score(make_pipeline(PCA(n_components=1),
                                     LogisticRegression(max_iter=800)),
                       X2, y2, cv=5).mean()
lda1 = cross_val_score(make_pipeline(LinearDiscriminantAnalysis(n_components=1),
                                     LogisticRegression(max_iter=800)),
                       X2, y2, cv=5).mean()
print(f"\nall 10 features {base:.3f} | PCA 1 comp {pca1:.3f} | LDA 1 comp {lda1:.3f}")
# PCA throws the signal away: the informative direction has the SMALLEST
# variance. LDA, which uses the labels, keeps it. This is PCA's core limitation.

# =====================================================================
# 8. IT IS LINEAR -- a rotation cannot unroll a circle
# =====================================================================
t = rng.uniform(0, 2*np.pi, 600)
r = np.r_[rng.normal(1, .08, 300), rng.normal(3, .08, 300)]
circles = np.c_[r*np.cos(t), r*np.sin(t)]
y3 = (r > 2).astype(int)

lin = cross_val_score(make_pipeline(PCA(n_components=1),
                                    LogisticRegression()), circles, y3, cv=5).mean()
ker = cross_val_score(make_pipeline(KernelPCA(n_components=1, kernel="rbf", gamma=1.0),
                                    LogisticRegression()), circles, y3, cv=5).mean()
print(f"\nconcentric circles: PCA {lin:.3f}   KernelPCA(rbf) {ker:.3f}")

# =====================================================================
# 9. IN A PIPELINE -- scale, reduce, model; k tuned by CV
# =====================================================================
y4 = (Xh[:, :3].sum(axis=1) + rng.normal(0, .8, 600) > 0).astype(int)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(Xh, y4, test_size=.25, random_state=0)

gs = GridSearchCV(
    make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), PCA(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)),
    {"pca__n_components": [2, 5, 10, 20, 30]},
    cv=5, scoring="roc_auc", n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print("\nbest k:", gs.best_params_, round(gs.best_score_, 4))
print("test auc:", round(gs.score(X_te, y_te), 4))

# The transform is FITTED -- means and eigenvectors are learned from train:
fitted = gs.best_estimator_.named_steps["pca"]
print("stored mean (first 4):", fitted.mean_[:4].round(3))
print("components shape:", fitted.components_.shape)
# Applied UNCHANGED to test and production. Never fit_transform on test.

q.q: Explain PCA in one minute.
q.a:
Centre the data, compute the covariance matrix, and take its eigenvectors. The
eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue is the direction of greatest variance —
the first principal component — and its eigenvalue is the variance it captures.
Project onto the top $k$ eigenvectors to reduce from $p$ dimensions to $k$ while
keeping as much variance as possible.

q.q: Why are the principal components orthogonal?
q.a:
Because the covariance matrix is real and symmetric, and the spectral theorem
guarantees such a matrix has an orthogonal eigenbasis. Orthogonality is not an
extra constraint imposed on the optimisation — it falls out of it.

q.q: Why must you scale before PCA?
q.a:
Because PCA maximises variance and variance carries the square of the unit.
Salary in rupees has variance around $10^8$, age in years around $10^2$, so PC1
would be the salary axis regardless of relevance — and re-expressing salary in
lakhs would change the answer.

q.q: Can PCA hurt a supervised model?
q.a:
Yes. It is unsupervised, so it maximises variance rather than class separation.
If the discriminative direction happens to have small variance — a low-variance
signal buried among high-variance noise — PCA discards exactly the component you
needed. LDA, which uses the labels, is the supervised alternative.

q.q: How do you choose the number of components?
q.a:
Cumulative explained variance against a threshold (typically 95%), the elbow of
the scree plot, the Kaiser criterion ($\lambda>1$ on standardised data), or — the
most defensible — treat $k$ as a hyperparameter and tune it against the
downstream metric by cross-validation.

q.q: Why do libraries use SVD rather than eigendecomposition?
q.a:
Forming $X^{\top}X$ squares the condition number, losing about half the
available precision, and building a $p\times p$ matrix is wasteful when $p\gg n$.
The SVD of $X$ gives the same eigenvectors directly, with $\lambda_k=s_k^2/n$.

q.q: Your data lies on two concentric circles. Will PCA separate them?
q.a:
No. PCA can only rotate, and no rotation makes concentric circles linearly
separable. You need a non-linear method — kernel PCA with an RBF kernel, t-SNE,
or UMAP.

34.idea: Fit a line y = mx + c that minimises the sum of squared residuals. Ordinary least squares gives the closed-form answer.
34.intuition: Each point pulls the line vertically toward itself. Squaring the errors makes big misses count much more, and the best line balances all the pulls.
34.formula: m = Σ(x−x̄)(y−ȳ) / Σ(x−x̄)² ; c = ȳ − m x̄ ; SSE = Σ(y − ŷ)²

Compute the numerator S_xy and denominator S_xx.
Slope m = S_xy / S_xx.
Intercept c = ȳ − m x̄.
Predict with ŷ = mx + c and check residuals.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, SGDRegressor
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error, r2_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 200
cgpa = rng.uniform(5, 10, n)
pkg  = 1.9 * cgpa - 5.5 + rng.normal(0, 1.1, n)      # true m=1.9, c=-5.5

# =====================================================================
# 1. THE CLOSED FORM, DERIVED BY HAND
# =====================================================================
x_bar, y_bar = cgpa.mean(), pkg.mean()

num = np.sum((cgpa - x_bar) * (pkg - y_bar))         # covariance numerator
den = np.sum((cgpa - x_bar) ** 2)                    # variance numerator
m = num / den
c = y_bar - m * x_bar                                 # c = y_bar - m*x_bar

print(f"m = {m:.6f}   c = {c:.6f}")
print("matches sklearn:",
      np.allclose([m, c], [LinearRegression().fit(cgpa.reshape(-1,1), pkg).coef_[0],
                           LinearRegression().fit(cgpa.reshape(-1,1), pkg).intercept_]))

# The slope IS covariance over variance:
print(f"cov/var = {np.cov(cgpa, pkg, bias=True)[0,1] / np.var(cgpa):.6f}")

# And it is the correlation rescaled into the units of y per unit of x:
r = np.corrcoef(cgpa, pkg)[0, 1]
print(f"r * (sy/sx) = {r * pkg.std() / cgpa.std():.6f}")

# =====================================================================
# 2. THE LINE PASSES THROUGH THE CENTROID -- a consequence of dE/dc = 0
# =====================================================================
print(f"\npredicted at x_bar: {m*x_bar + c:.6f}   y_bar: {y_bar:.6f}")

# =====================================================================
# 3. AS A CLASS
# =====================================================================
class SimpleLinearRegression:
    def fit(self, x, y):
        x, y = np.asarray(x).ravel(), np.asarray(y).ravel()
        xb, yb = x.mean(), y.mean()
        self.m_ = np.sum((x - xb) * (y - yb)) / np.sum((x - xb) ** 2)
        self.c_ = yb - self.m_ * xb
        return self

    def predict(self, x):
        return self.m_ * np.asarray(x).ravel() + self.c_

mine = SimpleLinearRegression().fit(cgpa, pkg)
print(f"\nscratch  m {mine.m_:.6f}  c {mine.c_:.6f}")
print(f"R2 {r2_score(pkg, mine.predict(cgpa)):.4f}")

# =====================================================================
# 4. WHY SQUARED AND NOT ABSOLUTE -- differentiability
# =====================================================================
grid = np.linspace(m - 1.5, m + 1.5, 601)
sq  = [np.sum((pkg - (mm*cgpa + c))**2) for mm in grid]
ab  = [np.sum(np.abs(pkg - (mm*cgpa + c))) for mm in grid]

d_sq = np.gradient(sq, grid); d_ab = np.gradient(ab, grid)
print(f"\nsquared loss: smooth, 2nd derivative constant "
      f"({np.std(np.gradient(d_sq, grid)):.2e} variation)")
print(f"absolute loss: kinked, gradient jumps by "
      f"{np.max(np.abs(np.diff(d_ab))):.2f} at the minimum")
# Only the smooth one lets you set dE/dm = 0 and solve.

# But absolute loss is ROBUST -- add three bad points and compare:
cg2 = np.r_[cgpa, [5.2, 5.4, 5.1]]
pk2 = np.r_[pkg,  [40.,  42.,  38.]]
print(f"\nOLS slope with 3 outliers: "
      f"{np.polyfit(cg2, pk2, 1)[0]:.3f}   (true 1.9)")
from sklearn.linear_model import HuberRegressor
print(f"Huber slope with 3 outliers: "
      f"{HuberRegressor().fit(cg2.reshape(-1,1), pk2).coef_[0]:.3f}")

# =====================================================================
# 5. THE MATRIX FORM -- the same answer, and how to compute it properly
# =====================================================================
X = np.c_[np.ones(n), cgpa]                          # add the intercept column

beta_bad  = np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X) @ X.T @ pkg       # the FORMULA
beta_ok   = np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ pkg)      # solve, do not invert
beta_best = np.linalg.lstsq(X, pkg, rcond=None)[0]   # SVD -- what sklearn uses

print("\ninverse :", beta_bad.round(6))
print("solve   :", beta_ok.round(6))
print("lstsq   :", beta_best.round(6))
print(f"cond(X)     {np.linalg.cond(X):.2e}")
print(f"cond(X'X)   {np.linalg.cond(X.T @ X):.2e}   <- SQUARED, precision lost")

# =====================================================================
# 6. THE GEOMETRY -- residuals are orthogonal to the columns of X
# =====================================================================
resid = pkg - X @ beta_best
print(f"\nsum of residuals        {resid.sum():.2e}   (0 because c is fitted)")
print(f"resid . x               {(resid @ cgpa):.2e}   (orthogonal projection)")
print(f"corr(resid, fitted)     {np.corrcoef(resid, X @ beta_best)[0,1]:.2e}")

# =====================================================================
# 7. CHECKING THE ASSUMPTIONS
# =====================================================================
from scipy import stats
fitted = X @ beta_best

# linearity + homoscedasticity: look for structure in the residual plot
sl, _, rr, pv, _ = stats.linregress(fitted, np.abs(resid))
print(f"\n|resid| vs fitted slope {sl:+.4f} (p={pv:.3f}) "
      f"{'-> heteroscedastic' if pv < .05 else '-> constant variance, OK'}")

# normality of errors -- needed for p-values, not for the point estimate
print(f"residual normality p = {stats.normaltest(resid)[1]:.3f}")

# standard errors, from the same matrix
sigma2 = (resid @ resid) / (n - X.shape[1])
se = np.sqrt(np.diag(sigma2 * np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X)))
t = beta_best / se
print(f"\n{'coef':>10s} {'std err':>10s} {'t':>8s} {'p':>10s}")
for name, b_, s_, t_ in zip(["intercept", "cgpa"], beta_best, se, t):
    p_ = 2 * (1 - stats.t.cdf(abs(t_), n - X.shape[1]))
    print(f"{name:>10s} {b_:10.4f} {s_:10.4f} {t_:8.2f} {p_:10.2e}")

# =====================================================================
# 8. OLS vs GRADIENT DESCENT -- the notes' rule, measured
# =====================================================================
import time
print(f"\n{'p':>6s} {'OLS':>10s} {'SGD':>10s}")
for p in [1, 10, 100, 1000, 3000]:
    Xd = rng.normal(0, 1, (4000, p))
    yd = Xd @ rng.normal(0, 1, p) + rng.normal(0, .5, 4000)
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); LinearRegression().fit(Xd, yd); a = time.perf_counter()-t0
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); SGDRegressor(max_iter=60, tol=None).fit(Xd, yd)
    b = time.perf_counter()-t0
    print(f"{p:6d} {a:9.4f}s {b:9.4f}s")
# OLS is O(p^3): unbeatable when p is small, impractical when p is large.

q.q: Derive the slope of a simple linear regression.
q.a:
Write $E=\sum(y_i-mx_i-c)^2$. Set $\partial E/\partial c=0$ to get
$c=\bar y-m\bar x$. Substitute into $\partial E/\partial m=0$ and collect terms
to get $m=\sum(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)/\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2$ — covariance over
variance.

q.q: Why squared error rather than absolute error?
q.a:
Differentiability. The closed-form solution comes from setting derivatives to
zero, and $|d|$ is not differentiable at zero. Squared error also has a clean
statistical interpretation — it is the maximum-likelihood estimator under
Gaussian noise — at the cost of sensitivity to outliers.

q.q: When would you use gradient descent instead of the closed form?
q.a:
When the number of features is large (the closed form is $O(p^3)$), when the data
does not fit in memory or arrives as a stream, or when the loss has no closed
form at all — logistic regression and neural networks.

q.q:
What does it mean that the residuals are orthogonal to the
predictors?
q.a:
That $X\hat\beta$ is the orthogonal projection of $y$ onto the column space of
$X$ — the closest point in the space of achievable predictions. Practically: the
residuals sum to zero when an intercept is fitted, and they are uncorrelated with
every predictor. Any pattern in a residual plot means the model has missed
structure.

q.q: What is Gauss–Markov, and does it require normality?
q.a:
It states that under linearity, exogeneity, homoscedasticity and uncorrelated
errors, OLS is the Best Linear Unbiased Estimator — minimum variance among
unbiased linear estimators. It does not require normality; that is needed
only for $t$-tests, $p$-values and confidence intervals.

q.q: Your residual plot shows a funnel shape. What does that mean?
q.a:
Heteroscedasticity — the error variance grows with the fitted value. The
coefficients remain unbiased, but the standard errors are wrong, so all inference
is invalid. Fix by transforming the target (log), using weighted least squares, or
using robust standard errors.

35.idea: MAE averages absolute errors. MSE and RMSE punish large errors more. R² is the share of variance explained. Adjusted R² penalises extra features.
35.intuition: Pick the metric that matches the cost: MAE if each unit of error costs the same, RMSE if big misses are disproportionately bad, MAPE if you need percent error.
35.formula: MAE = Σ|e|/n ; MSE = Σe²/n ; RMSE = √MSE ; R² = 1 − SSE/SST ; R²_adj = 1 − (1−R²)(n−1)/(n−p−1)
steps: Compute errors e = y − ŷ.
MAE, MSE and RMSE from the errors.
SST = Σ(y − ȳ)²; R² = 1 − SSE/SST.
Adjust R² for n rows and p predictors.
pitfalls: R² never falls when you add features; use adjusted R².
MAPE breaks when any true value is zero.
35.tip: Explain why RMSE is larger than MAE: squaring weights big errors.
35.hook: R² = 1 − SSE/SST. Adjusted R² penalises extra features.
35.pit: R² always rises when you add features; use adjusted R².
35.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import (mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error,
                             r2_score, mean_absolute_percentage_error)
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.dummy import DummyRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 500
x = rng.uniform(0, 10, (n, 1))
y = 3 * x.ravel() + 5 + rng.normal(0, 2, n)
model = LinearRegression().fit(x, y)
pred = model.predict(x)

# =====================================================================
# 1. EVERY FORMULA, FROM SCRATCH
# =====================================================================
err = y - pred
mae  = np.abs(err).mean()
mse  = (err ** 2).mean()
rmse = np.sqrt(mse)
r2   = 1 - np.sum(err**2) / np.sum((y - y.mean())**2)
k    = x.shape[1]
r2a  = 1 - (1 - r2) * (n - 1) / (n - 1 - k)
mape = np.mean(np.abs(err / y)) * 100
wmape = np.sum(np.abs(err)) / np.sum(y) * 100

print(f"MAE   {mae:8.4f}   sklearn {mean_absolute_error(y, pred):8.4f}")
print(f"MSE   {mse:8.4f}   sklearn {mean_squared_error(y, pred):8.4f}")
print(f"RMSE  {rmse:8.4f}   sklearn {mean_squared_error(y, pred)**.5:8.4f}")
print(f"R2    {r2:8.4f}   sklearn {r2_score(y, pred):8.4f}")
print(f"AdjR2 {r2a:8.4f}")
print(f"MAPE  {mape:8.4f}%  sklearn "
      f"{mean_absolute_percentage_error(y, pred)*100:8.4f}%")
print(f"WMAPE {wmape:8.4f}%")

# =====================================================================
# 2. RMSE >= MAE ALWAYS -- and the ratio is a diagnostic
# =====================================================================
uniform = rng.normal(0, 2, 400)                       # all errors similar
spiky   = np.r_[rng.normal(0, .4, 396), [22., -20., 25., -24.]]  # a few huge
for name, e in [("uniform errors", uniform), ("a few huge errors", spiky)]:
    a, r = np.abs(e).mean(), np.sqrt((e**2).mean())
    print(f"{name:20s} MAE {a:6.2f}  RMSE {r:6.2f}  ratio {r/a:5.2f}")
# ratio ~1.25 = uniform;  ratio > 3 = go and look at the tail.

# =====================================================================
# 3. MAE IS ROBUST, MSE IS NOT
# =====================================================================
y_out    = y.copy();    y_out[:5] += 60               # 1% of rows corrupted
pred_out = LinearRegression().fit(x, y_out).predict(x)
print(f"\n{'':14s} {'clean':>10s} {'1% corrupted':>14s}")
print(f"{'MAE':14s} {mean_absolute_error(y, pred):10.3f} "
      f"{mean_absolute_error(y_out, pred_out):14.3f}")
print(f"{'RMSE':14s} {mean_squared_error(y, pred)**.5:10.3f} "
      f"{mean_squared_error(y_out, pred_out)**.5:14.3f}")
# RMSE roughly doubles; MAE moves far less.

# WHAT EACH ONE OPTIMISES: mean vs median
z = np.r_[rng.normal(0, 1, 300), [12.]]
grid = np.linspace(-1, 12, 2000)
print(f"\nMSE-optimal constant {grid[np.argmin([(np.mean((z-g)**2)) for g in grid])]:.3f} "
      f"(mean {z.mean():.3f})")
print(f"MAE-optimal constant {grid[np.argmin([(np.mean(np.abs(z-g))) for g in grid])]:.3f} "
      f"(median {np.median(z):.3f})")

# =====================================================================
# 4. R2 ALWAYS RISES; ADJUSTED R2 DOES NOT
# =====================================================================
m = 60
Xs = rng.normal(0, 1, (m, 3))
ys = Xs @ [2, -1, .5] + rng.normal(0, 1, m)

print(f"\n{'features':>9s} {'R2':>8s} {'AdjR2':>8s}")
for kk in [1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 40, 55]:
    Xk = np.c_[Xs, rng.normal(0, 1, (m, max(kk-3, 0)))][:, :kk]
    p_ = LinearRegression().fit(Xk, ys).predict(Xk)
    r  = r2_score(ys, p_)
    ra = 1 - (1 - r) * (m - 1) / (m - 1 - kk)
    print(f"{kk:9d} {r:8.4f} {ra:8.4f}")
# Only the first 3 features are real. R2 climbs to 1.0 (a perfect fit to
# noise); adjusted R2 peaks near 3 and then collapses.

# R2 CAN BE NEGATIVE on held-out data:
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(Xs, ys, test_size=.4, random_state=0)
bad = LinearRegression().fit(np.c_[X_tr, rng.normal(0,1,(len(X_tr),30))], y_tr)
print("\ntest R2 of an overfitted model:",
      round(r2_score(y_te, bad.predict(np.c_[X_te, rng.normal(0,1,(len(X_te),30))])), 3))
# Negative means WORSE than predicting the mean.

# =====================================================================
# 5. MAPE vs WMAPE -- the demand-forecasting case
# =====================================================================
actual = np.array([   2,    3,    1, 1000, 1200,  950])   # 3 tiny, 3 large SKUs
predic = np.array([   1,    5,    2, 1010, 1180,  960])

per_item = np.abs((actual - predic) / actual) * 100
print("\nper-item % error:", per_item.round(1))
print(f"MAPE  {per_item.mean():6.2f}%   <- dominated by the three tiny SKUs")
print(f"WMAPE {np.sum(np.abs(actual-predic))/np.sum(actual)*100:6.2f}%   "
      f"<- weighted by volume, which is what the business feels")
print(f"total units mis-forecast: {np.abs(actual-predic).sum()} of {actual.sum()}")

# MAPE IS UNDEFINED AT ZERO:
with_zero = np.array([0., 5., 10.])
print("\nMAPE with a zero actual:",
      np.mean(np.abs((with_zero - np.array([1., 5., 9.])) /
                     np.where(with_zero == 0, np.nan, with_zero))))
print("WMAPE handles it:",
      round(np.sum(np.abs(with_zero - np.array([1.,5.,9.])))/np.sum(with_zero)*100, 2), "%")

# MAPE IS ASYMMETRIC -- which teaches a model to under-forecast:
a = np.array([100.])
print(f"\nover-forecast by 50:  MAPE {abs((a-150)/a)[0]*100:.0f}%")
print(f"under-forecast by 50: MAPE {abs((a-50)/a)[0]*100:.0f}%")
print("over-forecast by 500: MAPE", f"{abs((a-600)/a)[0]*100:.0f}%",
      "-- unbounded above, capped at 100% below")

# =====================================================================
# 6. ALWAYS COMPARE AGAINST A BASELINE
# =====================================================================
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(x, y, test_size=.25, random_state=0)
base = DummyRegressor(strategy="mean").fit(X_tr, y_tr)
mdl  = LinearRegression().fit(X_tr, y_tr)

print(f"\n{'':10s} {'baseline':>10s} {'model':>10s} {'improvement':>13s}")
for name, fn in [("MAE",  mean_absolute_error),
                 ("RMSE", lambda a_, b_: mean_squared_error(a_, b_) ** .5)]:
    bl = fn(y_te, base.predict(X_te)); md = fn(y_te, mdl.predict(X_te))
    print(f"{name:10s} {bl:10.3f} {md:10.3f} {1-md/bl:12.1%}")
print(f"{'R2':10s} {r2_score(y_te, base.predict(X_te)):10.3f} "
      f"{r2_score(y_te, mdl.predict(X_te)):10.3f}")
# An RMSE of 2.0 means nothing until you know the baseline scored 8.7.

q.q: MAE or RMSE?
q.a:
MAE when you want an interpretable typical error and outliers should not dominate.
RMSE when large errors are disproportionately costly — an ETA that is 40 minutes
wrong is far worse than four that are 10 minutes wrong. Report both: the ratio
tells you whether the errors are uniform or driven by a few extremes.

q.q: Why is MSE used as a loss function but MAE reported as a metric?
q.a:
MSE is differentiable everywhere, which is what closed-form and gradient-based
optimisation require; MAE has a kink at zero. But MSE is in squared units, so it
is meaningless to a stakeholder — MAE or RMSE is what you report.

q.q: Why does $R^2$ always increase when you add a feature?
q.a:
Because least squares minimises over a larger column space, and the previous
solution is still available (set the new coefficient to zero). The minimum error
can only fall, and $SS_{mean}$ is unchanged. Adjusted $R^2$ divides by
$n-1-k$, so a useless feature costs a degree of freedom and lowers the score.

q.q: Can $R^2$ be negative?
q.a:
Yes, on held-out data. It means the model is worse than always predicting the
training mean — typically severe overfitting, or a target distribution that
shifted between train and test.

q.q: Your demand forecast has MAPE 45% but WMAPE 6%. What is going on?
q.a:
The large percentage errors are concentrated on low-volume SKUs, where a
one-unit miss is a huge percentage. WMAPE weights by volume, so it reflects what
the business actually feels. Report WMAPE, and if the small SKUs genuinely matter,
report their error separately rather than letting them distort the headline.

q.q: Why does optimising MAPE make a model under-forecast?
q.a:
Because MAPE is asymmetric: under-forecasting caps at 100% error while
over-forecasting is unbounded. The optimiser learns that predicting low is safer,
which systematically biases the forecast downward.

q.q: $R^2 = 0.95$. Is the model good?
q.a:
Not established. $R^2$ says nothing about whether the functional form is right —
Anscombe's quartet gives four wildly different datasets identical $R^2$. Check the
residual plot for structure, check the error in business units, and compare
against a baseline.

36.idea: Several features predict one target. Each coefficient is the effect of that feature holding the others fixed. The solution is the normal equation or gradient descent.
36.intuition: Each feature gets its own slope, and the slopes are chosen jointly, so a feature's effect is the part no other feature already explains.
36.formula: ŷ = β0 + β1x1 + … + βp xp ; β = (XᵀX)⁻¹ Xᵀ y
steps: Add a column of ones for the intercept.
Form XᵀX and Xᵀy.
Solve the linear system for β.
Check that XᵀX is invertible (no perfect multicollinearity).
pitfalls: Correlated features make individual coefficients unstable.
Coefficients are only comparable when features share a scale.
36.tip: Say that a coefficient is conditional on the other features in the model.
36.code:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, Ridge
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
from scipy import stats

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
m = 600
exp = rng.uniform(0, 20, m)                 # years of experience
edu = rng.uniform(10, 20, m)                # years of education
age = 22 + exp + rng.normal(0, 1.5, m)      # nearly determined by experience!
sal = 3.0*exp + 5.0*edu + 20 + rng.normal(0, 6, m)   # true betas: 3.0 and 5.0

# =====================================================================
# 1. THE NORMAL EQUATIONS, FROM SCRATCH
# =====================================================================
X = np.c_[np.ones(m), exp, edu]             # the leading column of ones
beta = np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ sal)  # solve, do not invert
print("beta (intercept, exp, edu):", beta.round(4))
print("true:                       [20.0, 3.0, 5.0]")

sk = LinearRegression().fit(np.c_[exp, edu], sal)
print("sklearn:", np.r_[sk.intercept_, sk.coef_].round(4))

# The second derivative 2 X'X is positive definite -> unique minimum:
print("eigenvalues of X'X all > 0:", (np.linalg.eigvalsh(X.T @ X) > 0).all())

# =====================================================================
# 2. "HOLDING THE OTHERS CONSTANT" -- simple vs multiple coefficients
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'feature':10s} {'simple':>9s} {'multiple':>10s} {'true':>7s}")
for name, col, truth in [("exp", exp, 3.0), ("edu", edu, 5.0)]:
    simple = np.polyfit(col, sal, 1)[0]
    print(f"{name:10s} {simple:9.3f} {sk.coef_[['exp','edu'].index(name)]:10.3f} "
          f"{truth:7.1f}")
# Fitting one at a time attributes the shared variation to whichever
# feature you happened to include.

# =====================================================================
# 3. STANDARDISED COEFFICIENTS -- the only comparable ones
# =====================================================================
Xz = StandardScaler().fit_transform(np.c_[exp, edu])
bz = LinearRegression().fit(Xz, sal).coef_
print(f"\nraw coefficients:          {sk.coef_.round(3)}")
print(f"standardised coefficients: {bz.round(3)}  <- rank importance with THESE")
# beta_std_j = beta_j * sd(x_j) / sd(y) is the manual conversion:
print("manual conversion:", (sk.coef_ * np.c_[exp, edu].std(axis=0)).round(3))

# =====================================================================
# 4. MULTICOLLINEARITY -- age is nearly a copy of experience
# =====================================================================
def vif(Xdf: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.Series:
    out = {}
    for c in Xdf.columns:
        r2 = LinearRegression().fit(Xdf.drop(columns=c), Xdf[c]).score(
                 Xdf.drop(columns=c), Xdf[c])
        out[c] = np.inf if r2 >= 1 else 1 / (1 - r2)
    return pd.Series(out).sort_values(ascending=False)

D = pd.DataFrame({"exp": exp, "edu": edu, "age": age})
print("\nVIF:\n", vif(D).round(2))
print("corr(exp, age):", np.corrcoef(exp, age)[0, 1].round(4))

good = LinearRegression().fit(D[["exp", "edu"]], sal)
bad  = LinearRegression().fit(D[["exp", "edu", "age"]], sal)
print(f"\nwithout age: exp {good.coef_[0]:7.3f}  R2 {good.score(D[['exp','edu']], sal):.4f}")
print(f"with    age: exp {bad.coef_[0]:7.3f}  age {bad.coef_[2]:7.3f}  "
      f"R2 {bad.score(D[['exp','edu','age']], sal):.4f}")
# R2 is essentially unchanged -- PREDICTION is fine.
# But the exp coefficient has moved far from 3.0 and may even flip sign.

# INSTABILITY: refit on bootstrap samples and watch the coefficients swing
coefs_stable, coefs_collinear = [], []
for _ in range(200):
    idx = rng.integers(0, m, m)
    coefs_stable.append(LinearRegression().fit(D.iloc[idx][["exp","edu"]],
                                               sal[idx]).coef_[0])
    coefs_collinear.append(LinearRegression().fit(D.iloc[idx][["exp","edu","age"]],
                                                  sal[idx]).coef_[0])
print(f"\nbootstrap sd of the 'exp' coefficient:")
print(f"  without age {np.std(coefs_stable):.3f}")
print(f"  with    age {np.std(coefs_collinear):.3f}   <- far less stable")

# THE REMEDIES
print("\ndrop one:  ", LinearRegression().fit(D[["exp","edu"]], sal).coef_.round(3))
print("ridge:     ", Ridge(alpha=10).fit(D[["exp","edu","age"]], sal).coef_.round(3))
# Ridge adds lambda*I to X'X, making it well-conditioned by construction (T41).

# PERFECT collinearity -- the inverse simply does not exist
sqft = rng.uniform(500, 3000, m)
sqm  = sqft * 0.092903                        # an exact linear function
Xp = np.c_[np.ones(m), sqft, sqm]
print(f"\nrank of X {np.linalg.matrix_rank(Xp)} of {Xp.shape[1]} columns")
try:
    np.linalg.inv(Xp.T @ Xp)
except np.linalg.LinAlgError as e:
    print("X'X is singular:", e)
print("lstsq still returns AN answer (minimum-norm):",
      np.linalg.lstsq(Xp, sal, rcond=None)[0].round(4))
# Note it is A solution, not THE solution -- infinitely many fit identically.

# =====================================================================
# 5. STANDARD ERRORS, t AND p -- straight from (X'X)^-1
# =====================================================================
X2 = np.c_[np.ones(m), exp, edu]
b2 = np.linalg.solve(X2.T @ X2, X2.T @ sal)
resid = sal - X2 @ b2
dof = m - X2.shape[1]
sigma2 = resid @ resid / dof
se = np.sqrt(np.diag(sigma2 * np.linalg.inv(X2.T @ X2)))
tvals = b2 / se

print(f"\n{'':>10s} {'coef':>9s} {'std err':>9s} {'t':>8s} {'p':>10s}")
for nm, b_, s_, t_ in zip(["intercept", "exp", "edu"], b2, se, tvals):
    p_ = 2 * (1 - stats.t.cdf(abs(t_), dof))
    print(f"{nm:>10s} {b_:9.4f} {s_:9.4f} {t_:8.2f} {p_:10.2e}")

# =====================================================================
# 6. DIAGNOSTICS
# =====================================================================
fitted = X2 @ b2

# linearity / homoscedasticity
sl, _, _, pv, _ = stats.linregress(fitted, np.abs(resid))
print(f"\n|resid| vs fitted: slope {sl:+.4f} p={pv:.3f} "
      f"{'HETEROSCEDASTIC' if pv < .05 else 'constant variance, OK'}")

# normality of errors (needed for the p-values above, not for the estimates)
print(f"residual normality p = {stats.normaltest(resid)[1]:.3f}")

# influential points: leverage and Cook's distance
H = X2 @ np.linalg.inv(X2.T @ X2) @ X2.T
lev = np.diag(H)
cook = resid**2 / (X2.shape[1] * sigma2) * lev / (1 - lev)**2
print(f"high leverage rows (h > 2p/n): {(lev > 2*X2.shape[1]/m).sum()}")
print(f"influential rows (Cook's D > 4/n): {(cook > 4/m).sum()}")

# adjusted R2 -- the honest comparison across feature counts (Topic 35)
def adj_r2(y_, p_, k):
    r = r2_score(y_, p_)
    return 1 - (1 - r) * (len(y_) - 1) / (len(y_) - 1 - k)

for cols in [["exp"], ["exp", "edu"], ["exp", "edu", "age"]]:
    mm = LinearRegression().fit(D[cols], sal)
    print(f"{str(cols):28s} R2 {mm.score(D[cols], sal):.4f}  "
          f"adjR2 {adj_r2(sal, mm.predict(D[cols]), len(cols)):.4f}")

q.q: How do you interpret a coefficient in multiple regression?
q.a:
As the expected change in $y$ for a one-unit increase in that feature, with
every other feature held constant. That conditioning is what makes it differ
from the simple-regression coefficient, which absorbs the effects of everything
correlated with it.

q.q: Two features are correlated at 0.95. Does it matter?
q.a:
For prediction, barely — $\hat y$ and $R^2$ are stable. For interpretation, a
great deal: the coefficients become unstable, signs can flip between bootstrap
samples, and standard errors inflate so that genuinely important features look
insignificant. Detect with VIF and act only if the coefficients matter.

q.q: What happens if two columns are perfectly collinear?
q.a:
$X$ is rank-deficient, $X^{\top}X$ is singular, and there is no unique
solution — infinitely many coefficient vectors give identical predictions.
lstsq still returns the minimum-norm solution, which is a solution but not
the solution.

q.q: Can you compare coefficient magnitudes to rank feature importance?
q.a:
Not from raw coefficients — they carry the units of their features. Standardise
the features first, so the coefficients are in units of standard deviations. Even
then, importance is conditional on the model and on which other features are
present.

q.q: Why does the intercept get its own column of ones?
q.a:
So that $\beta_0$ is estimated by the same normal equations as every slope. It
also means the fitted plane is not forced through the origin, and it is what makes
the residuals sum to zero.

q.q:
Your model has $R^2=0.85$ but every coefficient is insignificant.
What is going on?
q.a:
Classic multicollinearity. The features jointly explain the target well, but they
are so correlated that no individual coefficient can be pinned down — the
standard errors are inflated, so each $t$-statistic is small. Check VIF and either
drop, combine, or regularise.

37.t: Gradient Descent I: Intuition and Mathematics
37.idea: Gradient descent repeatedly moves parameters opposite to the gradient of the loss, which points uphill. The learning rate sets the step size.
37.intuition: Standing on a foggy hillside, you feel which way is down and take a step. Steps shrink automatically near the bottom because the slope flattens.
37.formula: θ ← θ − η ∇L(θ) ; for L = mean (y − mx)²: ∂L/∂m = −(2/n) Σ x(y − mx)
steps: Start at θ = 0 (or a random value).
Compute the gradient on the data.
Update θ ← θ − η grad.
Repeat until the loss stops changing.
Too large η overshoots; too small η is slow.
pitfalls: Too large a learning rate makes the loss explode.
A flat region or saddle can stall progress.
37.tip: Draw the bowl: the gradient is the slope, and the step is opposite to it.
37.pit: Too large a learning rate overshoots and diverges.

steps: Start w = 0, b = 0, learning rate 0.05. Each epoch uses all 5 rows once (batch).
Epoch 1: predictions all 0. MSE = mean of y squared = 17.2. Gradient gw = -26.4, gb = -8.0. Update: w = 1.32, b = 0.40.
Epoch 2: predictions 1.72, 3.04, 4.36, 5.68, 7.00. MSE = 1.65. Gradient gw = 5.04, gb = 0.72. Update: w = 1.07, b = 0.36.
Loss falls each epoch and converges toward the OLS answer (m = 0.6, c = 2.2) with more epochs.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, SGDRegressor
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 200
x = rng.uniform(0, 10, n)
y = 2.4 * x + 3 + rng.normal(0, 2, n)          # true m=2.4, c=3

# =====================================================================
# 1. THE ALGORITHM, EXACTLY AS THE NOTES DESCRIBE IT
# =====================================================================
def gradient_descent(x, y, lr=0.01, epochs=1000, m=5.0, c=10.0, verbose=False):
    n = len(x)
    history = []
    for epoch in range(epochs):
        # STEP 2: predict, and compute the error
        y_pred = m * x + c
        error  = y - y_pred

        # STEP 3: the gradients, from the derivation
        dm = -(2 / n) * np.sum(x * error)      # dL/dm
        dc = -(2 / n) * np.sum(error)          # dL/dc

        # STEP 5: new = old - lr * slope
        m -= lr * dm
        c -= lr * dc

        loss = np.mean(error ** 2)
        history.append(loss)

        # STEP 6: stop when the slope is almost zero
        if np.hypot(dm, dc) < 1e-7:
            if verbose: print(f"converged at epoch {epoch}")
            break
    return m, c, history

m_gd, c_gd, hist = gradient_descent(x, y, lr=0.01, epochs=5000, verbose=True)
print(f"gradient descent: m {m_gd:.6f}  c {c_gd:.6f}")

ols = LinearRegression().fit(x.reshape(-1, 1), y)
print(f"OLS closed form : m {ols.coef_[0]:.6f}  c {ols.intercept_:.6f}")
# The SAME answer -- gradient descent just reaches it iteratively.

# =====================================================================
# 2. VERIFY THE GRADIENTS NUMERICALLY -- always do this
# =====================================================================
def loss(m, c):  return np.mean((y - (m*x + c)) ** 2)
def grads(m, c):
    e = y - (m*x + c)
    return -(2/len(x))*np.sum(x*e), -(2/len(x))*np.sum(e)

m0, c0, eps = 1.7, 2.3, 1e-5
an_m, an_c = grads(m0, c0)
nu_m = (loss(m0+eps, c0) - loss(m0-eps, c0)) / (2*eps)
nu_c = (loss(m0, c0+eps) - loss(m0, c0-eps)) / (2*eps)
print(f"\ndL/dm analytic {an_m:.8f}  numeric {nu_m:.8f}  diff {abs(an_m-nu_m):.2e}")
print(f"dL/dc analytic {an_c:.8f}  numeric {nu_c:.8f}  diff {abs(an_c-nu_c):.2e}")

# =====================================================================
# 3. EACH STEP REDUCES THE LOSS -- the Taylor argument, verified
# =====================================================================
m_, c_, lr = 5.0, 10.0, 0.01
print(f"\n{'epoch':>6s} {'m':>9s} {'c':>9s} {'loss':>12s} {'|grad|':>10s}")
for e in range(7):
    gm, gc = grads(m_, c_)
    print(f"{e:6d} {m_:9.4f} {c_:9.4f} {loss(m_,c_):12.4f} {np.hypot(gm,gc):10.4f}")
    m_ -= lr*gm; c_ -= lr*gc
# Note the gradient magnitude SHRINKING -- the steps self-regulate.

# =====================================================================
# 4. THE LEARNING RATE
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'lr':>8s} {'final loss':>14s} {'behaviour'}")
for lr in [0.0001, 0.001, 0.01, 0.026, 0.05]:
    mm, cc, h = gradient_descent(x, y, lr=lr, epochs=400)
    final = h[-1]
    if not np.isfinite(final):        note = "DIVERGED"
    elif final > 100:                 note = "diverging"
    elif h[-1] > h[-2] * 0.999:       note = "converged (or stalled)"
    else:                             note = "still improving -- too slow"
    print(f"{lr:8.4f} {final:14.4f}   {note}")

# THE CONVERGENCE CONDITION: eta < 2 / lambda_max(H)
X = np.c_[x, np.ones(n)]
H = 2 / n * X.T @ X
lmax = np.linalg.eigvalsh(H).max()
print(f"\nlambda_max(H) = {lmax:.4f}  ->  eta must be < {2/lmax:.6f}")

# =====================================================================
# 5. THE MATRIX FORM -- one line for any number of features
# =====================================================================
def gd_matrix(X, y, lr=0.05, epochs=2000):
    Xb = np.c_[np.ones(len(X)), X]                 # intercept column
    w = np.zeros(Xb.shape[1])
    for _ in range(epochs):
        grad = -(2/len(y)) * Xb.T @ (y - Xb @ w)   # the whole algorithm
        w -= lr * grad
    return w

Xm = rng.normal(0, 1, (400, 5))
ym = Xm @ np.array([2., -1., .5, 3., -2.]) + 7 + rng.normal(0, .5, 400)
w = gd_matrix(Xm, ym)
print(f"\ngradient descent : {w.round(4)}")
print(f"OLS              : "
      f"{np.r_[LinearRegression().fit(Xm, ym).intercept_, LinearRegression().fit(Xm, ym).coef_].round(4)}")

# =====================================================================
# 6. WHY SCALING IS MANDATORY -- the condition number
# =====================================================================
x1 = rng.normal(0, 1, 400)
x2 = rng.normal(0, 1, 400) * 1000                  # 1000x larger scale
Xu = np.c_[x1, x2]
Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(Xu)
yy = 2*x1 + 0.003*x2 + rng.normal(0, .3, 400)

for tag, Xd in [("unscaled", Xu), ("scaled", Xs)]:
    Xb = np.c_[np.ones(400), Xd]
    H = 2/400 * Xb.T @ Xb
    ev = np.linalg.eigvalsh(H)
    print(f"\n{tag:9s} lambda_max {ev.max():.4e}  lambda_min {ev.min():.4e}")
    print(f"{'':9s} condition number kappa = {ev.max()/ev.min():.3e}")
    print(f"{'':9s} max safe eta = {2/ev.max():.3e}")
    print(f"{'':9s} contraction per step ~ "
          f"{(np.sqrt(ev.max()/ev.min())-1)/(np.sqrt(ev.max()/ev.min())+1):.6f}")
# Unscaled: kappa ~ 1e6, so eta must be ~1e-6 AND each step barely moves.
# Scaled:   kappa ~ 1,   so eta can be ~0.1 and each step makes real progress.

# =====================================================================
# 7. STOPPING CRITERIA
# =====================================================================
def gd_with_stopping(x, y, lr=0.01, max_iter=100_000, tol=1e-9, grad_tol=1e-7):
    m, c, prev = 0.0, 0.0, np.inf
    for it in range(max_iter):
        gm, gc = (lambda e: (-(2/len(x))*np.sum(x*e), -(2/len(x))*np.sum(e)))(
                   y - (m*x + c))
        m -= lr*gm; c -= lr*gc
        cur = np.mean((y - (m*x + c))**2)

        if np.hypot(gm, gc) < grad_tol:  return m, c, it, "gradient ~ 0"
        if abs(prev - cur) < tol:        return m, c, it, "loss stopped improving"
        prev = cur
    return m, c, max_iter, "hit max_iter"

m2, c2, iters, why = gd_with_stopping(x, y)
print(f"\nstopped after {iters} iterations: {why}")
print(f"m {m2:.6f}  c {c2:.6f}")

# =====================================================================
# 8. SKLEARN'S VERSION -- always inside a scaling pipeline
# =====================================================================
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
sgd = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                    SGDRegressor(loss="squared_error", learning_rate="constant",
                                 eta0=0.01, max_iter=5000, tol=1e-6,
                                 random_state=0)).fit(x.reshape(-1,1), y)
print("\nsklearn SGD prediction at x=5:", sgd.predict([[5.0]]).round(4))
print("OLS prediction at x=5        :", ols.predict([[5.0]]).round(4))

q.q: Why use gradient descent if there is a closed-form solution?
q.a:
Because the closed form costs $O(p^3)$ and needs a $p\times p$ matrix in memory,
which is impossible past tens of thousands of features. It also fails when
features are collinear, cannot handle streaming data, and does not exist at all
for logistic regression, SVMs or neural networks.

q.q: Why is there a minus sign in the update?
q.a:
The gradient points towards steepest ascent. We want to descend, so we move
against it. A first-order Taylor expansion shows
$L(\theta-\eta\nabla L)\approx L(\theta)-\eta\|\nabla L\|^2$, so each step reduces
the loss provided $\eta$ is small enough.

q.q: What happens if the learning rate is too large?
q.a:
The step overshoots the minimum and lands somewhere with a larger
gradient, so the next step overshoots further. The loss oscillates and then
diverges to inf or nan. The formal condition is
$\eta<2/\lambda_{\max}(H)$.

q.q: Why does gradient descent need feature scaling when OLS does not?
q.a:
OLS solves the system exactly and does not care about conditioning (numerically it
does, but the answer is the same). Gradient descent's speed depends on the
condition number of the Hessian: unscaled features create a long, narrow valley in
which the algorithm zig-zags, and force a tiny learning rate to avoid divergence.

q.q: How do you know when to stop?
q.a:
When the gradient norm falls below a threshold ("the slope is almost 0"), when
the loss stops improving by more than tol, or — best in practice —
when the validation loss stops improving, which also acts as
regularisation.

q.q: Your loss becomes nan after a few epochs. What do you check?
q.a:
Learning rate first — almost always too large. Then whether the features are
scaled. Then the gradient implementation, verified numerically against a finite
difference. Then whether the data contains inf or nan already.

q.q: Does the starting point matter?
q.a:
Not for linear regression — the loss is convex, so every start reaches the same
global minimum. For neural networks it matters greatly: the loss is non-convex,
and initialising all weights identically makes every neuron learn the same thing.

38.t: Gradient Descent II: Batch, Stochastic and Mini-batch
38.idea: Batch uses all rows per update, stochastic uses one row, and mini-batch uses a small group. Each trades gradient accuracy against update speed and hardware efficiency.
38.intuition: Batch takes careful steps after reading the whole book. Stochastic takes a quick step after each sentence: noisy but fast. Mini-batch reads a paragraph at a time.
38.formula: Updates per epoch: batch = 1, mini-batch = n/b, stochastic = n.
steps: Batch: average gradient over all n rows, one update.
Stochastic: gradient on one row, update, next row.
Mini-batch: gradient on b rows, update, next batch; shuffle each epoch.
38.example: x = [1,2,3,4], y = 2x, η = 0.05. Batch after one epoch: m = 1.5 (1 update). Stochastic: m = 2.065 (4 updates). Mini-batch of 2: m = 2.375 (2 updates).
pitfalls: Stochastic updates need a decaying learning rate or they wander.
Forgetting to shuffle makes epochs biased.
38.tip: Mini-batch is the default in deep learning because GPUs process batches efficiently.
38.hook: Updates per epoch: batch 1, mini-batch n/b, stochastic n.
38.pit: Stochastic steps are noisy; they need a decaying learning rate.

steps: Batch: one update per epoch using all 5 rows. Epoch 1: 1 update, w = 1.32, b = 0.40.

Stochastic: 5 updates per epoch, one per row in file order. Row 1 moves w to 0.20, row 2 to 0.88, row 3 to 1.43, row 4 back to 0.46, row 5 to 1.58 (b = 0.70). The row 4 step overshoots because its error is large and positive.
Mini-batch of 2: batches rows 1-2, rows 3-4, row 5. Three updates per epoch. After batch 1: w = 0.50, b = 0.30. After batch 2: w = 1.32, b = 0.55. After batch 3: w = 0.25, b = 0.33.
Trade-off: batch is smooth, stochastic is noisy, mini-batch is the usual middle ground.
