q.q: Level-wise vs leaf-wise — which is better?
q.a:
Neither universally. Leaf-wise reaches a lower training loss for a fixed leaf
budget because it spends splits where they pay most, so it is faster to a given
accuracy on large data. On small data that same greediness overfits. Level-wise
is more symmetric and implicitly regularised.

q.q: How is GOSS different from row subsampling?
q.a:
Subsampling drops rows uniformly. GOSS keeps all large-gradient (poorly fitted)
rows and samples only among the small-gradient ones, then up-weights those
samples by $(1-a)/b$ so the gain estimate stays unbiased. It discards mostly
rows that carry no information.

q.q: Why does LightGBM overfit small datasets?
q.a:
Leaf-wise growth plus a num_leaves default of 31 and
max_depth=-1 means the tree can go very deep on one branch until a leaf
holds a handful of rows. Fix: cut num_leaves to 15–31, raise
min_child_samples, add reg_lambda, use early stopping.

q.q: What is target leakage in target encoding, and CatBoost's fix?
q.a:
A rare category's mean target is dominated by the row's own label, so the
feature predicts train labels but nothing else. CatBoost computes the encoding
from only the rows preceding it in a random permutation, smoothed towards the
global prior — an online, leak-free estimate.

q.q: What is prediction shift?
q.a:
Residuals during training are computed from a model that was itself trained on
those same rows, so they are biased small relative to what happens at
inference. Ordered boosting computes row $i$'s residual from a model that never
saw row $i$, aligning the two distributions.

q.q: What is an oblivious tree and why use one?
q.a:
Every node at a given depth shares the same feature and threshold, so the tree
is a lookup table indexed by $d$ bits. It regularises heavily and makes
inference extremely fast and vectorisable — valuable when you serve millions
of predictions per second.

q.q: When would you not use any of these?
q.a:
When the data is not tabular (images, audio, long text — use deep learning),
when you need a globally interpretable model with coefficients (use regularised
linear or a single tree), when you have very few rows relative to features
(regularised linear usually wins), or when extrapolation beyond the training
range is required — trees output constants and cannot extrapolate at all.

70.idea: Stacking trains a meta-model on out-of-fold predictions of base models. Blending does the same using a single hold-out split, which is simpler but uses less data.
70.intuition: Let the base models make predictions, then let a referee learn which base model to trust in which situation.
70.formula: Stacking meta-training rows = all n rows (out-of-fold). Blending meta rows = hold-out size only.
steps: Split into k folds (stacking) or train and blend sets (blending).
Train each base model; collect out-of-fold predictions.
Build the meta matrix: one column per base model.
Train the meta-model on that matrix.
For test, use base models retrained on all data.
70.example: 1000 rows, 4 folds of 250: each base model gives one out-of-fold prediction per row, giving a 1000 × 3 meta matrix. Blending with an 800/200 split: meta matrix 200 × 3.
pitfalls: Base models must not see rows used to train the meta-model.
Stacking costs k times more fits.
70.tip: Out-of-fold predictions are the key idea; say that first.
70.hook: Stacking meta rows = all rows; blending = hold-out rows only.
70.pit: Base models must not see the rows the meta-model is trained on.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import (train_test_split, StratifiedKFold,
                                     cross_val_predict, cross_val_score)
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression, RidgeCV
from sklearn.ensemble import (RandomForestClassifier, StackingClassifier,
                              StackingRegressor, GradientBoostingClassifier)
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=4000, n_features=25, n_informative=12,
                           n_redundant=5, flip_y=0.04, random_state=0)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3,
                                      stratify=y, random_state=0)

# ==================================================================
# 1. STACKING BY HAND -- so the OOF matrix is not a black box
# ==================================================================
base = [
    ("logreg", make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000))),
    ("knn"   , make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(25))),
    ("rf"    , RandomForestClassifier(300, random_state=0, n_jobs=4)),
    ("svc"   , make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC(probability=True, random_state=0))),
    ("nb"    , GaussianNB()),
]

cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
n, M = len(ytr), len(base)

Z_train = np.zeros((n, M))            # the out-of-fold matrix
Z_test  = np.zeros((len(yte), M))

for j, (name, model) in enumerate(base):
    # cross_val_predict gives EXACTLY the OOF predictions: each row is
    # predicted by the fold-model that did not train on it.
    Z_train[:, j] = cross_val_predict(model, Xtr, ytr, cv=cv,
                                      method="predict_proba", n_jobs=4)[:, 1]
    # refit on the FULL training set for the test-time column
    model.fit(Xtr, ytr)
    Z_test[:, j] = model.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]
    print(f"{name:7s} solo AUC {roc_auc_score(yte, Z_test[:, j]):.4f}")

meta = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(Z_train, ytr)
print("STACK   AUC", round(roc_auc_score(yte, meta.predict_proba(Z_test)[:, 1]), 4))
print("mean    AUC", round(roc_auc_score(yte, Z_test.mean(axis=1)), 4))
print("meta weights:", dict(zip([n_ for n_, _ in base], meta.coef_[0].round(3))))

# Diversity check -- this table tells you which members are earning their keep
print(np.corrcoef(Z_train.T).round(2))

# ==================================================================
# 2. THE LEAKY VERSION -- what NOT to do
# ==================================================================
Z_leak = np.zeros((n, M))
for j, (_, model) in enumerate(base):
    model.fit(Xtr, ytr)
    Z_leak[:, j] = model.predict_proba(Xtr)[:, 1]   # <-- IN-SAMPLE. WRONG.
meta_leak = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(Z_leak, ytr)
print("leaky  meta-train AUC",
      round(roc_auc_score(ytr, meta_leak.predict_proba(Z_leak)[:, 1]), 4))  # ~1.0
print("leaky  test       AUC",
      round(roc_auc_score(yte, meta_leak.predict_proba(Z_test)[:, 1]), 4))  # worse

# ==================================================================
# 3. THE SKLEARN WAY -- StackingClassifier does all of the above
# ==================================================================
stack = StackingClassifier(
        estimators      = base,
        final_estimator = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000),
        cv              = cv,        # how the OOF matrix is built
        stack_method    = "predict_proba",
        passthrough     = False,     # True -> also give the meta the raw X
        n_jobs          = 4)
stack.fit(Xtr, ytr)
print("sklearn stack AUC",
      round(roc_auc_score(yte, stack.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]), 4))

# Honest evaluation: cross-validate the WHOLE stack, not just the meta-model.
print("nested CV AUC:",
      cross_val_score(stack, X, y, cv=3, scoring="roc_auc", n_jobs=1).round(4))

# ==================================================================
# 4. BLENDING -- one holdout, no folds
# ==================================================================
Xa, Xhold, ya, yhold = train_test_split(Xtr, ytr, test_size=0.2,
                                        stratify=ytr, random_state=0)
H  = np.zeros((len(yhold), M))
T  = np.zeros((len(yte),   M))
for j, (_, model) in enumerate(base):
    model.fit(Xa, ya)                       # base models see 80% only
    H[:, j] = model.predict_proba(Xhold)[:, 1]
    T[:, j] = model.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]
blender = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(H, yhold)
print("BLEND   AUC", round(roc_auc_score(yte, blender.predict_proba(T)[:, 1]), 4))

# ==================================================================
# 5. REGRESSION + MULTI-LEVEL + SAFE FOLDS
# ==================================================================
from sklearn.datasets import make_regression
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
Xr, yr = make_regression(n_samples=3000, n_features=20, noise=15, random_state=0)
sreg = StackingRegressor(
        estimators=[("lin", LinearRegression()),
                    ("rf" , RandomForestRegressor(200, random_state=0, n_jobs=4))],
        final_estimator=RidgeCV(alphas=np.logspace(-3, 3, 13)),
        cv=5, n_jobs=4).fit(Xr[:2000], yr[:2000])
print("stacked R2:", round(sreg.score(Xr[2000:], yr[2000:]), 4))

# Level-2 stacks are just stacks whose members are stacks:
level2 = StackingClassifier(
        estimators=[("stack1", stack),
                    ("gb", GradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0))],
        final_estimator=LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000), cv=3, n_jobs=1)
# (expensive -- rarely worth more than 2 levels outside competitions)

# Grouped or temporal data: swap the fold generator, everything else is the same
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold, TimeSeriesSplit
# StackingClassifier(..., cv=GroupKFold(5))   # needs groups= passed to fit
# StackingClassifier(..., cv=TimeSeriesSplit(5))

q.q: How does stacking differ from bagging and boosting?
q.a:
Bagging: one algorithm, parallel, combined by a fixed average, attacks
variance. Boosting: one algorithm, sequential, fixed weighted sum, attacks
bias. Stacking: several different algorithms, and the combination itself
is a learned model.

q.q: Why must the meta-model be trained on out-of-fold predictions?
q.a:
In-sample predictions are unrealistically accurate, especially for
high-variance learners. The meta-model would learn weights calibrated to that
fiction. OOF predictions have the same error profile as unseen data, so the
learned weights transfer.

q.q: Stacking vs blending — when do you pick blending?
q.a:
When data is plentiful (a 10% holdout is still tens of thousands of rows),
when compute is tight, or when K-fold would leak — time series or grouped
data where a naive fold split puts related rows on both sides.

q.q: How do you choose base models?
q.a:
By inductive-bias diversity: linear, tree ensemble, distance-based,
probabilistic. Check the OOF correlation matrix — members correlated above
about 0.95 are redundant. A weaker but decorrelated model often contributes
more than a stronger duplicate.

q.q: Can a stack be worse than its best base model?
q.a:
Yes — from leakage in the OOF construction, from an overfit meta-model (too
flexible, or too few meta rows in blending), or from redundant members that
make the meta-features collinear. Always compare against both the best single
model and a plain average.

q.q: What does passthrough=True do?
q.a:
It gives the meta-model the original features alongside the base predictions,
so it can learn region-dependent trust ("in this part of feature space, prefer
the forest"). More expressive, more overfitting risk; needs a regularised or
tree-based meta-model and more data.

q.q: Why can a meta-coefficient be negative?
q.a:
Because the meta-model is doing regression, not averaging. If a model has a
systematic bias correlated with another member's error, subtracting it removes
that error. This is expressive power a simple average does not have — and one
reason a stack can beat every member.

71.idea: KNN predicts from the k closest training points, using majority vote for classification or average for regression. It has no training step; all the work happens at prediction.
71.intuition: You are the average of the people you spend time with. Look at the nearest examples and copy the majority.
71.formula: Euclidean distance: d = √Σ(x_i − z_i)² ; prediction = majority of k nearest labels.
steps: Scale the features.
Compute the distance from the query to every training row.
Select the k smallest.
Vote (classification) or average (regression).
71.example: Query (3,2), nearest three are (2,2), (2,1), (1,1), all class A, so predict A. Distances 1.00, 1.41, 2.24, then class B at 4.24.
pitfalls: Unscaled features make the largest-range feature dominate distance.
Prediction is slow on large data, since distances are computed to every row.
71.tip: Small k is flexible but noisy; large k is smooth but blurred.
71.pit: Unscaled features; slow prediction on large data.

steps: Scale with training mean and std. Query (7.0, 108) becomes standardised.
Distances computed to all 8 training rows; the three smallest are rows 2, 6, 7.
Labels 1, 0, 1: majority is 1, so predict placed = 1.
Row 8 (distance 1.28) is ignored; with k = 1 the answer would be the same (row 2).

import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons, load_wine
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, GridSearchCV, cross_val_score
from sklearn.neighbors import (KNeighborsClassifier, KNeighborsRegressor,
                               NearestNeighbors, RadiusNeighborsClassifier)
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report

# ==================================================================
# 1. KNN FROM SCRATCH -- the algorithm is 10 lines
# ==================================================================
class MyKNN:
    def __init__(self, k=5, p=2, weights="uniform"):
        self.k, self.p, self.weights = k, p, weights

    def fit(self, X, y):
        self.X, self.y = np.asarray(X, float), np.asarray(y)   # "just store it"
        self.classes_ = np.unique(self.y)
        return self

    def _dist(self, q):
        # Minkowski distance from q to every stored point
        return (np.abs(self.X - q) ** self.p).sum(axis=1) ** (1 / self.p)

    def predict(self, Q):
        out = []
        for q in np.asarray(Q, float):
            d   = self._dist(q)
            idx = np.argpartition(d, self.k)[:self.k]     # O(n), not a full sort
            w   = np.ones(self.k) if self.weights == "uniform" else 1.0 / (d[idx] + 1e-12)
            # weighted majority vote
            scores = {c: w[self.y[idx] == c].sum() for c in self.classes_}
            out.append(max(scores, key=scores.get))
        return np.array(out)

X, y = make_moons(400, noise=0.28, random_state=0)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)
print("scratch:", (MyKNN(5).fit(Xtr, ytr).predict(Xte) == yte).mean())
print("sklearn:",  KNeighborsClassifier(5).fit(Xtr, ytr).score(Xte, yte))

# ==================================================================
# 2. THE CORRECT PIPELINE -- scaler INSIDE, so it never sees the val fold
# ==================================================================
pipe = Pipeline([("sc",  StandardScaler()),
                 ("knn", KNeighborsClassifier())])

grid = {
    "knn__n_neighbors": list(range(1, 41, 2)),   # odd values for binary
    "knn__weights":     ["uniform", "distance"],
    "knn__p":           [1, 2],                  # Manhattan / Euclidean
    "knn__metric":      ["minkowski"],
}
wine = load_wine()
gs = GridSearchCV(pipe, grid, cv=5, scoring="accuracy", n_jobs=4)
gs.fit(wine.data, wine.target)
print("best params:", gs.best_params_)
print("best CV    :", round(gs.best_score_, 4))

# What scaling was worth, measured:
raw = cross_val_score(KNeighborsClassifier(**{k.split("__")[1]: v
        for k, v in gs.best_params_.items()}), wine.data, wine.target, cv=5).mean()
print("unscaled CV:", round(raw, 4), " scaled CV:", round(gs.best_score_, 4))

# ==================================================================
# 3. REGRESSION
# ==================================================================
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
Xr = np.sort(rng.uniform(0, 10, 200))[:, None]
yr = np.sin(Xr.ravel()) + rng.normal(0, 0.2, 200)
for w in ("uniform", "distance"):
    r = KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=9, weights=w).fit(Xr[:150], yr[:150])
    print(w, "R2:", round(r.score(Xr[150:], yr[150:]), 4))

# ==================================================================
# 4. RADIUS NEIGHBOURS -- fixed radius instead of fixed k
# ==================================================================
# Better when density varies a lot: dense regions vote with many neighbours,
# sparse regions with few. Points with an EMPTY radius need outlier_label.
rn = RadiusNeighborsClassifier(radius=1.0, weights="distance",
                               outlier_label="most_frequent").fit(Xtr, ytr)
print("radius-KNN:", round(rn.score(Xte, yte), 4))

# ==================================================================
# 5. USING THE NEIGHBOUR STRUCTURE DIRECTLY
# ==================================================================
nn = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=6, algorithm="ball_tree").fit(Xtr)
dist, idx = nn.kneighbors(Xte[:3])
print("distances to 6 nearest:", dist.round(3))

# The k-distance plot -- used to pick eps for DBSCAN (Topic 78) and to
# spot outliers: points whose k-th neighbour is unusually far away.
d_k = np.sort(nn.kneighbors(Xtr)[0][:, -1])
print("90th percentile k-distance:", round(np.percentile(d_k, 90), 3))

# ==================================================================
# 6. SCALING TO LARGE n  -- exact vs approximate
# ==================================================================
big = rng.normal(size=(100000, 12))
lab = (big[:, 0] + big[:, 1] > 0).astype(int)
exact = KNeighborsClassifier(10, algorithm="ball_tree", n_jobs=4).fit(big, lab)
# For millions of rows, exact search stops being viable. Use an approximate
# nearest-neighbour library instead -- faiss, hnswlib, annoy, scann -- which
# trade a small recall loss for orders-of-magnitude speed.

q.q: Why is KNN called a lazy learner?
q.a:
Because fit() does no generalisation — it only stores the data. All
computation is deferred to prediction. The consequence is $O(1)$ training and
$O(nd)$ per query, the reverse of every eager learner.

q.q: How do you choose k?
q.a:
Cross-validation over a range of odd values. Never training error — it is
minimised at $k=1$ by construction, since each point is its own nearest
neighbour. A rough starting point is $k\approx\sqrt{n}$, then tune around it.

q.q: Why must features be scaled?
q.a:
Distance is a sum over features, so a feature with a large numeric range
dominates it and the others are ignored. Unlike a linear model, KNN has no
weights that can rescale a feature's influence.

q.q: What is the curse of dimensionality for KNN?
q.a:
As $d$ grows, all pairwise distances converge to the same value, so the nearest
neighbours are not meaningfully nearer than random points. Data density also
falls exponentially, so a "local" neighbourhood covers most of each feature's
range. KNN needs low dimension or aggressive feature selection.

q.q: Euclidean or Manhattan?
q.a:
Euclidean by default. Manhattan is more robust when individual features have
outliers and often works better in higher dimensions, since it concentrates
less. Treat $p$ as a hyperparameter and tune it.

q.q: How does KNN handle imbalanced classes?
q.a:
Badly, by default — the majority class wins on raw counts even when the
minority is closer. Use weights="distance", resample, or use
RadiusNeighborsClassifier so density rather than count decides.

q.q: KNN vs K-Means — what is the relationship?
q.a:
None, beyond the letter K. KNN is supervised classification/regression with $k$
= number of neighbours consulted. K-Means is unsupervised clustering with $k$ =
number of clusters. They share no objective, no training procedure, and no
output type.

q.q: Can KNN give probabilities?
q.a:
Yes — the fraction of the $k$ neighbours in each class (weighted, if
weights="distance"). They are coarse, taking only $k+1$ distinct values
with uniform weights, and are poorly calibrated for small $k$.

q.q: How would you deploy KNN with 50 million rows?
q.a:
Not exactly. Use an approximate nearest-neighbour index (FAISS, HNSW, ScaNN)
which trades a little recall for sub-linear queries, reduce dimension first
with PCA or a learned embedding, and consider replacing KNN with a model whose
prediction cost does not grow with the training set.

72.t: SVM I: Hard Margin and the Maximal Margin Classifier
72.idea: A support vector machine finds the separating line (hyperplane) with the widest margin to the nearest points, which are the support vectors.
72.intuition: Instead of any line that separates the classes, choose the one that leaves the widest empty street between them.
72.formula: Constraint: y_i (w·x_i + b) ≥ 1 ; margin width = 2 / ‖w‖ ; minimise ½‖w‖²
steps: Write the constraints for all training points.
Minimise ½‖w‖² (equivalent to maximising the margin).
Support vectors are the points where the constraint holds with equality.
Prediction uses sign(w·x + b).
72.example: Points (1,1) labelled −1 and (3,3) labelled +1: w = (0.5, 0.5), b = −2, margin width 2.83.
pitfalls: Hard margin fails when classes overlap, since no separator exists.
Sensitive to outliers that define the margin.
72.tip: Margin = 2/‖w‖: a smaller weight vector means a wider street.
72.pit: Hard margin fails when classes overlap.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

X, y = make_blobs(n_samples=60, centers=2, cluster_std=1.05, random_state=6)

# ==================================================================
# 1. HARD MARGIN via a huge C
# ==================================================================
clf = SVC(kernel="linear", C=1e10).fit(X, y)
w, b = clf.coef_[0], clf.intercept_[0]
print("w =", w.round(3), " b =", round(b, 3))
print("margin width 2/||w|| =", round(2 / np.linalg.norm(w), 4))

# The support vectors, and the duals
print("n support vectors:", clf.n_support_)      # per class
print("support indices  :", clf.support_)
print("dual coefs a_i*y_i:", clf.dual_coef_.round(3))
# NOTE: sklearn stores alpha_i * y_i together, so signs encode the class.

# Verify w = sum_i alpha_i y_i x_i  -- the stationarity condition
w_rebuilt = (clf.dual_coef_ @ clf.support_vectors_).ravel()
print("rebuilt w matches:", np.allclose(w, w_rebuilt))

# Verify every support vector sits exactly on a margin line: y(wx+b) == 1
fm = y[clf.support_] * (clf.support_vectors_ @ w + b)
print("functional margins of SVs:", fm.round(6))   # all 1.0

# Verify NON-support vectors are strictly outside: y(wx+b) > 1
mask = np.ones(len(X), bool); mask[clf.support_] = False
print("min functional margin of the rest:",
      round((y[mask] * (X[mask] @ w + b)).min(), 4))     # > 1

# ==================================================================
# 2. THE HEADLINE CLAIM: ONLY SUPPORT VECTORS MATTER
# ==================================================================
sv_only = SVC(kernel="linear", C=1e10).fit(clf.support_vectors_, y[clf.support_])
print("same hyperplane:", np.allclose(sv_only.coef_[0] / np.linalg.norm(sv_only.coef_[0]),
                                      w / np.linalg.norm(w), atol=1e-3))

# ...and deleting a non-support vector changes nothing
keep = np.ones(len(X), bool); keep[np.where(mask)[0][0]] = False
dropped = SVC(kernel="linear", C=1e10).fit(X[keep], y[keep])
print("unchanged after dropping a non-SV:",
      np.allclose(dropped.coef_[0], w, atol=1e-3))

# ==================================================================
# 3. SOLVING THE DUAL DIRECTLY WITH cvxopt-STYLE QP (here: scipy)
#    max  sum(a) - 0.5 * a^T Q a     with Q_ij = y_i y_j <x_i,x_j>
#    s.t. a >= 0,  sum(a_i y_i) = 0
# ==================================================================
from scipy.optimize import minimize
K = X @ X.T                             # the linear kernel / Gram matrix
Q = np.outer(y_pm := np.where(y == 1, 1.0, -1.0), y_pm) * K

def neg_dual(a):
    return 0.5 * a @ Q @ a - a.sum()
def neg_dual_grad(a):
    return Q @ a - np.ones_like(a)

res = minimize(neg_dual, np.zeros(len(X)), jac=neg_dual_grad, method="SLSQP",
               bounds=[(0, None)] * len(X),
               constraints=[{"type": "eq",
                             "fun": lambda a: a @ y_pm,
                             "jac": lambda a: y_pm}],
               options={"maxiter": 500, "ftol": 1e-12})
alpha = res.x
sv = alpha > 1e-6
print("dual found", sv.sum(), "support vectors; sklearn found", len(clf.support_))

w_dual = ((alpha * y_pm)[sv] @ X[sv])
b_dual = np.mean(y_pm[sv] - X[sv] @ w_dual)
print("w from dual:", w_dual.round(3), " (sklearn:", w.round(3), ")")

# ==================================================================
# 4. DISTANCE TO THE BOUNDARY, AND PREDICTION
# ==================================================================
# decision_function returns w.x + b  -- the FUNCTIONAL margin.
# Divide by ||w|| to get the true GEOMETRIC distance in feature units.
f = clf.decision_function(X)
geometric = f / np.linalg.norm(w)
print("closest point is", round(np.abs(geometric).min(), 4), "units away")
print("prediction = sign(w.x + b):", np.array_equal(clf.predict(X), (f > 0).astype(int)))

# ==================================================================
# 5. ALWAYS SCALE
# ==================================================================
# ||w||^2 is measured in feature units, so a feature with a huge range
# dominates the objective exactly as it dominates a distance in KNN.
svm = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC(kernel="linear", C=1.0))
svm.fit(X, y)

q.q: What exactly is the margin, and why maximise it?
q.a:
The perpendicular distance from the hyperplane to the nearest training point of
either class; the "street" has width $2/\|w\|$. Maximising it maximises the
distance to the closest data, which bounds generalisation error and makes the
classifier robust to small perturbations of the inputs.

q.q: Why $\frac12\|w\|^2$ instead of maximising $2/\|w\|$?
q.a:
$2/\|w\|$ is non-convex and non-differentiable at 0. Since $t \mapsto 1/t$ is
monotone decreasing, maximising $2/\|w\|$ equals minimising $\|w\|$, and
squaring plus the $\frac12$ makes it a smooth convex quadratic whose gradient
is simply $w$ — ideal for QP solvers.

q.q: Why label the classes $\pm1$?
q.a:
It merges "correct side" and "how far" into one expression:
$y_i(w^Tx_i+b)\ge1$ handles both classes with one inequality. With ${0,1}$
you would need two separate cases.

q.q: What is a support vector?
q.a:
A training point with $\alpha_i>0$; equivalently one lying exactly on a margin
line, $y_i(w^Tx_i+b)=1$. They alone determine $w$. All other points can be
deleted without changing the model.

q.q: Why derive the dual at all?
q.a:
Two reasons. It exposes the sparsity (most $\alpha_i$ vanish, so the model is
compact and prediction is cheap). And it expresses everything through inner
products $\langle x_i,x_j\rangle$, which is the only reason the kernel trick
exists. The dual also has $n$ variables rather than $d$, so it is preferable
when features outnumber rows.

q.q: Is the SVM solution unique?
q.a:
The optimal $w$ is unique because the objective is strictly convex in $w$. The
set of $\alpha$ achieving it need not be unique when data points are duplicated
or collinear, but the resulting hyperplane is the same.

q.q: What happens if the data is not linearly separable?
q.a:
The hard-margin feasible set is empty and the problem has no solution. You must
either introduce slack variables (soft margin, Topic 73) or map to a space
where separation is possible (kernels, Topic 74).

q.q: Is SVM affected by feature scaling?
q.a:
Yes, strongly. The objective $\|w\|^2$ and the geometric margin are both
measured in feature units, so a large-range feature dominates. Always
standardise, inside a pipeline.

q.q: How does SVM compare to logistic regression?
q.a:
Logistic regression optimises log loss over all points, so every point
influences the boundary and it outputs calibrated probabilities. SVM optimises
hinge loss, so points beyond the margin contribute exactly zero, the solution
depends only on support vectors, and the output is a signed distance rather
than a probability. SVM tends to be better with few samples and many features;
logistic regression scales better and gives probabilities directly.

73.t: SVM II: Soft Margin and the C Parameter
73.idea: A soft margin allows some points inside the margin or on the wrong side. The parameter C trades margin width against violations: small C tolerates more, large C fits more strictly.
73.intuition: C is the price of a violation. Cheap violations give a wide, forgiving street; expensive violations force the street to bend around the points.
73.formula: Objective = ½‖w‖² + C Σ max(0, 1 − y_i f(x_i)) (hinge loss)
steps: Choose C, usually on a log scale.
Each point contributes hinge loss max(0, 1 − margin).
Optimiser balances wide margin against total hinge loss.
Cross-validate C.
73.example: Hinge losses [0, 0, 0.6, 1.5]. Wide candidate (½‖w‖² = 0.5, hinge total 2.1) beats narrow (4.0, 0) at C = 0.1 (0.71 vs 4.0). At C = 10 the narrow one wins (21.5 vs 4.0).
pitfalls: Large C fits training noise (high variance).
Tuning C without scaling features.
73.tip: Small C = wide, tolerant margin; large C = narrow, strict margin.
73.hook: Objective = ½||w||² + C Σ max(0, 1 − y f(x))
73.pit: Large C fits training noise (high variance).

import numpy as np
from sklearn.svm import SVC, LinearSVC
from sklearn.linear_model import SGDClassifier
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, GridSearchCV, cross_val_score
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline, make_pipeline
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=1500, n_features=20, n_informative=8,
                           flip_y=0.12, class_sep=0.9, random_state=0)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)

# ==================================================================
# 1. TUNING C -- on a LOG scale, with the scaler inside the pipeline
# ==================================================================
pipe = Pipeline([("sc", StandardScaler()),
                 ("svm", SVC(kernel="linear"))])

gs = GridSearchCV(pipe, {"svm__C": np.logspace(-3, 3, 13)},
                  cv=5, scoring="accuracy", n_jobs=4, return_train_score=True)
gs.fit(Xtr, ytr)
print("best C:", gs.best_params_["svm__C"], " CV:", round(gs.best_score_, 4))

# Read the bias-variance story straight off the grid:
for C, tr, te in zip(gs.cv_results_["param_svm__C"],
                     gs.cv_results_["mean_train_score"],
                     gs.cv_results_["mean_test_score"]):
    print(f"C={float(C):8.3f}  train {tr:.4f}  cv {te:.4f}  gap {tr-te:+.4f}")

# ==================================================================
# 2. INSPECTING THE THREE KINDS OF SUPPORT VECTOR
# ==================================================================
C = 1.0
m = SVC(kernel="linear", C=C).fit(StandardScaler().fit_transform(Xtr), ytr)

alpha = np.abs(m.dual_coef_).ravel()          # sklearn stores alpha_i * y_i
free    = (alpha > 1e-8) & (alpha < C - 1e-8) # ON the margin, xi = 0
bounded = alpha >= C - 1e-8                   # violators, xi > 0
print(f"total points      : {len(ytr)}")
print(f"support vectors   : {len(m.support_)}")
print(f"  free (on margin): {free.sum()}")
print(f"  bounded (xi > 0): {bounded.sum()}")
print(f"non-SVs           : {len(ytr) - len(m.support_)}")

# Slack for every training point, computed by hand
Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(Xtr)
f  = m.decision_function(Xs)
y_pm = np.where(ytr == 1, 1.0, -1.0)
xi = np.maximum(0.0, 1.0 - y_pm * f)
print("sum of slack:", round(xi.sum(), 2),
      "| margin violations:", int((xi > 0).sum()),
      "| actual errors:",     int((xi > 1).sum()))
print("training errors agree:", (xi > 1).sum() == (m.predict(Xs) != ytr).sum())

# ==================================================================
# 3. SOFT MARGIN == HINGE LOSS + L2  -- verified three ways
# ==================================================================
# (a) the SVC objective, evaluated by hand
w = m.coef_[0]
obj = 0.5 * w @ w + C * xi.sum()
print("primal objective:", round(obj, 3))

# (b) LinearSVC minimises the same thing with a different solver (liblinear)
lin = LinearSVC(C=C, loss="hinge", max_iter=20000).fit(Xs, ytr)
print("LinearSVC agrees:", round(lin.score(Xs, ytr), 4), round(m.score(Xs, ytr), 4))

# (c) SGDClassifier with hinge loss and alpha = 1/(C*n) is the SAME MODEL,
#     fitted by stochastic gradient descent -- the scalable route for big data.
sgd = SGDClassifier(loss="hinge", alpha=1.0 / (C * len(ytr)),
                    max_iter=5000, tol=1e-4, random_state=0).fit(Xs, ytr)
print("SGD hinge  :", round(sgd.score(Xs, ytr), 4))

# ==================================================================
# 4. CLASS IMBALANCE -- per-class C
# ==================================================================
Xi, yi = make_classification(n_samples=3000, n_features=15, n_informative=7,
                             weights=[0.93, 0.07], flip_y=0.02, random_state=1)
Xa, Xb, ya, yb = train_test_split(Xi, yi, test_size=0.3, stratify=yi, random_state=0)

for cw in (None, "balanced", {0: 1, 1: 20}):
    mm = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                       SVC(kernel="linear", C=1.0, class_weight=cw)).fit(Xa, ya)
    p = mm.predict(Xb)
    print(f"class_weight={str(cw):12s}",
          classification_report(yb, p, output_dict=True, zero_division=0)["1"])

# ==================================================================
# 5. WHICH IMPLEMENTATION TO USE
# ==================================================================
# SVC          : kernel-capable, O(n^2)-O(n^3). Fine up to ~10-20k rows.
# LinearSVC    : linear only, liblinear, scales to ~1e5-1e6 rows. NOTE it
#                penalises the intercept and defaults to squared_hinge.
# SGDClassifier: loss="hinge", scales to millions / out-of-core via partial_fit.
#                alpha = 1/(C*n_samples) maps SGD's regularisation onto SVC's C.
#
# All three optimise the SAME objective; they differ only in solver and scale.

# ==================================================================
# 6. SOFT MARGIN FOR REGRESSION -- SVR and the epsilon-tube
# ==================================================================
from sklearn.svm import SVR
from sklearn.datasets import make_regression
Xr, yr = make_regression(n_samples=800, n_features=10, noise=15, random_state=0)
# epsilon defines a tube: errors smaller than epsilon cost NOTHING (the
# regression analogue of hinge loss's flat region). C prices the rest.
svr = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                    SVR(kernel="linear", C=10.0, epsilon=1.0)).fit(Xr[:600], yr[:600])
print("SVR R2:", round(svr.score(Xr[600:], yr[600:]), 4))

q.q: What does $C$ control?
q.a:
The price of margin violations. It is the inverse of regularisation strength:
the soft-margin objective is hinge loss $+ \frac{1}{2C}\|w\|^2$ after
rescaling. Large $C$ = weak regularisation = narrow margin = overfit; small $C$
= strong regularisation = wide margin = underfit.

q.q: What is a slack variable?
q.a:
$\xi_i \ge 0$ measuring how far point $i$ intrudes past its own margin line, in
functional-margin units. $\xi_i \in (0,1]$ means it is inside the margin but
still correctly classified; $\xi_i > 1$ means it is on the wrong side.

q.q: How does the dual change from hard to soft margin?
q.a:
Only by the upper bound: $\alpha_i \le C$ instead of $\alpha_i$ unbounded. The
objective is unchanged, which is why kernels apply identically.

q.q: What is the difference between a free and a bounded support vector?
q.a:
Free ($0<\alpha_i<C$) lies exactly on the margin with $\xi_i=0$ — these are
used to recover $b$. Bounded ($\alpha_i=C$) has $\xi_i>0$ and lies inside the
margin or on the wrong side; the optimiser has capped its influence.

q.q: How is an SVM related to logistic regression?
q.a:
Both minimise a convex loss plus L2. Hinge loss is exactly zero beyond the
margin, so only nearby points matter and the solution is sparse in support
vectors; log loss is positive everywhere, so all points contribute and the
output is a calibrated probability. Hinge is not a proper scoring rule, which
is why SVC needs Platt scaling to produce probabilities.

q.q: Why is probability=True discouraged in SVC?
q.a:
It runs internal 5-fold cross-validation to fit a Platt sigmoid, making training
roughly five times slower, and the resulting probabilities can be inconsistent
with predict() (the argmax of the probabilities may disagree with the
sign of the decision function). Use decision_function for ranking, or
CalibratedClassifierCV if you genuinely need probabilities.

q.q: Number of support vectors: what does it tell you?
q.a:
It is a rough capacity measure — the leave-one-out error is bounded by
$#SV/n$. Nearly all points being support vectors means $C$ is too small
or the kernel is too wide (heavy underfitting); very few means $C$ is large and
the model may be brittle.

q.q: How do you scale SVMs to a million rows?
q.a:
Not with SVC — its kernel solver is between $O(n^2)$ and $O(n^3)$. Use
LinearSVC for linear problems, SGDClassifier(loss="hinge") for
out-of-core, or approximate the kernel explicitly with Nystroem or
RBFSampler followed by a linear model.

74.idea: A kernel computes the dot product in a higher-dimensional feature space directly from the original inputs, so the SVM can draw curved boundaries without ever building the high-dimensional vectors.
74.intuition: Some classes are separable only after lifting the data (for example, a ring inside a disc). The kernel lets you lift implicitly.
74.formula: Polynomial: k(x,z) = (x·z + c)ᵈ ; RBF: k(x,z) = exp(−γ ‖x − z‖²) ; linear: x·z
steps: Choose a kernel: linear, polynomial, RBF (default), or sigmoid.
Scale the features.
Tune γ (RBF width) and C together.
Predict from kernel values to the support vectors.
74.example: x = (1,2), z = (3,1): (x·z)² = 25. The explicit map (x1², √2 x1x2, x2²) gives 25 as well.
pitfalls: RBF with large γ overfits; small γ underfits.
Kernels on unscaled data are dominated by the largest-range feature.
74.tip: A kernel is a similarity measure; the trick is that only dot products are needed.
74.pit: Kernels need scaled inputs; RBF γ too large overfits.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.datasets import make_circles, make_moons, make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, GridSearchCV
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline, make_pipeline
from sklearn.kernel_approximation import Nystroem, RBFSampler
from sklearn.linear_model import SGDClassifier

# ==================================================================
# 1. PROVING THE TRICK -- explicit lift vs kernel, same answer
# ==================================================================
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.normal(size=(6, 2))

def phi(x):                       # feature map for K(x,z) = (x.z + 1)^2
    x1, x2 = x[:, 0], x[:, 1]
    return np.column_stack([x1**2, x2**2, np.sqrt(2)*x1*x2,
                            np.sqrt(2)*x1, np.sqrt(2)*x2, np.ones_like(x1)])

K_explicit = phi(X) @ phi(X).T            # lift, THEN dot product  (6-D)
K_trick    = (X @ X.T + 1) ** 2           # dot product in 2-D, then square
print("identical:", np.allclose(K_explicit, K_trick))   # True
print("dims: explicit 6, kernel 2 -- and this gap explodes with degree")

# For d=100 features at degree 5 the explicit space has
print("features at d=100, p=5:", int(np.math.comb(100 + 5, 5)))   # ~96 million

# ==================================================================
# 2. CIRCLES: linear fails, RBF succeeds
# ==================================================================
Xc, yc = make_circles(600, factor=0.42, noise=0.09, random_state=0)
Xa, Xb, ya, yb = train_test_split(Xc, yc, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)
for kern in ("linear", "rbf"):
    m = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC(kernel=kern, C=1)).fit(Xa, ya)
    print(f"{kern:7s} test acc {m.score(Xb, yb):.4f}")
# linear ~0.50 (chance), rbf ~0.99 -- the boundary is a circle.

# The manual lift gives the same result, at the cost of building the feature:
Xlift_a = np.column_stack([Xa, (Xa**2).sum(1)])
Xlift_b = np.column_stack([Xb, (Xb**2).sum(1)])
print("manual lift + linear SVM:",
      round(SVC(kernel="linear", C=1).fit(Xlift_a, ya).score(Xlift_b, yb), 4))

# ==================================================================
# 3. TUNING gamma AND C JOINTLY -- never one at a time
# ==================================================================
X, y = make_classification(n_samples=2000, n_features=15, n_informative=8,
                           flip_y=0.05, random_state=0)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)

pipe = Pipeline([("sc", StandardScaler()), ("svm", SVC(kernel="rbf"))])
grid = {"svm__C":     np.logspace(-2, 3, 6),
        "svm__gamma": np.logspace(-4, 1, 6)}
gs = GridSearchCV(pipe, grid, cv=5, n_jobs=4).fit(Xtr, ytr)
print("best:", gs.best_params_, round(gs.best_score_, 4))

# The heatmap of the joint grid is what you should always look at:
sc = gs.cv_results_["mean_test_score"].reshape(len(grid["svm__C"]), -1)
print(np.round(sc, 3))

# ==================================================================
# 4. A CUSTOM KERNEL -- any PSD function works
# ==================================================================
def my_rbf(A, B, gamma=0.5):
    # ||a-b||^2 = ||a||^2 + ||b||^2 - 2 a.b   (avoids a python loop)
    sq = (A**2).sum(1)[:, None] + (B**2).sum(1)[None, :] - 2 * A @ B.T
    return np.exp(-gamma * np.maximum(sq, 0))

custom = SVC(kernel=my_rbf).fit(StandardScaler().fit_transform(Xtr), ytr)
print("custom kernel works:", round(custom.score(
      StandardScaler().fit(Xtr).transform(Xte), yte), 4))

# You can also precompute the Gram matrix yourself -- useful for kernels over
# non-vector objects (strings, graphs, sets), where there are no "features".
Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(Xtr)
Gtr = my_rbf(Xs, Xs)
pre = SVC(kernel="precomputed").fit(Gtr, ytr)
Xts = StandardScaler().fit(Xtr).transform(Xte)
print("precomputed:", round(pre.score(my_rbf(Xts, Xs), yte), 4))

# ==================================================================
# 5. WHAT THE MODEL STORES  -- there is no w in kernel space
# ==================================================================
m = SVC(kernel="rbf", C=1, gamma="scale").fit(Xs, ytr)
print("support vectors:", m.support_vectors_.shape)   # the model IS these points
try:
    m.coef_
except AttributeError as e:
    print("no coef_ for a nonlinear kernel:", type(e).__name__)
# Prediction: f(x) = sum_i alpha_i y_i K(x_i, x) + b, over support vectors only
manual = (m.dual_coef_ @ my_rbf(m.support_vectors_, Xts[:5],
          gamma=1/(Xs.shape[1]*Xs.var()))).ravel() + m.intercept_
print("decision_function:", m.decision_function(Xts[:5]).round(3))

# ==================================================================
# 6. SCALING UP -- approximate the kernel, then use a linear model
# ==================================================================
Xbig, ybig = make_classification(n_samples=200000, n_features=20,
                                 n_informative=10, random_state=0)
fast = make_pipeline(
        StandardScaler(),
        Nystroem(kernel="rbf", gamma=0.05, n_components=400, random_state=0),
        SGDClassifier(loss="hinge", alpha=1e-5, max_iter=30, tol=1e-3))
fast.fit(Xbig[:150000], ybig[:150000])
print("Nystroem + linear SVM on 150k rows:",
      round(fast.score(Xbig[150000:], ybig[150000:]), 4))
# RBFSampler (random Fourier features) is the cheaper, slightly weaker sibling.

q.q: Explain the kernel trick.
q.a:
The SVM dual depends on the data only through inner products. A kernel
$K(x,z)$ computes the inner product of two points after a feature map
$\phi$, without ever evaluating $\phi$. So we get the expressiveness of a
high- or infinite-dimensional space at the computational cost of the original
one.

q.q: What makes a function a valid kernel?
q.a:
Symmetry plus positive semi-definiteness of the Gram matrix for every finite
sample (Mercer's condition). That guarantees an implicit $\phi$ exists and the
dual stays convex.

q.q: Why is the RBF kernel infinite-dimensional?
q.a:
Factor $e^{-\frac12\|x-z\|^2}$ into $e^{-\|x\|^2/2}e^{-\|z\|^2/2}e^{x^Tz}$ and
Taylor-expand $e^{x^Tz}=\sum_k (x^Tz)^k/k!$. Every polynomial degree appears
with a positive weight, so the feature space has infinitely many coordinates.

q.q: What does $\gamma$ do?
q.a:
It sets the width of the Gaussian, i.e. how far a single training point's
influence extends. Large $\gamma$ = narrow influence = wiggly boundary and
overfitting (approaching 1-NN); small $\gamma$ = broad influence = nearly
linear boundary and underfitting.

q.q: How do $\gamma$ and $C$ interact?
q.a:
Both increase effective capacity, so they must be tuned jointly. Large $\gamma$
plus large $C$ memorises the training set; small $\gamma$ plus small $C$
underfits badly. The good region is a diagonal band in the $(\log C,\log\gamma)$
plane, which a joint grid search finds and a sequential search does not.

q.q: Which kernel would you start with?
q.a:
Linear if $d \gg n$ (text, genomics) or if you need interpretable coefficients
— it is also far faster. Otherwise RBF, which subsumes the polynomial family
and needs only two hyperparameters. Polynomial when you specifically want
bounded-degree feature interactions; sigmoid essentially never.

q.q: Can you get $w$ from a kernel SVM?
q.a:
Not explicitly, unless the kernel is linear — $w$ lives in the implicit
feature space, which may be infinite-dimensional. The model is stored as the
support vectors, their dual coefficients $\alpha_iy_i$, and $b$; prediction is
$f(x)=\sum_{i\in SV}\alpha_iy_iK(x_i,x)+b$.

q.q: Where else does the kernel trick appear?
q.a:
Kernel PCA, kernel ridge regression, Gaussian processes (the covariance
function is a kernel), spectral clustering, and one-class SVM for
anomaly detection. Any algorithm expressible purely in inner products can be
kernelised.

q.q: Kernel SVM or gradient boosting on tabular data?
q.a:
Boosting, almost always: it handles mixed types and missing values, scales to
large $n$, and needs no scaling. Kernel SVMs remain competitive on small,
dense, well-scaled numeric data — especially when $d>n$ — and on structured
inputs where a bespoke kernel encodes real domain knowledge.

75.idea: Naive Bayes applies Bayes' theorem, assuming features are independent given the class. It is fast and works well for text, even when the assumption is false.
75.intuition: Update your prior belief about a class with the evidence. Multiply the likelihoods of each feature, as if each clue were independent.
75.formula: P(C|x) ∝ P(C) ∏_j P(x_j | C) ; Bayes: P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B)
steps: Estimate priors P(C) from class frequencies.
Estimate P(x_j | C) for each feature.
For a new point, compute the product for each class.
Predict the class with the largest posterior.
75.example: Weather: lost, Mumbai, sunny. Posterior for Won 0.3 versus Lost 0.2, so classify Won.
pitfalls: Independence rarely holds, yet ranking often works.
Zero counts give zero probability: use Laplace smoothing.
75.tip: Naive = conditional independence; it is naive yet often competitive for text.
75.pit: The independence assumption is often false, but it still ranks well.

steps: Query (sunny, hot). Among yes rows: P(sunny | yes) = 1/4, P(hot | yes) = 1/4. Score yes = 0.667 x 0.25 x 0.25 = 0.042.
Among no rows: P(sunny | no) = 1/2, P(hot | no) = 1/2. Score no = 0.333 x 0.5 x 0.5 = 0.083.
Posterior yes = 0.042 / (0.042 + 0.083) = 0.333, so predict no.
Note: with (sunny, cool) the scores tie at 0.083, so the example is not informative. Use Laplace smoothing when a count is zero.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.naive_bayes import (GaussianNB, MultinomialNB,
                                 BernoulliNB, ComplementNB)
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification, load_iris
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, GridSearchCV, cross_val_score
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer, TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.calibration import CalibratedClassifierCV
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report, brier_score_loss

# ==================================================================
# 1. GAUSSIAN NAIVE BAYES FROM SCRATCH -- fit is just mean and variance
# ==================================================================
class MyGaussianNB:
    def fit(self, X, y):
        self.classes_ = np.unique(y)
        self.prior_ = np.array([(y == c).mean() for c in self.classes_])
        self.mu_    = np.array([X[y == c].mean(axis=0) for c in self.classes_])
        self.var_   = np.array([X[y == c].var(axis=0) + 1e-9
                                for c in self.classes_])
        return self

    def _log_likelihood(self, X):
        # log N(x | mu, var), summed over features -- the naive product in logs
        out = []
        for k in range(len(self.classes_)):
            ll = -0.5 * (np.log(2 * np.pi * self.var_[k])
                         + (X - self.mu_[k]) ** 2 / self.var_[k])
            out.append(ll.sum(axis=1) + np.log(self.prior_[k]))
        return np.array(out).T                       # (n, n_classes)

    def predict(self, X):
        return self.classes_[self._log_likelihood(X).argmax(axis=1)]

    def predict_proba(self, X):
        L = self._log_likelihood(X)
        L -= L.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)            # log-sum-exp for stability
        P = np.exp(L)
        return P / P.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)

iris = load_iris()
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(iris.data, iris.target,
                                      test_size=0.3, stratify=iris.target,
                                      random_state=0)
print("scratch:", (MyGaussianNB().fit(Xtr, ytr).predict(Xte) == yte).mean())
print("sklearn:", GaussianNB().fit(Xtr, ytr).score(Xte, yte))

# What the model actually stores -- 2 numbers per feature per class. That's it.
g = GaussianNB().fit(Xtr, ytr)
print("theta_ (means)  shape:", g.theta_.shape)
print("var_            shape:", g.var_.shape)
print("class_prior_          :", g.class_prior_.round(3))

# ==================================================================
# 2. TEXT: the classic use case
# ==================================================================
docs = ["win money now free lottery",  "meeting at ten tomorrow",
        "free free cash prize claim",  "project deadline meeting notes",
        "claim your free prize now",   "lunch meeting with the team"]
labels = [1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0]            # 1 = spam

# CountVectorizer -> MultinomialNB is the textbook pipeline
spam = make_pipeline(CountVectorizer(), MultinomialNB(alpha=1.0)).fit(docs, labels)
print(spam.predict(["free money claim now", "team meeting notes"]))

# Inspect the learned log-likelihoods -- feature_log_prob_ is log P(word | class)
vec = spam.named_steps["countvectorizer"]
nb  = spam.named_steps["multinomialnb"]
words = np.array(vec.get_feature_names_out())
spammy = words[np.argsort(nb.feature_log_prob_[1] - nb.feature_log_prob_[0])[-4:]]
print("most spam-indicative words:", spammy)

# ==================================================================
# 3. TUNING alpha -- usually the ONLY hyperparameter
# ==================================================================
X, y = make_classification(n_samples=3000, n_features=200, n_informative=40,
                           n_classes=4, n_clusters_per_class=1, random_state=0)
Xc = np.abs(X)                            # MultinomialNB needs non-negative
gs = GridSearchCV(MultinomialNB(),
                  {"alpha": [1e-4, 1e-3, 1e-2, 0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 5.0, 20.0]},
                  cv=5, n_jobs=4).fit(Xc, y)
print("best alpha:", gs.best_params_, round(gs.best_score_, 4))

# alpha=0 is MLE and will produce -inf logs for unseen combinations.
# alpha=1 is Laplace/add-one; alpha<1 is Lidstone and often better for text.

# ==================================================================
# 4. THE VARIANTS COMPARED ON THE SAME COUNTS
# ==================================================================
corpus = ["a b c a", "b b d", "c c c a", "d d e", "a e e b", "c d e a"]
target = [0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0]
counts = CountVectorizer().fit_transform(corpus)
for M in (MultinomialNB, BernoulliNB, ComplementNB):
    print(M.__name__, round(cross_val_score(M(alpha=0.5), counts, target,
                                            cv=3).mean(), 3))

# BernoulliNB binarises internally (binarize=0.0 by default). It uses the
# ABSENCE of a word as evidence too, which Multinomial ignores entirely.

# ==================================================================
# 5. CALIBRATION -- NB ranks well but its probabilities are extreme
# ==================================================================
X, y = make_classification(n_samples=4000, n_features=20, n_informative=8,
                           n_redundant=6, random_state=0)   # redundancy hurts NB
Xa, Xb, ya, yb = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.4, random_state=0)

raw = GaussianNB().fit(Xa, ya)
cal = CalibratedClassifierCV(GaussianNB(), method="isotonic", cv=5).fit(Xa, ya)
print("raw  Brier:", round(brier_score_loss(yb, raw.predict_proba(Xb)[:, 1]), 4))
print("cal  Brier:", round(brier_score_loss(yb, cal.predict_proba(Xb)[:, 1]), 4))
# Accuracy barely moves; the probabilities become usable.

# ==================================================================
# 6. STREAMING -- partial_fit for data that does not fit in memory
# ==================================================================
stream = MultinomialNB(alpha=0.5)
classes = np.unique(y)
for start in range(0, 4000, 500):
    chunk = np.abs(X[start:start + 500])
    stream.partial_fit(chunk, y[start:start + 500], classes=classes)
print("streamed model trained on 8 chunks:", round(stream.score(np.abs(X), y), 4))

q.q: What is "naive" about Naive Bayes?
q.a:
The assumption that features are conditionally independent given the class:
$P(x_1,\dots,x_d|c)=\prod_j P(x_j|c)$. It reduces the parameter count from
exponential to linear in $d$, at the price of an assumption that is usually
false.

q.q: Why can we ignore the denominator $P(X)$?
q.a:
It is the same for every class, so it cannot change which class maximises the
posterior. We do need it if we want normalised probabilities, and it is
recovered by dividing by the sum of the class scores.

q.q: Why does it work when the assumption is violated?
q.a:
Classification only requires the correct arg-max. Dependency effects often
inflate all class scores in a similar way and cancel in the comparison. The
probability magnitudes are wrong; the ranking frequently is not.

q.q: What is the zero-frequency problem?
q.a:
If a feature value never co-occurs with a class in training, its estimated
likelihood is 0 and the whole product collapses to 0, vetoing that class. Fixed
by Laplace/Lidstone smoothing: add $\alpha$ to every count and $\alpha|V|$ to
the denominator.

q.q: Why work in log space?
q.a:
Multiplying thousands of probabilities each around $10^{-4}$ underflows to
exactly zero in float64. Logs turn the product into a sum, which is numerically
stable; converting back to probabilities uses log-sum-exp.

q.q: Multinomial vs Bernoulli for text?
q.a:
Multinomial models how many times each word occurs and ignores absent
words. Bernoulli models presence/absence and explicitly uses the absence of a
word as evidence. Bernoulli tends to win on short documents (tweets, subject
lines); Multinomial on longer ones.

q.q: Is Naive Bayes a linear classifier?
q.a:
Multinomial and Bernoulli NB are: the log-posterior is linear in the counts, so
the boundary is a hyperplane. GaussianNB is linear only if the per-class
variances are equal; otherwise the quadratic terms survive and the boundary is
a conic.

q.q: Naive Bayes vs logistic regression?
q.a:
They are a generative/discriminative pair over the same model family. NB models
$P(x|c)P(c)$ and solves in closed form from counts; logistic regression models
$P(c|x)$ directly and optimises it. Ng and Jordan showed NB reaches its
(higher) asymptotic error much faster, so it wins with little data while
logistic regression wins with plenty.

q.q: Can Naive Bayes learn XOR?
q.a:
No. Each feature contributes an independent additive term to the log-posterior,
so the model is additive and cannot represent an interaction where the effect of
$x_1$ depends on $x_2$. You would have to engineer the interaction feature
yourself.

q.q: How would you improve a Naive Bayes text classifier?
q.a:
Tune $\alpha$; use TF-IDF instead of raw counts; add bigrams; remove or merge
near-duplicate features to reduce double-counting; use ComplementNB if the
classes are imbalanced; and calibrate the output if downstream code consumes
probabilities.

76.t: K-Means Clustering and the Elbow Method
76.idea: K-means alternates two steps: assign each point to its nearest centroid, then move each centroid to the mean of its points. It minimises within-cluster sum of squares (inertia).
76.intuition: Drop k flags on the map, let each house join its nearest flag, move each flag to the middle of its houses, and repeat until nothing changes.
76.formula: Inertia = Σ_clusters Σ_x ‖x − c‖² ; choose k where inertia stops dropping sharply (elbow).
steps: Choose k and initialise centroids (k-means++ is better).
Assign each point to its nearest centroid.
Recompute centroids as cluster means.
Repeat until assignments stop changing.
Run several restarts; plot inertia against k to find the elbow.
76.example: Points A(1,1), B(2,1), C(1,2) and D(5,5), E(6,5), F(5,6): centroids move to (1.33, 1.33) and (5.33, 5.33) after one update; inertia 2.67.
pitfalls: Assumes round clusters of similar size.
Sensitive to initialisation and to outliers.
76.tip: Describe the two alternating steps, then the elbow.
76.hook: Minimise inertia = Σ ||x − c||² ; plot inertia vs k to find the elbow.
76.pit: Assumes round clusters of similar size; sensitive to start.

steps: Start centroids c1 = (1,1), c2 = (5,5).
Assign: A, B, C are closer to c1 (distances 0, 1, 1). D, E, F to c2.
Iteration 2 gives the same labels: converged.
Inertia = 2.67: sum of squared distances to each point's centroid.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans, MiniBatchKMeans
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.metrics import (silhouette_score, silhouette_samples,
                             calinski_harabasz_score, davies_bouldin_score,
                             adjusted_rand_score)

X, y_true = make_blobs(n_samples=1500, centers=4, cluster_std=1.0, random_state=7)

# ==================================================================
# 1. LLOYD'S ALGORITHM FROM SCRATCH -- the whole thing is two lines in a loop
# ==================================================================
def kmeans(X, k, iters=100, tol=1e-6, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    C = X[rng.choice(len(X), k, replace=False)]        # naive init
    for it in range(iters):
        # --- ASSIGN: every point to its nearest centroid ---------------
        d2  = ((X[:, None, :] - C[None, :, :]) ** 2).sum(-1)   # (n, k)
        lab = d2.argmin(axis=1)
        wcss = d2.min(axis=1).sum()

        # --- UPDATE: every centroid to the mean of its cluster ---------
        newC = np.array([X[lab == j].mean(axis=0) if (lab == j).any() else C[j]
                         for j in range(k)])
        shift = np.linalg.norm(newC - C)
        C = newC
        if shift < tol:                                # centroids stopped moving
            break
    return C, lab, wcss, it + 1

C, lab, wcss, n_it = kmeans(X, 4, seed=3)
print(f"converged in {n_it} iterations, WCSS = {wcss:.1f}")

km = KMeans(n_clusters=4, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit(X)
print("sklearn inertia_ (= WCSS):", round(km.inertia_, 1))
print("agreement with scratch:", round(adjusted_rand_score(lab, km.labels_), 3))

# ==================================================================
# 2. k-means++ INITIALISATION, BY HAND
# ==================================================================
def kmeanspp(X, k, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    C = [X[rng.integers(len(X))]]                      # first centre: uniform
    for _ in range(k - 1):
        D2 = np.min(((X[:, None, :] - np.array(C)[None, :, :]) ** 2).sum(-1), axis=1)
        probs = D2 / D2.sum()                          # proportional to D(x)^2
        C.append(X[rng.choice(len(X), p=probs)])
    return np.array(C)

# Measured: how much better than random seeding?
rand_w = [KMeans(4, init="random",    n_init=1, random_state=s).fit(X).inertia_
          for s in range(30)]
pp_w   = [KMeans(4, init="k-means++", n_init=1, random_state=s).fit(X).inertia_
          for s in range(30)]
print(f"random init : mean {np.mean(rand_w):8.1f}  worst {max(rand_w):8.1f}")
print(f"k-means++   : mean {np.mean(pp_w):8.1f}  worst {max(pp_w):8.1f}")

# ==================================================================
# 3. CHOOSING k -- four criteria at once
# ==================================================================
print(f"{'k':>3} {'WCSS':>10} {'silhouette':>11} {'CH':>9} {'DB':>7}")
for k in range(2, 9):
    m = KMeans(k, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit(X)
    print(f"{k:3d} {m.inertia_:10.1f} {silhouette_score(X, m.labels_):11.4f} "
          f"{calinski_harabasz_score(X, m.labels_):9.1f} "
          f"{davies_bouldin_score(X, m.labels_):7.3f}")
# WCSS never stops falling. Silhouette and CH peak; DB is minimised.

# Elbow located programmatically -- the "knee": maximum distance from the
# straight line joining the first and last point of the curve.
ks = np.arange(1, 11)
w  = np.array([KMeans(k, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit(X).inertia_ for k in ks])
p1, p2 = np.array([ks[0], w[0]]), np.array([ks[-1], w[-1]])
line = p2 - p1
dists = np.abs(np.cross(line, np.column_stack([ks, w]) - p1)) / np.linalg.norm(line)
print("elbow at k =", ks[dists.argmax()])

# ==================================================================
# 4. SCALING -- inside a pipeline, always
# ==================================================================
Xu = X.copy(); Xu[:, 1] *= 60                    # one feature in different units
print("unscaled ARI:", round(adjusted_rand_score(
      y_true, KMeans(4, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(Xu)), 3))
pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KMeans(4, n_init=10, random_state=0))
print("scaled   ARI:", round(adjusted_rand_score(y_true, pipe.fit_predict(Xu)), 3))

# ==================================================================
# 5. PREDICTING, TRANSFORMING, AND THE CENTROIDS AS FEATURES
# ==================================================================
km = KMeans(4, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit(X)
print("centres:\n", km.cluster_centers_.round(2))
print("assign new points:", km.predict([[0, 0], [5, 5]]))
# transform() gives the distance to every centroid -- a useful k-dimensional
# feature for a downstream supervised model ("cluster distance features").
print("distance features shape:", km.transform(X[:3]).round(2))

# ==================================================================
# 6. SCALING TO LARGE n -- MiniBatchKMeans
# ==================================================================
Xbig, _ = make_blobs(n_samples=500000, centers=8, random_state=0)
mb = MiniBatchKMeans(n_clusters=8, batch_size=2048, n_init=5,
                     random_state=0).fit(Xbig)
print("minibatch inertia:", round(mb.inertia_, 1))
# Updates centroids from small random batches. Roughly an order of magnitude
# faster, with slightly worse WCSS. Supports partial_fit for streaming.

# ==================================================================
# 7. SILHOUETTE DIAGNOSTICS -- find the badly-placed points
# ==================================================================
s = silhouette_samples(X, km.labels_)
print("points with negative silhouette:", int((s < 0).sum()))
for j in range(4):
    print(f"cluster {j}: n={np.sum(km.labels_ == j):4d}  mean s={s[km.labels_ == j].mean():.3f}")

q.q: Explain K-Means in three sentences.
q.a:
Pick $k$ centroids, assign every point to its nearest one, then move each
centroid to the mean of the points assigned to it, and repeat until nothing
moves. Each step provably lowers the within-cluster sum of squares, so it
converges. The result is a local optimum that depends on the initial centroids.

q.q: Why the mean, and not the median?
q.a:
Because the objective is squared Euclidean distance, whose minimiser is
the mean. With absolute distance the minimiser is the median — that is
K-Medians, and it is more robust to outliers.

q.q: Does K-Means always converge? To the best answer?
q.a:
It always converges, because both steps weakly decrease a bounded objective and
there are finitely many assignments. It does not converge to the global
optimum — the problem is NP-hard, and different seeds give different local
optima. Mitigate with k-means++ and multiple restarts.

q.q: Weakness of the elbow method?
q.a:
WCSS decreases monotonically and reaches zero at $k=n$, so there is no maximum
or minimum to find — you are visually detecting a change of slope, which is
subjective and often absent on real data. Silhouette or the gap statistic give
an actual optimum.

q.q: What is the silhouette coefficient?
q.a:
$s_i=(b_i-a_i)/\max(a_i,b_i)$, where $a_i$ is the mean distance to points in
its own cluster and $b_i$ the mean distance to the nearest other cluster. It
combines cohesion and separation, ranges over $[-1,1]$, and negative values flag
probable misassignments.

q.q: Why does K-Means fail on the two-moons dataset?
q.a:
Because it assigns points to the nearest centroid, the clusters are Voronoi
cells — always convex. A crescent is not convex and cannot be a Voronoi cell,
so K-Means cuts both moons in half. Use DBSCAN or spectral clustering.

q.q: How does k-means++ work and why is it better?
q.a:
It picks seeds one at a time with probability proportional to the squared
distance to the nearest already-chosen seed, so centres start far apart and in
different clusters. It guarantees an expected WCSS within $O(\log k)$ of
optimal, and empirically both converges faster and finds better optima.

q.q: Relationship to Gaussian mixture models?
q.a:
K-Means is the limiting case of a GMM fitted by EM with hard assignments and
shared spherical covariance $\sigma^2 I$ as $\sigma\to0$. GMMs allow soft
memberships and per-cluster full covariances, which is why they handle
elongated and overlapping clusters that K-Means cannot.

q.q: How do you cluster categorical or mixed data?
q.a:
Not with K-Means — the mean of categories is undefined. Use K-Modes
(categorical), K-Prototypes (mixed), hierarchical clustering with Gower
distance, or embed the categories first.

q.q: How would you evaluate a clustering when you do have labels?
q.a:
Adjusted Rand Index or Normalised Mutual Information — both are invariant to
label permutation, which raw accuracy is not. Without labels, use internal
measures (silhouette, Calinski–Harabasz, Davies–Bouldin) plus stability under
resampling.

77.idea: Agglomerative clustering starts with each point as its own cluster and repeatedly merges the two closest clusters. The merge history is a dendrogram; cutting it at a height gives clusters.
77.intuition: Build a family tree from the bottom up. The height of each join says how far apart the two groups were.
77.formula: Linkage: single = min pairwise distance; complete = max; average = mean.
steps: Compute the distance matrix.
Merge the closest pair under the chosen linkage.
Update distances to the new cluster.
Repeat until one cluster remains.
Cut the dendrogram at a chosen height or number of clusters.
77.example: Points 1, 2, 6, 8: merge {1,2} at height 1, {6,8} at 2. Final merge: single 4, average 5.5, complete 7.
pitfalls: Slow on large data: quadratic memory.
Linkage choice changes the clusters, sometimes dramatically.
77.tip: Read the dendrogram height as the distance at which two groups joined.
77.hook: Linkage: single = min distance, complete = max, average = mean.
77.pit: Slow on large data; linkage choice changes the result.

steps: Smallest distance 1: merge {1,2} at height 1.
Next smallest 2: merge {6,8} at height 2.
Last merge between {1,2} and {6,8}: single = 4 (min), average = 5.5 (mean of 5,7,4,6), complete = 7 (max).
Cutting at height 3 gives two clusters, the same for all linkages.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import (dendrogram, linkage, fcluster,
                                     cophenet, set_link_color_palette)
from scipy.spatial.distance import pdist, squareform
from sklearn.cluster import AgglomerativeClustering
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score, adjusted_rand_score
from sklearn.neighbors import kneighbors_graph

X, y_true = make_blobs(n_samples=500, centers=5, cluster_std=1.0, random_state=11)
Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)

# ==================================================================
# 1. THE SCIPY ROUTE -- gives you the tree, which sklearn hides
# ==================================================================
Z = linkage(Xs, method="ward")     # Z is the (n-1) x 4 merge history:
# columns: [cluster_i, cluster_j, distance_at_merge, size_of_new_cluster]
print("first 3 merges:\n", Z[:3].round(3))
print("last  3 merges:\n", Z[-3:].round(3))

# Cut the tree -- two equivalent ways
labels_k = fcluster(Z, t=5,   criterion="maxclust")  # "give me exactly 5"
labels_d = fcluster(Z, t=25.0, criterion="distance") # "cut at height 25"
print("ARI:", round(adjusted_rand_score(y_true, labels_k), 3))

# ==================================================================
# 2. READING k OFF THE MERGE HEIGHTS -- the biggest jump
# ==================================================================
heights = Z[:, 2]
gaps    = np.diff(heights)                # increase from one merge to the next
idx     = int(np.argmax(gaps[-10:])) + len(gaps) - 10
k_suggested = len(Xs) - idx - 1
print("largest gap suggests k =", k_suggested)

for k in range(2, 9):
    lab = fcluster(Z, k, criterion="maxclust")
    print(f"k={k}  silhouette={silhouette_score(Xs, lab):.4f}")

# ==================================================================
# 3. DRAWING THE DENDROGRAM
# ==================================================================
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4))
dendrogram(Z,
           ax=ax,
           truncate_mode="lastp",   # show only the last p merges
           p=20,                    # ...otherwise 500 leaves is unreadable
           show_leaf_counts=True,   # "(37)" = a collapsed subtree of 37 points
           color_threshold=Z[-4, 2],# colour below this height
           leaf_rotation=90)
ax.axhline(Z[-4, 2], color="red", linestyle="--")
ax.set_ylabel("merge distance")
# plt.savefig("dendrogram.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")

# ==================================================================
# 4. COPHENETIC CORRELATION -- is the tree faithful?
# ==================================================================
D = pdist(Xs)                              # original pairwise distances
for method in ("single", "complete", "average", "ward"):
    c, _ = cophenet(linkage(Xs, method), D)
    print(f"{method:9s} cophenetic corr = {c:.4f}")
# Highest is not automatically "best" -- but a low value means the dendrogram
# is a poor summary of the actual geometry.

# ==================================================================
# 5. THE SKLEARN ROUTE -- fits the pipeline API, no tree returned
# ==================================================================
ac = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=5, linkage="ward").fit(Xs)
print("sklearn ARI:", round(adjusted_rand_score(y_true, ac.labels_), 3))

# Threshold instead of a count: "anything closer than 2.0 is the same thing"
ac2 = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=None, distance_threshold=2.0,
                              linkage="ward").fit(Xs)
print("threshold gave", ac2.n_clusters_, "clusters")

# Non-Euclidean metrics need a non-ward linkage
cos = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=5, metric="cosine",
                              linkage="average").fit(Xs)

# ==================================================================
# 6. CONNECTIVITY CONSTRAINTS -- only merge neighbours
# ==================================================================
# Restricts merges to the kNN graph: much faster, and encodes structure
# (spatial adjacency in images, road networks, time order in a series).
conn = kneighbors_graph(Xs, n_neighbors=10, include_self=False)
ac3 = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=5, connectivity=conn,
                              linkage="ward").fit(Xs)
print("constrained ARI:", round(adjusted_rand_score(y_true, ac3.labels_), 3))

# ==================================================================
# 7. THERE IS NO predict()
# ==================================================================
try:
    ac.predict(Xs[:5])
except AttributeError:
    print("AgglomerativeClustering has no predict -- assign new points by "
          "nearest centroid, or by 1-NN against the labelled training set.")

centroids = np.array([Xs[ac.labels_ == j].mean(axis=0)
                      for j in range(ac.n_clusters_)])
def assign(new):
    return np.argmin(((new[:, None, :] - centroids[None]) ** 2).sum(-1), axis=1)
print("assigned new points:", assign(Xs[:5]))

# ==================================================================
# 8. CLUSTERING FROM A PRECOMPUTED DISTANCE MATRIX
# ==================================================================
# Useful when your objects are not vectors (strings, graphs, users) but you
# can define a distance between them.
Dm = squareform(pdist(Xs[:200], metric="cityblock"))
ac4 = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=4, metric="precomputed",
                              linkage="average").fit(Dm)
print("precomputed labels:", np.bincount(ac4.labels_))

q.q: What is a dendrogram and how do you read it?
q.a:
A tree of the merge history. Leaves are individual points; the height of each
join is the distance at which those two clusters merged. A horizontal cut
produces a clustering, and the number of vertical lines it crosses is the number
of clusters. Tall vertical segments mean well-separated clusters.

q.q: Advantage over K-Means?
q.a:
You do not have to pick $k$ up front — you get every $k$ at once and choose
afterwards. It is deterministic (no seed dependence), it works with any distance
metric or a precomputed distance matrix, and the dendrogram itself is an
interpretable artefact showing structure at all scales.

q.q: Disadvantage?
q.a:
$O(n^2)$ memory and at least $O(n^2\log n)$ time, so it stops at around
$10^4$ points. Merges are greedy and irreversible — a bad early merge can
never be undone. And there is no predict() for new data.

q.q: What is the chaining effect?
q.a:
Single linkage measures cluster distance by the closest pair, so a thin bridge
of a few points joins two otherwise well-separated clusters into one long
straggly chain. It is the flip side of single linkage's ability to find
non-convex shapes.

q.q: Which linkage would you choose and why?
q.a:
Ward by default — compact, balanced clusters, and the objective matches
K-Means. Single if I expect elongated or curved clusters and the data is clean.
Average when I need a non-Euclidean metric such as cosine. Complete when I want
clusters with a bounded diameter.

q.q: Explain Ward's linkage.
q.a:
It merges the pair whose union increases total within-cluster variance least;
the increase equals $\frac{|A||B|}{|A|+|B|}\|\mu_A-\mu_B\|^2$. The size factor
penalises merging two large clusters even if their centres are close, producing
balanced results. It requires Euclidean distance.

q.q: How do you pick the number of clusters from a dendrogram?
q.a:
Look for the largest vertical gap between consecutive merges and cut just below
it — a big jump means the algorithm was forced to join dissimilar groups.
Confirm with silhouette across candidate cuts, and use domain knowledge.

q.q: What is cophenetic correlation?
q.a:
The correlation between the merge height at which two points first join and
their actual pairwise distance. It quantifies how much the tree distorts the
original geometry; a low value warns that the dendrogram is misleading.

q.q: How would you cluster a million points hierarchically?
q.a:
You would not, directly. Options: subsample and cluster the sample; run
MiniBatchKMeans with a few thousand centroids and cluster those
hierarchically; use BIRCH, which builds a compact CF-tree in one pass and then
clusters its summaries; or add a connectivity constraint so only neighbouring
points can ever merge.

78.idea: DBSCAN groups points that sit in dense regions. A core point has at least minPts neighbours within radius eps. Points reachable from cores form clusters; the rest are noise.
78.intuition: Clusters are crowds separated by quiet space. DBSCAN finds crowds of any shape, and labels lonely points as noise rather than forcing them into a group.
78.formula: Core if |neighbourhood within eps| ≥ minPts (including the point itself).
steps: For each point, count neighbours within eps.
Points with enough neighbours are core points.
Connect core points that are within eps of each other: that forms a cluster.
Attach border points (non-core but near a core) to a cluster.
Everything else is noise.
78.example: eps = 1, minPts = 3: a 2 × 2 block of points forms one cluster; the point (1.4, 0) is a border point; (3,3) and (10,10) are noise.
pitfalls: Struggles when clusters have very different densities.
eps is hard to choose; use a k-distance plot.
78.tip: Core, border, noise: say that three-way split.
78.pit: Struggles when clusters have different densities.

steps: Each point counts itself. Core needs at least 3 neighbours.
Points 1 to 4 are core and join one cluster.
Point 7 has 2 neighbours, so it is not core, but it is within 1 of core point 2: border.
Points 5 and 6 have no neighbours: noise.
