import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN, OPTICS, HDBSCAN
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons, make_blobs
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.metrics import adjusted_rand_score, silhouette_score

X, y_true = make_moons(n_samples=1000, noise=0.07, random_state=0)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = np.vstack([X, rng.uniform([-1.5, -1.0], [2.5, 1.6], (60, 2))])  # add noise
y_true = np.r_[y_true, np.full(60, -1)]
Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)          # ALWAYS scale first

# ==================================================================
# 1. CHOOSING eps FROM THE k-DISTANCE PLOT
# ==================================================================
min_samples = 8                                  # ~2*d for d=2, bumped for noise
k = min_samples - 1
dist, _ = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=k).fit(Xs).kneighbors(Xs)
kdist = np.sort(dist[:, -1])                     # distance to the k-th neighbour

# Locate the knee automatically: the point furthest from the chord joining
# the first and last points of the curve.
i  = np.arange(len(kdist))
p1, p2 = np.array([0, kdist[0]]), np.array([len(kdist) - 1, kdist[-1]])
line = p2 - p1
d_perp = np.abs(np.cross(line, np.column_stack([i, kdist]) - p1)) / np.linalg.norm(line)
eps = kdist[d_perp.argmax()]
print("knee suggests eps =", round(eps, 4))

# ==================================================================
# 2. FITTING, AND READING THE OUTPUT
# ==================================================================
db = DBSCAN(eps=eps, min_samples=min_samples).fit(Xs)
labels = db.labels_                              # -1 means NOISE

n_clusters = len(set(labels)) - (1 if -1 in labels else 0)
n_noise    = int((labels == -1).sum())
print(f"{n_clusters} clusters, {n_noise} noise points "
      f"({100*n_noise/len(labels):.1f}%)")

# core_sample_indices_ tells you exactly which points were CORE
core = np.zeros(len(labels), bool)
core[db.core_sample_indices_] = True
border = (~core) & (labels != -1)
print(f"core: {core.sum()}   border: {border.sum()}   noise: {n_noise}")

# Silhouette must EXCLUDE noise -- otherwise it is meaningless
m = labels != -1
print("silhouette (clustered points only):",
      round(silhouette_score(Xs[m], labels[m]), 4))

# ==================================================================
# 3. DBSCAN FROM SCRATCH -- the flood fill, ~25 lines
# ==================================================================
def dbscan(X, eps, min_samples):
    n   = len(X)
    nn  = NearestNeighbors(radius=eps).fit(X)
    nbr = nn.radius_neighbors(X, return_distance=False)
    is_core = np.array([len(v) >= min_samples for v in nbr])

    labels  = np.full(n, -1)                     # -1 = noise / unassigned
    cid     = 0
    visited = np.zeros(n, bool)

    for p in range(n):
        if visited[p] or not is_core[p]:
            continue                             # only core points seed clusters
        # --- flood fill from this core point ---------------------------
        stack = [p]
        visited[p] = True
        labels[p]  = cid
        while stack:
            q = stack.pop()
            for r in nbr[q]:
                if labels[r] == -1:              # noise or unassigned -> absorb
                    labels[r] = cid              # (border points join here)
                if not visited[r] and is_core[r]:
                    visited[r] = True            # only CORE points keep expanding
                    stack.append(r)
        cid += 1
    return labels

mine = dbscan(Xs, eps, min_samples)
print("scratch vs sklearn ARI:", round(adjusted_rand_score(mine, labels), 4))

# ==================================================================
# 4. THE VARYING-DENSITY PROBLEM, AND HDBSCAN
# ==================================================================
Xv, yv = make_blobs(n_samples=[500, 500, 500],
                    centers=[[0, 0], [6, 0], [12, 0]],
                    cluster_std=[0.4, 1.6, 0.4], random_state=0)
Xv = StandardScaler().fit_transform(Xv)

for e in (0.15, 0.30, 0.60):
    l = DBSCAN(eps=e, min_samples=8).fit_predict(Xv)
    print(f"eps={e}: {len(set(l))-(1 if -1 in l else 0)} clusters, "
          f"{100*(l==-1).mean():5.1f}% noise, ARI={adjusted_rand_score(yv, l):.3f}")
# No single eps gets all three: small eps buries the diffuse middle cluster in
# noise, large eps merges the two tight ones.

h = HDBSCAN(min_cluster_size=25).fit(Xv)
print("HDBSCAN ARI:", round(adjusted_rand_score(yv, h.labels_), 3),
      " noise:", f"{100*(h.labels_ == -1).mean():.1f}%")
print("membership probabilities available:", h.probabilities_[:5].round(2))

# OPTICS: computes the whole reachability structure once, then you can extract
# a DBSCAN clustering at ANY eps without refitting.
op = OPTICS(min_samples=8, xi=0.05, min_cluster_size=25).fit(Xv)
print("OPTICS ARI:", round(adjusted_rand_score(yv, op.labels_), 3))

# ==================================================================
# 5. DBSCAN AS AN OUTLIER DETECTOR
# ==================================================================
# The -1 label is a perfectly good unsupervised anomaly flag.
outliers = X[labels == -1]
print("flagged", len(outliers), "anomalies")

# ==================================================================
# 6. PREDICTING FOR NEW POINTS
# ==================================================================
# DBSCAN has no predict(). The standard approximation: a new point joins the
# cluster of any CORE point within eps, else it is noise.
def dbscan_predict(db, X_train, X_new, eps):
    core_pts    = X_train[db.core_sample_indices_]
    core_labels = db.labels_[db.core_sample_indices_]
    out = np.full(len(X_new), -1)
    for i, x in enumerate(X_new):
        d = np.linalg.norm(core_pts - x, axis=1)
        if d.min() <= eps:
            out[i] = core_labels[d.argmin()]
    return out

print("new points ->", dbscan_predict(db, Xs, Xs[:5], eps))

# ==================================================================
# 7. NON-EUCLIDEAN METRICS AND PRECOMPUTED DISTANCES
# ==================================================================
db_cos = DBSCAN(eps=0.2, min_samples=5, metric="cosine").fit(Xs)
# metric="precomputed" accepts an n x n distance matrix -- useful for
# clustering strings, graphs, or trajectories where there are no coordinates.

q.q: How is DBSCAN different from K-Means?
q.a:
K-Means partitions space into convex Voronoi cells around $k$ centroids and
forces every point into one. DBSCAN grows clusters through dense
neighbourhoods, so shapes are arbitrary, the number of clusters is discovered
rather than specified, and points in sparse regions are labelled noise instead
of being assigned.

q.q: Define core, border, and noise points.
q.a:
Core: at least MinPts points within $\epsilon$ (itself included). Border: not
core, but within $\epsilon$ of some core point. Noise: neither — it belongs to
no cluster and gets label $-1$.

q.q: How do you choose $\epsilon$?
q.a:
Plot each point's distance to its $k$th nearest neighbour ($k=$MinPts$-1$),
sorted ascending. The curve is flat for points inside clusters and rises
sharply for noise; take $\epsilon$ at the knee. Do this on scaled data.

q.q: How do you choose MinPts?
q.a:
At least $d+1$, commonly $2d$. Larger values demand denser clusters and produce
more noise, which is what you want on noisy data. It also sets the minimum
cluster size implicitly.

q.q: What is DBSCAN's main weakness?
q.a:
A single global $\epsilon$. If one cluster is dense and another diffuse, no
radius works for both. HDBSCAN solves this by considering all $\epsilon$ and
extracting the most persistent clusters.

q.q: Is DBSCAN deterministic?
q.a:
Almost. Core and noise assignments are order-independent. Border points
reachable from two clusters go to whichever is processed first, so their labels
can vary with row order.

q.q: Can DBSCAN be used for anomaly detection?
q.a:
Yes — the $-1$ label is exactly an unsupervised outlier flag, and unlike
Isolation Forest or LOF it comes free with a clustering. It works well when
anomalies are genuinely in sparse regions.

q.q: Why does DBSCAN struggle in high dimensions?
q.a:
Distances concentrate, so every point's $\epsilon$-neighbourhood contains either
everything or nothing, and the k-distance plot has no knee. Additionally,
spatial indexes stop pruning, so complexity degrades to $O(n^2)$. Reduce
dimension first.

q.q: How would you assign a new point without refitting?
q.a:
DBSCAN has no predict(). The standard approximation is to assign the new
point to the cluster of the nearest core point if it lies within $\epsilon$, and
call it noise otherwise. HDBSCAN provides approximate_predict for this.

q.q: How do you evaluate a DBSCAN clustering?
q.a:
Compute silhouette on the non-noise points only — including the noise label as
a "cluster" makes the score meaningless. Also report the noise fraction:
if 60% of the data is noise, $\epsilon$ is too small regardless of what the
silhouette says.

79.idea: t-SNE turns pairwise distances into neighbour probabilities in high dimensions, then finds a 2D or 3D layout that matches those probabilities. It is for visualisation only.
79.intuition: Keep neighbours neighbours. The Gaussian in high dimensions measures similarity; a heavy-tailed kernel in 2D lets distant points spread apart.
79.formula: p(j|i) ∝ exp(−‖x_i − x_j‖² / 2σ²) ; low-D q_ij ∝ (1 + ‖y_i − y_j‖²)⁻¹
steps: Choose perplexity (effective number of neighbours), typically 5 to 50.
Compute neighbour probabilities in high dimensions.
Initialise a 2D layout randomly.
Gradient-descend the KL divergence between the two sets of probabilities.
Plot the result, colouring by label.
79.example: Points 0, 1, 3 with σ = 1: from point 0, p(1|0) = 0.982 and p(3|0) = 0.018. Almost all probability sits on the near neighbour.
pitfalls: Cluster sizes and gaps between clusters are not meaningful.
Results change with perplexity and random seed; never use t-SNE coordinates as model features.
79.tip: t-SNE is a picture, not a measurement.
79.pit: Cluster sizes and gaps are not meaningful; never use it as features.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.manifold import TSNE
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import adjusted_rand_score
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

digits = load_digits()
X, y = digits.data, digits.target        # 1797 x 64

# ==================================================================
# 1. THE STANDARD PIPELINE: scale -> PCA -> t-SNE
# ==================================================================
Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
Xp = PCA(n_components=30, random_state=0).fit_transform(Xs)  # denoise + speed up
print("variance kept by 30 PCs:",
      round(PCA(30, random_state=0).fit(Xs).explained_variance_ratio_.sum(), 3))

emb = TSNE(
        n_components  = 2,
        perplexity    = 30,      # THE parameter. 5-50. ~ effective #neighbours
        early_exaggeration = 12, # inflate P for the first 250 iters
        learning_rate = "auto",  # = max(n/12/4, 50); do not leave at the old 200
        init          = "pca",   # far more stable than "random" -- use it always
        max_iter      = 1000,    # 250 minimum; 1000 is a safe default
        metric        = "euclidean",
        random_state  = 0,       # reproducibility -- t-SNE is stochastic
        method        = "barnes_hut",   # O(n log n); exact is O(n^2)
    ).fit_transform(Xp)

print("KL divergence at convergence:",
      round(TSNE(perplexity=30, init="pca", random_state=0).fit(Xp).kl_divergence_, 4))

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 6))
sc = plt.scatter(emb[:, 0], emb[:, 1], c=y, cmap="tab10", s=6)
plt.colorbar(sc); plt.title("t-SNE of digits")
# plt.savefig("tsne.png", dpi=150)

# ==================================================================
# 2. THERE IS NO transform()
# ==================================================================
t = TSNE(n_components=2, init="pca", random_state=0)
t.fit(Xp)
try:
    t.transform(Xp[:5])
except AttributeError as e:
    print("no transform:", type(e).__name__)
# The embedding exists ONLY for the fitted points. To place new data you must
# refit everything -- and every coordinate will change. This is why t-SNE
# output must never be used as model features.

# ==================================================================
# 3. THE INSTABILITY, MEASURED
# ==================================================================
runs = [TSNE(2, perplexity=30, init="random", random_state=s,
             max_iter=500).fit_transform(Xp[:500]) for s in range(3)]
# The layouts differ completely, but the CLUSTER STRUCTURE is stable:
for i, e in enumerate(runs):
    lab = KMeans(10, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(e)
    print(f"seed {i}: ARI vs true labels = {adjusted_rand_score(y[:500], lab):.3f}")
# Same ARI, different pictures. Judge t-SNE by what groups together,
# never by where things sit.

# ==================================================================
# 4. SWEEPING PERPLEXITY -- always do this
# ==================================================================
for p in (5, 30, 50, 100):
    e = TSNE(2, perplexity=p, init="pca", random_state=0, max_iter=500).fit_transform(Xp)
    lab = KMeans(10, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(e)
    print(f"perplexity {p:3d}: ARI {adjusted_rand_score(y, lab):.3f}")
# Structure that survives every perplexity is real. Structure that appears at
# only one value is an artefact of that bandwidth.

# ==================================================================
# 5. WHAT NOT TO DO
# ==================================================================
# WRONG -- t-SNE coordinates as features for a classifier:
#   emb = TSNE(2).fit_transform(X_train)
#   clf.fit(emb, y_train)          # cannot ever score X_test
#
# WRONG -- fitting train and test separately and comparing the plots:
#   e1 = TSNE(2).fit_transform(X_train)
#   e2 = TSNE(2).fit_transform(X_test)   # unrelated coordinate systems
#
# WRONG -- measuring the gap between two clusters in the plot.
#
# RIGHT -- t-SNE to LOOK at the data; PCA/UMAP/autoencoder to MODEL it.

# ==================================================================
# 6. UMAP -- the modern alternative (pip install umap-learn)
# ==================================================================
# import umap
# reducer = umap.UMAP(n_neighbors=15,    # analogous to perplexity
#                     min_dist=0.1,      # how tightly points may pack
#                     n_components=2,
#                     random_state=0)
# emb_train = reducer.fit_transform(Xp)
# emb_test  = reducer.transform(Xp_new)   # <-- t-SNE cannot do this
#
# UMAP is faster, keeps more global structure, and supports transform(), so it
# can (carefully) be used as a preprocessing step as well as for plotting.

# ==================================================================
# 7. VALIDATING WHAT YOU SEE
# ==================================================================
# Never trust a cluster you only saw in a t-SNE plot. Confirm it by clustering
# the ORIGINAL features and checking the groups agree.
lab_hi = KMeans(10, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(Xp)     # original space
lab_lo = KMeans(10, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(emb)    # t-SNE space
print("agreement between spaces:", round(adjusted_rand_score(lab_hi, lab_lo), 3))

q.q: How does t-SNE differ from PCA?
q.a:
PCA is a linear projection maximising retained variance; it preserves global
structure, is deterministic, invertible, and has a transform for new
data. t-SNE is a non-linear, stochastic optimisation that preserves local
neighbourhoods only, has no transform, and produces a different picture
every run. PCA is for modelling; t-SNE is for looking.

q.q: What is perplexity?
q.a:
$2^{H(P_i)}$ — a smooth measure of the effective number of neighbours each
point considers. It determines each point's Gaussian bandwidth $\sigma_i$ via
binary search, adaptively: small in dense regions, large in sparse ones.

q.q: Why the Student-t distribution in the low-dimensional space?
q.a:
To fix the crowding problem. High-dimensional space has far more room at
moderate distances than 2-D does, so those points would be crushed together.
The t-distribution's heavy tail means a given similarity corresponds to a larger
map distance, creating the extra space and letting clusters separate.

q.q: Why is KL divergence used, and why does its asymmetry matter?
q.a:
$\mathrm{KL}(P\|Q)=\sum p\log(p/q)$ heavily penalises small $q$ where $p$ is
large — pulling true neighbours apart — but barely penalises large $q$ where
$p$ is small. So t-SNE guards local structure and ignores global structure. That
single fact explains every caveat about reading the plots.

q.q: Can you interpret the distance between two clusters?
q.a:
No. The objective assigns almost no cost to where distant points land. Clusters
that are far apart in the original space may be drawn adjacent and vice versa.
Only "these points are neighbours" is trustworthy.

q.q: Can you interpret cluster sizes?
q.a:
No. The adaptive per-point bandwidth equalises density, so a tight cluster and a
diffuse one are drawn at similar sizes.

q.q: Why can't you use t-SNE for feature engineering?
q.a:
It has no out-of-sample extension — the embedding is defined only for the
fitted points, so test data cannot be projected without refitting, and refitting
changes every coordinate. Use PCA, an autoencoder, or UMAP instead.

q.q: What is early exaggeration?
q.a:
Multiplying all $p_{ij}$ by a factor (12 by default) for the first few hundred
iterations. It makes clusters form tightly with wide gaps between them early on,
which helps the non-convex optimisation avoid poor local minima.

q.q: Why run PCA before t-SNE?
q.a:
It removes noise dimensions so that Euclidean distances are more meaningful,
and it reduces the cost of the neighbour computation by an order of magnitude.
30–50 components is standard.

q.q: When would you use UMAP instead?
q.a:
When you need speed on large datasets, want more of the global structure
preserved, or need a transform for new points. UMAP is generally the
better default now; t-SNE remains the better-understood reference, and their
local structure usually agrees.

80.idea: When one class is rare, a model can score high accuracy by ignoring it. Remedies: class weights, undersampling, oversampling, SMOTE, and evaluating with precision, recall and PR-AUC.
80.intuition: A test that is always negative is 95% accurate on a disease with 5% prevalence and finds nothing. Rebalance the learning, not just the score.
80.formula: Balanced weight = n / (k · n_class); SMOTE point = x_i + λ (x_nn − x_i)
steps: Measure the class ratio.
Pick the evaluation metric first (precision, recall, PR-AUC).
Try class weights before resampling.
If needed, resample only the training folds.
Compare with a baseline that always predicts the majority class.
80.example: 1000 emails, 50 spam: weights 10 for spam, 0.526 for legitimate. SMOTE between (2,4) and (4,8) with λ = 0.4 gives (2.8, 5.6).
pitfalls: Accuracy is misleading.
Resampling before the train/test split leaks information.
80.tip: Class weights first, resampling second, and always inside cross-validation.
80.pit: Accuracy is misleading; judge by precision, recall and PR-AUC.
80.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import (train_test_split, StratifiedKFold,
                                     cross_val_score, GridSearchCV)
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.metrics import (classification_report, confusion_matrix,
                             precision_recall_curve, average_precision_score,
                             roc_auc_score, f1_score, make_scorer, fbeta_score)
from imblearn.over_sampling import (SMOTE, RandomOverSampler, ADASYN,
                                    BorderlineSMOTE, SMOTENC)
from imblearn.under_sampling import RandomUnderSampler, TomekLinks
from imblearn.combine import SMOTETomek, SMOTEENN
from imblearn.pipeline import Pipeline          # <-- imblearn's, NOT sklearn's
from imblearn.ensemble import BalancedRandomForestClassifier

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=20000, n_features=25, n_informative=10,
                           weights=[0.98, 0.02], flip_y=0.01, random_state=0)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3,
                                      stratify=y,        # ALWAYS stratify
                                      random_state=0)
print("train positives:", ytr.sum(), "of", len(ytr))

# ==================================================================
# 1. THE CORRECT PIPELINE -- sampler INSIDE, so it never touches validation
# ==================================================================
pipe = Pipeline([
    ("scaler",  StandardScaler()),
    ("sampler", SMOTE(random_state=0, k_neighbors=5)),   # fit only, not predict
    ("clf",     LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000)),
])

cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
ap = cross_val_score(pipe, Xtr, ytr, cv=cv, scoring="average_precision", n_jobs=4)
print("CV average precision:", ap.round(4), "mean", round(ap.mean(), 4))

# THE WRONG WAY -- do not do this:
#   X_res, y_res = SMOTE().fit_resample(X, y)          # leaks into the test set
#   train_test_split(X_res, y_res)                     # score is meaningless
#
# Also wrong: sklearn.pipeline.Pipeline with a sampler -- it would try to
# resample at predict time too. imblearn's Pipeline skips samplers on predict.

# ==================================================================
# 2. THRESHOLD TUNING -- the cheapest and usually biggest win
# ==================================================================
clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, class_weight="balanced")
clf.fit(StandardScaler().fit_transform(Xtr), ytr)
proba = clf.predict_proba(StandardScaler().fit(Xtr).transform(Xte))[:, 1]

prec, rec, thr = precision_recall_curve(yte, proba)
f1 = 2 * prec * rec / (prec + rec + 1e-12)
best = thr[np.nanargmax(f1[:-1])]
print(f"default 0.5 -> F1 {f1_score(yte, (proba >= 0.5).astype(int)):.4f}")
print(f"tuned {best:.3f} -> F1 {f1_score(yte, (proba >= best).astype(int)):.4f}")

# If you know the costs, optimise EXPECTED COST instead of F1 -- this is the
# only truly principled threshold.
COST_FN, COST_FP = 500.0, 10.0        # e.g. rupees per missed fraud / false alarm
costs = [((yte == 1) & (proba < t)).sum() * COST_FN +
         ((yte == 0) & (proba >= t)).sum() * COST_FP
         for t in np.linspace(0.01, 0.99, 99)]
t_star = np.linspace(0.01, 0.99, 99)[int(np.argmin(costs))]
print(f"cost-optimal threshold {t_star:.2f}, cost {min(costs):,.0f}")

# ==================================================================
# 3. CLASS WEIGHTS -- one parameter, no data distortion
# ==================================================================
for cw in (None, "balanced", {0: 1, 1: 30}):
    m = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, class_weight=cw)
    s = cross_val_score(m, StandardScaler().fit_transform(Xtr), ytr,
                        cv=cv, scoring="average_precision").mean()
    print(f"class_weight={str(cw):14s} AP={s:.4f}")

# "balanced" sets w_k = n / (n_classes * n_k) -- inversely proportional to
# frequency. Tree ensembles have it too; XGBoost uses scale_pos_weight.

# ==================================================================
# 4. COMPARING SAMPLERS PROPERLY
# ==================================================================
samplers = {
    "none":              None,
    "RandomOverSampler": RandomOverSampler(random_state=0),
    "SMOTE":             SMOTE(random_state=0),
    "BorderlineSMOTE":   BorderlineSMOTE(random_state=0),
    "ADASYN":            ADASYN(random_state=0),
    "RandomUnder":       RandomUnderSampler(random_state=0),
    "SMOTETomek":        SMOTETomek(random_state=0),
}
for name, s in samplers.items():
    steps = [("sc", StandardScaler())]
    if s is not None:
        steps.append(("samp", s))
    steps.append(("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000)))
    score = cross_val_score(Pipeline(steps), Xtr, ytr, cv=cv,
                            scoring="average_precision", n_jobs=4).mean()
    print(f"{name:18s} AP={score:.4f}")

# sampling_strategy controls HOW balanced -- full 1:1 is rarely optimal.
partial = SMOTE(sampling_strategy=0.3, random_state=0)   # minority -> 30% of majority

# ==================================================================
# 5. CATEGORICAL FEATURES -- plain SMOTE is WRONG
# ==================================================================
# SMOTE interpolates: the average of "Delhi" and "Mumbai" is meaningless.
# SMOTENC handles mixed data; SMOTEN handles all-categorical.
#   sm = SMOTENC(categorical_features=[3, 7, 11], random_state=0)

# ==================================================================
# 6. ENSEMBLES BUILT FOR IMBALANCE
# ==================================================================
brf = BalancedRandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=0,
                                     sampling_strategy="all",
                                     replacement=True, n_jobs=4).fit(Xtr, ytr)
print("BalancedRF AP:", round(average_precision_score(
      yte, brf.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]), 4))
# Each tree is grown on a balanced bootstrap -- no data is permanently lost,
# because different trees see different majority subsets.

# XGBoost's built-in handling:
#   scale_pos_weight = (y == 0).sum() / (y == 1).sum()

# ==================================================================
# 7. TUNING WITH THE RIGHT SCORER
# ==================================================================
f2 = make_scorer(fbeta_score, beta=2)      # beta > 1 weights RECALL higher
gs = GridSearchCV(
        Pipeline([("sc", StandardScaler()),
                  ("samp", SMOTE(random_state=0)),
                  ("clf", RandomForestClassifier(random_state=0, n_jobs=4))]),
        {"samp__sampling_strategy": [0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 1.0],
         "samp__k_neighbors":       [3, 5],
         "clf__n_estimators":       [200],
         "clf__max_depth":          [None, 12]},
        cv=cv, scoring="average_precision", n_jobs=4).fit(Xtr, ytr)
print("best:", gs.best_params_, round(gs.best_score_, 4))

# ==================================================================
# 8. EXTREME IMBALANCE (<0.1%) -- stop classifying, start detecting
# ==================================================================
from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest
iso = IsolationForest(contamination=0.02, random_state=0).fit(Xtr[ytr == 0])
scores = -iso.score_samples(Xte)          # higher = more anomalous
print("IsolationForest AP:", round(average_precision_score(yte, scores), 4))
# Trained on the majority class ONLY -- it never needs a labelled positive.

q.q: Why is accuracy the wrong metric here?
q.a:
Because predicting the majority class for everything achieves the majority
class's frequency as accuracy — 99% on a 1% positive problem — while
finding nothing. Accuracy is dominated by the $TN$ cell, which is exactly the
cell nobody cares about.

q.q: ROC-AUC or PR-AUC?
q.a:
PR-AUC when positives are rare. FPR $=FP/(FP+TN)$ has an enormous denominator
under imbalance, so thousands of false positives barely move the ROC curve.
Precision $=TP/(TP+FP)$ contains no $TN$ term and reflects the alerts a human
would actually have to triage.

q.q: How does SMOTE work, and when does it fail?
q.a:
It picks a minority point, picks one of its $k$ minority nearest neighbours, and
places a synthetic point randomly along the segment between them. It fails in
high dimensions (the segment crosses majority territory), with categorical
features (interpolation is meaningless — use SMOTENC), when the minority class
is very small (fewer than $k+1$ points), and when minority points are noise
(it amplifies them).

q.q: Where exactly must resampling happen?
q.a:
Inside the pipeline, on the training fold only. Resampling before the split
leaks synthetic points derived from training rows into the test set. Use
imblearn.pipeline.Pipeline, which applies samplers during fit and
skips them during predict.

q.q: Oversampling or undersampling?
q.a:
Oversampling when data is scarce — you cannot afford to discard majority rows.
Undersampling when data is plentiful and training cost matters; it is also much
faster. Combined approaches (SMOTETomek, SMOTEENN) usually beat either alone,
and BalancedRandomForest gets undersampling's speed without permanently
discarding anything.

q.q: What does class_weight="balanced" do?
q.a:
Sets $w_k = \frac{n}{K n_k}$, so each class contributes equally to the total
loss. It is mathematically similar to oversampling by duplication, but it
changes the loss rather than the data — no memory overhead and no synthetic
points.

q.q: Is 0.5 ever the right threshold?
q.a:
Only by coincidence. It is optimal for accuracy on a balanced problem with equal
error costs. Under imbalance or asymmetric costs the optimal threshold is
$\frac{C_{FP}}{C_{FP}+C_{FN}}$ for a calibrated model — often far below 0.5.

q.q: Does resampling change your probability estimates?
q.a:
Yes — it changes the class prior, so predicted probabilities are inflated for
the minority class and no longer calibrated. If probabilities matter downstream,
either correct for the prior shift, or avoid resampling and use class weights
with threshold tuning.

q.q: When would you not treat it as a classification problem at all?
q.a:
When the positive rate is below roughly 0.1%, or when positives are so
heterogeneous that "positive" is not really one class. Then use anomaly
detection — Isolation Forest, One-Class SVM, autoencoder reconstruction error
— which trains on the majority class alone and needs no labelled positives.

q.q:
Your model has 0.99 ROC-AUC but the business says it is useless.
What happened?
q.a:
Almost certainly precision. At the operating threshold the alert list is
dominated by false positives, because a tiny FPR times an enormous negative
count is still a large absolute number. Look at the PR curve, compute precision
at the actual alert volume the team can handle (precision@k), and tune the
threshold against expected cost rather than F1.

81.idea: Optuna searches hyperparameters by learning from past trials. It proposes new settings where previous trials scored well, and can prune hopeless trials early.
81.intuition: Grid search tries every cell on a map; random search throws darts; Optuna uses earlier throws to aim better.
81.formula: Log-uniform sampling: draw log10(lr) uniformly, so each decade is equally likely.
steps: Define the objective function returning a validation score.
Declare the search space, with log scale for rates and sizes.
Run trials; Optuna samples and records each.
Enable a pruner to stop weak trials early.
Refit the best parameters on all training data.
81.example: Learning rate in [0.001, 0.1]: uniform gives 9% chance of being below 0.01; log-uniform gives 50%.
pitfalls: Tuning on the test set.
Too few trials for a large space.
81.tip: Log scale for learning rates and regularisation; mention pruning.
81.hook: Log-uniform sampling gives each decade equal chance.
81.pit: Tuning on the test set; no pruning wastes compute.

import numpy as np
import optuna
import lightgbm as lgb
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import (train_test_split, cross_val_score,
                                     StratifiedKFold, GridSearchCV,
                                     RandomizedSearchCV)
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

optuna.logging.set_verbosity(optuna.logging.WARNING)

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=8000, n_features=25, n_informative=10,
                           flip_y=0.03, random_state=0)
# Hold out a test set BEFORE tuning. It is touched exactly once, at the end.
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2,
                                      stratify=y, random_state=0)
cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)

# ==================================================================
# 1. THE THREE APPROACHES, SAME BUDGET
# ==================================================================
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
grid = {"n_estimators": [100, 300, 500],
        "max_depth":    [5, 10, None],
        "min_samples_leaf": [1, 5, 10]}          # 27 combinations
gs = GridSearchCV(RandomForestClassifier(random_state=0, n_jobs=2),
                  grid, cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc", n_jobs=4).fit(Xtr, ytr)
print("grid  :", round(gs.best_score_, 4), gs.best_params_)

from scipy.stats import randint, uniform
rs = RandomizedSearchCV(RandomForestClassifier(random_state=0, n_jobs=2),
                        {"n_estimators": randint(100, 600),
                         "max_depth": randint(3, 25),
                         "min_samples_leaf": randint(1, 20),
                         "max_features": uniform(0.2, 0.8)},
                        n_iter=27, cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc",
                        random_state=0, n_jobs=4).fit(Xtr, ytr)
print("random:", round(rs.best_score_, 4), rs.best_params_)

# ==================================================================
# 2. OPTUNA -- the objective is just a function that returns a number
# ==================================================================
def objective(trial):
    params = dict(
        n_estimators      = trial.suggest_int("n_estimators", 100, 1500),
        num_leaves        = trial.suggest_int("num_leaves", 8, 256, log=True),
        learning_rate     = trial.suggest_float("learning_rate", 1e-3, 0.3, log=True),
        min_child_samples = trial.suggest_int("min_child_samples", 5, 100),
        subsample         = trial.suggest_float("subsample", 0.5, 1.0),
        subsample_freq    = 1,            # LightGBM ignores subsample without this
        colsample_bytree  = trial.suggest_float("colsample_bytree", 0.4, 1.0),
        reg_alpha         = trial.suggest_float("reg_alpha",  1e-8, 10.0, log=True),
        reg_lambda        = trial.suggest_float("reg_lambda", 1e-8, 10.0, log=True),
    )
    model = lgb.LGBMClassifier(**params, n_jobs=2, verbose=-1, random_state=0)
    return cross_val_score(model, Xtr, ytr, cv=cv,
                           scoring="roc_auc", n_jobs=2).mean()

study = optuna.create_study(
    direction    = "maximize",
    sampler      = optuna.samplers.TPESampler(seed=42, n_startup_trials=15),
    pruner       = optuna.pruners.MedianPruner(n_startup_trials=5, n_warmup_steps=2),
    study_name   = "lgbm_tuning",
    storage      = None,          # "sqlite:///opt.db" to persist and resume
    load_if_exists = True,
)
study.optimize(objective, n_trials=60, timeout=600, n_jobs=1,
               show_progress_bar=False)
print("optuna:", round(study.best_value, 4))
print("params:", study.best_params)

# ==================================================================
# 3. FINAL, HONEST EVALUATION -- the test set, used once
# ==================================================================
final = lgb.LGBMClassifier(**study.best_params, subsample_freq=1,
                           n_jobs=4, verbose=-1, random_state=0).fit(Xtr, ytr)
print("tuned CV :", round(study.best_value, 4), "  <- optimistically biased")
print("held-out :", round(roc_auc_score(yte, final.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]), 4))
# The gap between these two numbers IS the selection bias from tuning.

# ==================================================================
# 4. CONDITIONAL SEARCH SPACES -- the define-by-run advantage
# ==================================================================
def svm_objective(trial):
    kernel = trial.suggest_categorical("kernel", ["linear", "rbf", "poly"])
    params = {"C": trial.suggest_float("C", 1e-3, 1e3, log=True), "kernel": kernel}
    if kernel in ("rbf", "poly"):                       # only sampled if relevant
        params["gamma"] = trial.suggest_float("gamma", 1e-5, 1e1, log=True)
    if kernel == "poly":
        params["degree"] = trial.suggest_int("degree", 2, 5)
        params["coef0"]  = trial.suggest_float("coef0", 0.0, 2.0)
    pipe = Pipeline([("sc", StandardScaler()), ("svm", SVC(**params))])
    return cross_val_score(pipe, Xtr[:2000], ytr[:2000], cv=3,
                           scoring="roc_auc", n_jobs=2).mean()

svm_study = optuna.create_study(direction="maximize",
                                sampler=optuna.samplers.TPESampler(seed=0))
svm_study.optimize(svm_objective, n_trials=30, show_progress_bar=False)
print("SVM best:", svm_study.best_params)
# GridSearchCV would need a LIST of disjoint dicts to express this.

# ==================================================================
# 5. PRUNING -- report intermediate values, ask whether to stop
# ==================================================================
def pruned_objective(trial):
    lr = trial.suggest_float("learning_rate", 1e-3, 0.3, log=True)
    nl = trial.suggest_int("num_leaves", 8, 200, log=True)
    scores = []
    for step, (tr_i, va_i) in enumerate(cv.split(Xtr, ytr)):
        m = lgb.LGBMClassifier(n_estimators=400, learning_rate=lr, num_leaves=nl,
                               n_jobs=2, verbose=-1, random_state=0)
        m.fit(Xtr[tr_i], ytr[tr_i])
        scores.append(roc_auc_score(ytr[va_i], m.predict_proba(Xtr[va_i])[:, 1]))

        trial.report(float(np.mean(scores)), step)      # tell Optuna how it's going
        if trial.should_prune():                        # ...and let it stop you
            raise optuna.TrialPruned()
    return float(np.mean(scores))

pstudy = optuna.create_study(direction="maximize",
            pruner=optuna.pruners.MedianPruner(n_startup_trials=5, n_warmup_steps=1))
pstudy.optimize(pruned_objective, n_trials=40, show_progress_bar=False)
n_pruned = sum(t.state == optuna.trial.TrialState.PRUNED for t in pstudy.trials)
print(f"{n_pruned} of {len(pstudy.trials)} trials pruned early")

# ==================================================================
# 6. UNDERSTANDING THE STUDY
# ==================================================================
imp = optuna.importance.get_param_importances(study)   # fANOVA
for k, v in imp.items():
    print(f"{k:20s} {v:.4f}")
# Drop the parameters at the bottom and re-run with a tighter range around the
# top ones -- this is how you get the most out of a second tuning pass.

df = study.trials_dataframe()          # every trial as a pandas DataFrame
print(df[["number", "value", "state"]].tail())

# Visualisations (need plotly):
#   optuna.visualization.plot_optimization_history(study)
#   optuna.visualization.plot_param_importances(study)
#   optuna.visualization.plot_slice(study)
#   optuna.visualization.plot_parallel_coordinate(study)
#   optuna.visualization.plot_contour(study, params=["learning_rate", "num_leaves"])

# ==================================================================
# 7. PRACTICALITIES
# ==================================================================
# Persist and resume / parallelise across machines:
#   study = optuna.create_study(storage="sqlite:///study.db",
#                               study_name="run1", load_if_exists=True)
#   ...then launch the same script in several processes; they share the study.
#
# Multi-objective (accuracy AND latency):
#   study = optuna.create_study(directions=["maximize", "minimize"])
#   return auc, inference_ms          # gives a Pareto front via study.best_trials
#
# Warm start from configurations you already trust:
#   study.enqueue_trial({"learning_rate": 0.05, "num_leaves": 31})

# ==================================================================
# 8. NESTED CV -- the unbiased (expensive) estimate
# ==================================================================
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score as cvs
outer = StratifiedKFold(3, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
scores = []
for tr_i, te_i in outer.split(X, y):
    inner_study = optuna.create_study(direction="maximize",
                    sampler=optuna.samplers.TPESampler(seed=0))
    Xi, yi = X[tr_i], y[tr_i]
    inner_study.optimize(lambda t: cvs(
        lgb.LGBMClassifier(
            learning_rate=t.suggest_float("learning_rate", 1e-3, 0.3, log=True),
            num_leaves=t.suggest_int("num_leaves", 8, 128, log=True),
            n_estimators=300, n_jobs=2, verbose=-1, random_state=0),
        Xi, yi, cv=3, scoring="roc_auc", n_jobs=2).mean(),
        n_trials=15, show_progress_bar=False)
    best = lgb.LGBMClassifier(**inner_study.best_params, n_estimators=300,
                              n_jobs=4, verbose=-1, random_state=0).fit(Xi, yi)
    scores.append(roc_auc_score(y[te_i], best.predict_proba(X[te_i])[:, 1]))
print("nested CV:", np.round(scores, 4), "mean", round(np.mean(scores), 4))

q.q: Why is random search usually better than grid search?
q.a:
Because objective functions have low effective dimensionality — only a few
hyperparameters matter. A grid spends its budget uniformly and projects onto few
distinct values per parameter, while random search gives $n$ distinct values of
every parameter for the same $n$ trials. It also scales to any dimension without
the combinatorial explosion.

q.q: How many random trials do you need?
q.a:
$1-(1-p)^n$ is the probability of hitting the top-$p$ fraction. For the top 5%
with 95% confidence, $n=60$ — independent of the number of hyperparameters.

q.q: How does Bayesian optimisation differ from random search?
q.a:
It builds a probabilistic model of the objective from completed trials and uses
it to choose the next point, balancing exploitation (near known good regions)
with exploration (where the model is uncertain). Random search never learns; its
$n$th trial is as uninformed as its first.

q.q: Explain TPE.
q.a:
Split completed trials into a good group and a bad group at a quantile, fit a
kernel density to each — $\ell(x)$ and $g(x)$ — and sample the candidate
maximising $\ell(x)/g(x)$, which is equivalent to Expected Improvement. Unlike a
Gaussian process it models $p(x\midscore)$ rather than
$p(score\mid x)$, so it costs $O(n)$ per suggestion and handles
categorical and conditional parameters naturally.

q.q: What is pruning and what is its risk?
q.a:
Stopping unpromising trials early using intermediate scores (fold-by-fold or
epoch-by-epoch). The risk is bias towards configurations that look good early:
a small learning rate with many iterations is slow to start and may be killed
before it wins. Use enough warmup steps.

q.q: Why sample the learning rate on a log scale?
q.a:
Because it is a scale parameter — 0.001 to 0.01 is as meaningful a change as
0.01 to 0.1. Uniform sampling on $[0.001,0.3]$ would almost never test the small
end. Log-uniform gives equal probability to each order of magnitude.

q.q: Why is the best CV score from tuning biased?
q.a:
Because you selected the maximum over many noisy estimates, so the winner
includes a favourable draw of noise. The more trials, the larger the inflation.
Report a held-out test score or use nested CV instead.

q.q: When is nested CV worth its cost?
q.a:
When the dataset is small (so a single held-out split is high-variance), when
you must publish an unbiased estimate of the whole modelling procedure, or when
comparing two tuning strategies fairly. For large data, one untouched test set
is cheaper and adequate.

q.q: How do you tune when a single fit takes hours?
q.a:
Tune on a stratified subsample or a subset of features first to localise the
good region, use aggressive pruning (Hyperband), reduce the CV folds during
search and validate properly only at the end, warm-start with known-good
configurations via enqueue_trial, and parallelise across machines with a
shared storage backend.

q.q: Which parameters should you actually tune?
q.a:
Check get_param_importances after a first pass. For gradient boosting:
learning rate and number of trees together, then tree complexity
(num_leaves/max_depth, min_child_samples), then
sampling and regularisation. Tuning everything at once with a small budget is
worse than tuning the top three well.

82.t: Model Deployment and the Production Checklist
82.idea: Deployment serves the model behind a stable interface, monitors inputs and predictions for drift, versions data and models, and keeps training and serving preprocessing identical.
82.intuition: A model is a product that decays. The world changes, so the checks are continuous, not one-off.
82.formula: Monitor: input drift (distribution shift), prediction drift, and performance drift when labels arrive.
steps: Package the full pipeline, not just the model weights.
Expose a stable API with input validation.
Log inputs, predictions and latency.
Compare live distributions with training (drift alarms).
Retrain on a schedule or when drift is detected; keep rollback ready.
82.example: A churn model scores daily. Monitoring shows the share of customers over 60 jumped after a pricing change: drift alarm, then retrain.
pitfalls: Training-serving skew: preprocessing differs between training and serving.
No rollback plan when a new model underperforms.
82.tip: Name the three kinds of drift and one alarm for each.
82.hook: Monitor input drift, prediction drift, and metric drift.
82.pit: Training-serving skew: preprocessing differs between training and serving.

# ==================================================================
# 1. TRAIN AND SAVE  -- train.py
# ==================================================================
import json, hashlib, joblib, sklearn, numpy as np, pandas as pd
from pathlib import Path
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, classification_report

df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")
NUM = ["age", "income", "tenure"]
CAT = ["city", "plan"]
X, y = df[NUM + CAT], df["churn"]
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2,
                                      stratify=y, random_state=0)

# EVERY transformation lives inside the pipeline. This is the whole point:
# one artefact, one code path, no possibility of training/serving skew.
pipe = Pipeline([
    ("prep", ColumnTransformer([
        ("num", Pipeline([("imp", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
                          ("sc",  StandardScaler())]), NUM),
        ("cat", Pipeline([("imp", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
                          ("oh",  OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"))]), CAT),
    ], remainder="drop")),                      # unknown columns are ignored
    ("clf", RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=0, n_jobs=-1)),
])
pipe.fit(Xtr, ytr)

proba = pipe.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]
auc   = roc_auc_score(yte, proba)

# Choose the threshold HERE, from validation data -- not 0.5 by default,
# and never re-derived at serving time.
from sklearn.metrics import precision_recall_curve
prec, rec, thr = precision_recall_curve(yte, proba)
f1 = 2 * prec * rec / (prec + rec + 1e-12)
THRESHOLD = float(thr[np.nanargmax(f1[:-1])])

Path("artifacts").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
joblib.dump(pipe, "artifacts/model.joblib", compress=3)

# The metadata file is not optional. Without it you cannot reproduce,
# validate, or safely roll back.
meta = {
    "version":         "1.4.0",
    "trained_at":      pd.Timestamp.utcnow().isoformat(),
    "sklearn_version": sklearn.__version__,
    "numpy_version":   np.__version__,
    "features":        NUM + CAT,               # ORDER MATTERS
    "numeric":         NUM,
    "categorical":     CAT,
    "threshold":       THRESHOLD,
    "test_auc":        float(auc),
    "n_train":         int(len(Xtr)),
    "data_hash":       hashlib.md5(
                          pd.util.hash_pandas_object(Xtr).values).hexdigest(),
    # the reference distribution used later for drift detection
    "reference_stats": {c: {"mean": float(Xtr[c].mean()),
                            "std":  float(Xtr[c].std()),
                            "q":    Xtr[c].quantile(np.linspace(0, 1, 11)).tolist()}
                        for c in NUM},
}
Path("artifacts/metadata.json").write_text(json.dumps(meta, indent=2))
print("saved v", meta["version"], "AUC", round(auc, 4))

# ==================================================================
# 2. SERVE  -- app.py  (FastAPI)
# ==================================================================
"""
import json, joblib, numpy as np, pandas as pd, sklearn, logging, time, uuid
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing import Literal, Optional

app   = FastAPI(title="Churn model", version="1.4.0")
model = joblib.load("artifacts/model.joblib")
META  = json.load(open("artifacts/metadata.json"))

# Fail loudly at startup if the environment does not match the training env.
if sklearn.__version__ != META["sklearn_version"]:
    raise RuntimeError(
        f"sklearn mismatch: trained {META['sklearn_version']}, "
        f"running {sklearn.__version__}")

class Customer(BaseModel):
    # Pydantic IS your schema validation -- types and ranges enforced at the edge.
    age:    int   = Field(..., ge=18, le=120)
    income: float = Field(..., ge=0)
    tenure: int   = Field(..., ge=0, le=600)
    city:   str
    plan:   Literal["basic", "pro", "enterprise"]

class Prediction(BaseModel):
    request_id:      str
    churn_probability: float
    churn:           bool
    threshold:       float
    model_version:   str
    latency_ms:      float

@app.get("/health")                 # liveness probe for the orchestrator
def health():
    return {"status": "ok", "version": META["version"]}

@app.get("/ready")                  # readiness: can it actually predict?
def ready():
    try:
        model.predict_proba(pd.DataFrame([{
            "age": 30, "income": 5e5, "tenure": 12,
            "city": "delhi", "plan": "pro"}]))
        return {"status": "ready"}
    except Exception as e:
        raise HTTPException(503, str(e))

@app.post("/predict", response_model=Prediction)
def predict(c: Customer):
    t0  = time.perf_counter()
    rid = str(uuid.uuid4())
    # Reindex to the EXACT training column order -- never trust dict ordering.
    row = pd.DataFrame([c.model_dump()])[META["features"]]
    p   = float(model.predict_proba(row)[0, 1])
    out = Prediction(request_id=rid, churn_probability=round(p, 6),
                     churn=p >= META["threshold"], threshold=META["threshold"],
                     model_version=META["version"],
                     latency_ms=round((time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000, 2))
    # LOG THE INPUTS TOO -- without them you cannot compute drift or retrain.
    logging.info(json.dumps({"rid": rid, "in": c.model_dump(),
                             "p": p, "v": META["version"]}))
    return out

@app.post("/predict_batch")         # batching amortises per-call overhead
def predict_batch(rows: list[Customer]):
    frame = pd.DataFrame([r.model_dump() for r in rows])[META["features"]]
    return {"probabilities": model.predict_proba(frame)[:, 1].round(6).tolist()}
"""

# 3. CONTAINERISE  -- Dockerfile
# ==================================================================
"""
FROM python:3.11-slim
WORKDIR /app
# Install dependencies first so this layer is cached across code changes
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY artifacts/ artifacts/
COPY app.py .
RUN useradd -m appuser && chown -R appuser /app
USER appuser                        # never run as root
EXPOSE 8000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s CMD curl -f http://localhost:8000/health
CMD ["uvicorn", "app:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000", "--workers", "2"]
"""
# requirements.txt must PIN exact versions:
#   scikit-learn==1.9.0
#   numpy==2.1.3
#   pandas==2.2.3
#   fastapi==0.115.0
#   uvicorn[standard]==0.32.0
#   joblib==1.4.2

# ==================================================================
# 4. MONITOR  -- monitor.py
# ==================================================================
from scipy.stats import ks_2samp

def psi(reference, current, bins=10):
    """Population Stability Index. <0.1 stable, 0.1-0.25 watch, >0.25 retrain."""
    q = np.quantile(reference, np.linspace(0, 1, bins + 1))
    q[0], q[-1] = -np.inf, np.inf
    e = np.histogram(reference, bins=q)[0] / len(reference) + 1e-6
    a = np.histogram(current,   bins=q)[0] / len(current)   + 1e-6
    return float(((a - e) * np.log(a / e)).sum())

def drift_report(reference_df, current_df, numeric_cols):
    rows = []
    for c in numeric_cols:
        ks = ks_2samp(reference_df[c], current_df[c])
        p  = psi(reference_df[c].values, current_df[c].values)
        rows.append({"feature": c,
                     "ks_stat": round(ks.statistic, 4),
                     "ks_pval": float(ks.pvalue),
                     "psi":     round(p, 4),
                     "action":  "RETRAIN" if p > 0.25 else
                                "WATCH"   if p > 0.10 else "ok"})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("psi", ascending=False)

# print(drift_report(Xtr, production_batch, NUM))

# Also monitor WITHOUT labels:
#   - the distribution of predicted probabilities (a sudden shift is a red flag)
#   - the fraction of predictions above the threshold (the alert rate)
#   - p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate, and unknown-category counts
#   - null rates per feature   <-- an upstream pipeline break shows up here first

# ==================================================================
# 5. THE RETRAINING LOOP
# ==================================================================
"""
Triggers -- pick explicitly, do not improvise:
  * scheduled      : weekly/monthly, simple and predictable
  * drift-based    : PSI > 0.25 on any important feature
  * performance    : live metric falls below an agreed floor (needs labels)
  * volume-based   : every N new labelled examples

Before promoting the retrained model:
  1. Score the OLD model and the NEW model on the SAME fresh holdout.
  2. Require a real improvement, not noise -- and check subgroup metrics too.
  3. Shadow-deploy, compare live predictions for a period.
  4. Canary 5% of traffic, then ramp.
  5. Keep the previous artefact and a one-command rollback path.

# ==================================================================

def test_pipeline_roundtrip(tmp_path):
    """A reloaded model must give BIT-IDENTICAL predictions."""
    p = tmp_path / "m.joblib"
    joblib.dump(pipe, p)
    reloaded = joblib.load(p)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(pipe.predict_proba(Xte),
                               reloaded.predict_proba(Xte), rtol=0, atol=0)

def test_unseen_category_does_not_crash():
    """handle_unknown='ignore' must actually handle it."""
    row = Xte.iloc[[0]].copy()
    row["city"] = "a_city_never_seen_in_training"
    assert 0.0 <= pipe.predict_proba(row)[0, 1] <= 1.0

def test_column_order_independence():
    """Reordered input columns must not change the prediction."""
    a = pipe.predict_proba(Xte.iloc[[0]])
    b = pipe.predict_proba(Xte.iloc[[0]][list(reversed(Xte.columns))][Xte.columns])
    np.testing.assert_allclose(a, b)

def test_missing_values_handled():
    row = Xte.iloc[[0]].copy(); row["income"] = np.nan
    assert np.isfinite(pipe.predict_proba(row)[0, 1])

def test_latency_budget():
    row = Xte.iloc[[0]]
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(100):
        pipe.predict_proba(row)
    assert (time.perf_counter() - t0) / 100 * 1000 < 50   # ms per call

def test_no_target_leakage_in_features():

q.q: Why save the pipeline instead of the model?
q.a:
Because the scaler, imputer and encoders learned parameters from the training
data and must be applied identically at serving time. Saving only the estimator
forces you to reimplement preprocessing in the serving code, and any divergence
— a refitted scaler, a different category mapping, a reordered column —
produces training/serving skew that no offline test will catch.

q.q: What is training/serving skew and how do you prevent it?
q.a:
Any difference between the transformations applied during training and during
inference. Prevent it structurally: one Pipeline object used in both
paths, features requested by name in a fixed order, and a round-trip test
asserting bit-identical predictions after reload.

q.q: Data drift vs concept drift?
q.a:
Data drift: $P(X)$ changes while $P(Y|X)$ holds — detectable without labels
via KS or PSI. Concept drift: $P(Y|X)$ itself changes, so the learned
relationship is wrong — requires labels and is far more damaging.

q.q: How do you detect drift without labels?
q.a:
Compare each feature's production distribution to the training reference using
KS statistics or PSI, monitor the distribution of predicted probabilities, watch
the alert rate above the threshold, and track null rates and unknown-category
counts — an upstream pipeline break usually shows up in the nulls first.

q.q: How often should you retrain?
q.a:
It depends on how fast the domain moves. Set an explicit trigger rather than a
habit: on a schedule, on PSI exceeding 0.25 for an important feature, on the
live metric falling below an agreed floor, or after $N$ new labelled examples.
Always compare old and new on the same fresh holdout before promoting.

q.q: How would you deploy a model that must respond in under 10ms?
q.a:
Prefer a simpler model (logistic regression, a shallow ensemble, or a compiled
tree), quantise or convert to ONNX, keep the process warm, batch where possible,
cache repeated inputs, and precompute anything that does not depend on the
request. The right-hand panel of the trade-off figure is the decision you are
actually making — and the most accurate model often loses.

q.q: What do you monitor in production?
q.a:
Model: prediction distribution, feature drift, live metrics once labels arrive,
subgroup performance. System: p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput, error rate,
memory. Data: null rates, unknown categories, schema violations, volume.

q.q: How do you roll out a new model version safely?
q.a:
Shadow first — run it on live traffic without acting on the output and compare
against the incumbent. Then canary 1–5% of traffic while watching the metrics,
then ramp. Keep the previous artefact and a rehearsed one-command rollback.

q.q: Batch or online serving?
q.a:
Batch whenever latency permits: it is simpler, cheaper, easier to monitor, and
easier to reprocess when something goes wrong. Online only when a prediction is
genuinely needed per request within an interactive budget.

q.q: What are the security concerns?
q.a:
joblib/pickle execute arbitrary code on load, so never load an
artefact from an untrusted source. Validate and bound all inputs. Rate-limit the
endpoint — an open prediction API can be probed to extract the model or infer
training data. Do not return raw internal scores or error traces to callers. Run
containers as a non-root user with pinned dependencies.

q.q: Your model's offline AUC improved but revenue did not. Why?
q.a:
Offline metrics are a proxy. Possibilities: the improvement is inside a region of
the score distribution nobody acts on; the threshold was not re-tuned; the
business metric depends on precision at a fixed alert volume rather than
ranking; there is feedback — the model changes the very behaviour it predicts;
or the offline evaluation leaked. Measure the business metric with a proper A/B
test, not offline.
